flashcards.back: A system in which model calls and tools are orchestrated along code paths the developer fixed in advance, so the sequence of steps is predictable and the model fills in content rather than choosing the route.
flashcards.detail: Pick it when the steps are known ahead of time and you want predictability, lower latency and easier testing. The contrast is an agent, where the model chooses the path.

flashcards.back: A system in which the model itself decides, turn by turn, which tools to call and when the task is finished, steering its own process from the results it sees instead of following a fixed script.
flashcards.detail: Reach for it when the path cannot be predicted in advance, and accept higher cost, latency and variance. Start with the simplest design that works and add autonomy only when it earns its keep.

flashcards.back: A pattern that splits a task into a fixed sequence of model calls, each consuming the previous output, often with a programmatic check between steps to catch errors early.
flashcards.detail: Example: draft an outline, validate it in code, then write the document from the approved outline. It trades a little latency for accuracy on each smaller step.

flashcards.back: A pattern in which an initial step classifies the incoming request and sends it to the specialised prompt, model or handler best suited to it, keeping each downstream path simple.
flashcards.detail: Example: easy questions go to a small fast model and hard ones to a larger one, or refunds go to one prompt and technical faults to another.

flashcards.back: A pattern that runs model calls at the same time, either on independent slices of one job (sectioning) or on the same job several times so the answers can be compared (voting), and then merges the results in code.
flashcards.detail: Use it for speed or confidence. The slices must be independent and known in advance, which is what separates it from orchestrator-workers.

flashcards.back: A pattern where a central model call analyses the task, decides at run time how to split it into subtasks, hands them to worker calls and then synthesises what comes back.
flashcards.detail: Example: a code change touching an unknown number of files. Unlike fixed parallelization, the decomposition is not known in advance, so the orchestrator must create it.

flashcards.back: A pattern with two roles in a loop: one model call produces a draft and another critiques it against clear criteria, and the feedback drives revision until the draft passes or an iteration cap is reached.
flashcards.detail: It pays off only when criteria are explicit and feedback really improves the result. Always cap the number of rounds so the loop cannot run forever.

flashcards.back: A multi-agent structure in which a coordinating agent receives the goal, delegates pieces to specialist agents, and combines their reports into the final answer, so specialists do not negotiate with the user or each other.
flashcards.detail: Every layer adds latency and cost. Justify it with real differences in tools, prompts, permissions or context between the specialists, not by default.

flashcards.back: A separate agent instance, started by a main agent, that works on one focused subtask in its own fresh context window and returns only its final message to the caller.
flashcards.detail: Benefits are context isolation, parallelism, tailored instructions and restricted tools. It does not see the parent conversation, so the task prompt must carry everything it needs.

flashcards.back: Passing every fact a delegated worker needs, such as file paths, error text and decisions already made, inside the task prompt itself, because the worker starts without the delegator's conversation history.
flashcards.detail: Classic failure: the parent assumes the helper "knows" what was discussed. The delegation prompt is the only channel from parent to subagent.

flashcards.back: The cycle in which the model replies with a tool request, the surrounding code runs the tool, the result is appended to the conversation, and the model is called again, repeating until a reply arrives with no tool request.
flashcards.detail: With the raw Messages API you keep looping while stop_reason is tool_use. Any other stop reason leaves the loop and must be handled.

flashcards.back: The runtime code wrapped around the model that runs the loop, executes tools, enforces permissions, manages context and persists state; the model supplies decisions while this layer supplies capability and control.
flashcards.detail: Claude Code is a harness. The Agent SDK exposes the same one as a library, and Managed Agents runs a harness for you on Anthropic infrastructure.

flashcards.back: Guard-rail options on an agent run that stop the loop after a set number of tool-using rounds or once estimated spend reaches a cap, so an open-ended task cannot run forever or overspend.
flashcards.detail: In the Agent SDK these are max_turns and max_budget_usd. Hitting one returns a result with an error subtype, and spend can overshoot by up to one response. The budget also counts subagents.

flashcards.back: A control point where the agent pauses before a consequential action, such as a payment or a destructive command, and waits for a person to approve, edit or reject it.
flashcards.detail: Implement it with a permission callback or a manual tool loop. Match the strictness of approval to the severity of the action rather than prompting for everything.

flashcards.back: A store the agent reads and writes outside the context window, such as files in a memory directory, so facts and learnings survive across sessions and context resets.
flashcards.detail: It complements the context window, which is short-lived and size-limited. Examples: the memory tool, Claude Code auto memory, and memory stores in Managed Agents.

flashcards.back: A Python and TypeScript library that embeds the same agent loop, built-in tools, permissions, sessions, hooks and subagents that power Claude Code inside an application you run yourself.
flashcards.detail: Choose it for a ready-made harness in your own process, the Messages API for a fully custom loop, and Managed Agents when Anthropic should host the harness.

flashcards.back: A tool-use cycle you write yourself against the Messages API: send the tools, check stop_reason, run each requested tool, append the results and call again, owning every decision about limits, approval and logging.
flashcards.detail: More code than a ready-made harness, but the right choice when you need human approval steps, custom logging, conditional execution or unusual control flow.

flashcards.back: A beta helper in the client SDKs that runs the tool-use cycle automatically: it calls the model, executes your decorated or typed tool functions, feeds results back, and returns when the model stops asking for tools.
flashcards.detail: It removes loop boilerplate. Use the manual loop instead when you need approval gates, custom logging or conditional execution.

flashcards.back: An Anthropic-hosted agent harness, configured through the API, that runs the loop, tools and a sandbox for you; work happens in persistent sessions that stream events, which suits long-running and asynchronous tasks.
flashcards.detail: It is in beta and the SDK sets the beta header. Because state is stored server-side it is not currently eligible for zero data retention.

flashcards.back: The configuration that says where a managed agent's work runs: an Anthropic-managed cloud sandbox with packages and network settings, or a self-hosted sandbox on infrastructure you operate.
flashcards.detail: One of four core concepts, with the agent (model, prompt, tools), the session and the events exchanged between your app and the agent.

flashcards.back: A running instance of an agent inside an environment, performing one task; messages and tool activity travel as events and history is persisted server-side so work can resume after a pause.
flashcards.detail: You send user events, stream responses over server-sent events, and can steer or interrupt mid-run. You can delete a session when its data should go.

flashcards.back: A Managed Agents option where tool execution, files and network traffic stay on infrastructure you control, served by a worker you run, while orchestration of the loop remains on Anthropic's side.
flashcards.detail: Use it for data that cannot leave your network or internal services that are not publicly routable. Tool inputs and results still reach Anthropic so the model can see them.

flashcards.back: Callbacks or commands the harness runs at fixed points, such as before a tool call, after it returns, when the run stops or when a subagent starts, giving deterministic control outside the model's judgment.
flashcards.detail: They run in your process, not inside the context window, so they cost no tokens. Use them where a rule must hold every time.

flashcards.front: PreToolUse hook (gate before a tool runs)
flashcards.back: A lifecycle hook that fires before a tool executes and can allow the call, modify its input or deny it; a denial reaches the model as a rejection message instead of running the tool.
flashcards.detail: The standard place to block dangerous shell commands or writes to protected files, because it works regardless of what the model decides.

flashcards.back: Guaranteeing a rule by placing it in code the harness runs every time, such as a hook, permission rule, schema validation or sandbox, rather than asking the model in a prompt, which only makes compliance likely.
flashcards.detail: Exam principle: when consequences are severe or compliance must be certain, enforce in code. Prompts and CLAUDE.md are guidance.

flashcards.back: Settings that decide how much human approval an SDK-run agent needs before using tools, ranging from asking for anything not pre-approved, through auto-approving file edits or planning only, to skipping prompts in isolated environments.
flashcards.detail: The modes are default, acceptEdits, plan, dontAsk, auto and bypassPermissions. Reserve bypassPermissions for containers and CI.

flashcards.back: Two agent options: one lists tools that run without asking, the other blocks listed tools whatever other settings say; any tool in neither list falls through to the permission mode.
flashcards.detail: An allow list is a convenience for read-only agents. A deny list is a hard stop. Scoped rules such as Bash(npm *) narrow a tool further.

flashcards.back: The final message of an SDK agent run, carrying the result text only on success, a subtype that says whether the loop finished or hit a limit, and the token usage, cost and session ID.
flashcards.detail: Check the subtype (success, error_max_turns, error_max_budget_usd, error_during_execution) before reading the result field.

flashcards.back: Using the ID from a finished SDK run to restore its full context and carry on, or to branch into a separate copy that explores another approach without changing the original.
flashcards.detail: Capture the ID from the final message. Resuming after hitting a turn limit lets the agent continue instead of starting over.

flashcards.back: Ways for one managed agent to hand work to others within a run: delegating to subagents it can follow up with, writing a program that fans many agents out in the background, or consulting an advisor model for guidance while it does the work itself.
flashcards.detail: Every agent in a run spends tokens, so set a session budget and tell the agent in its system prompt when a fan-out is warranted.

flashcards.back: A way to tell a managed agent what "done" looks like with a rubric; a separate grader, working in its own context window, scores the result against the rubric and returns feedback for another iteration.
flashcards.detail: It is an evaluator-optimizer loop built into the platform. Write gradeable criteria such as "the CSV has a numeric price column", not "the data looks good".

flashcards.back: A low-level orchestration framework and runtime that models an agent as a graph mixing deterministic code steps with model-driven steps, with durable state, streaming and human-in-the-loop interrupts.
flashcards.detail: Pick it for long-running, stateful flows that need explicit control and resumability. It focuses on orchestration, not on model or tool definitions.

flashcards.back: A Python agent framework from the team behind Pydantic that uses type hints and Pydantic models to define typed tools, dependencies and validated structured outputs, and works with many model providers.
flashcards.detail: Strength: type-checked, validated outputs and swappable models. Like other frameworks it still runs the tool-use loop underneath.

flashcards.back: An open-source toolkit, with Python and TypeScript versions, for building production agents with tools, multi-agent coordination, observability and deployment guides for AWS services.
flashcards.detail: Named in the exam guide with LangGraph and PydanticAI as examples of agentic abstraction frameworks. Know what a framework buys you, not each API.

flashcards.back: The choice between an agentic framework, which supplies loop, state, tracing and orchestration but adds abstraction and a dependency, and calling the Messages API directly, which gives full control and visibility for more code.
flashcards.detail: Start simple. Abstractions can hide prompts and responses and make debugging harder. The underlying contract is still tool_use and tool_result.

flashcards.back: Several independent tool requests returned by the model in a single reply, which the harness may run together and must answer, every one of them, in one follow-up user message.
flashcards.detail: A missing result for any tool_use ID is a 400 error. Read-only tools are safe to run concurrently; state-changing tools are usually run one after another.

flashcards.back: A system message the Agent SDK emits when it automatically summarises older history to free context space, a signal that early instructions may no longer be present word for word.
flashcards.detail: Put persistent rules in CLAUDE.md, which is re-injected on every request, rather than only in the first prompt of a long run.

flashcards.back: The core Claude endpoint, POST /v1/messages, which takes a model, an output cap and a list of role-tagged turns and returns one assistant turn made of content blocks.
flashcards.detail: Required request fields are model, max_tokens and messages. The SDKs wrap it, and the API is versioned with the anthropic-version header.

flashcards.back: A property of the Messages API: the server remembers nothing between requests, so the application resends the entire prior exchange, including earlier assistant turns, with every new call.
flashcards.detail: State lives in your app. You store, trim or summarise history yourself, and you may insert synthetic assistant turns when that helps.

flashcards.back: A request field kept apart from the messages list that holds standing instructions such as role, rules and output format, applying to the whole exchange rather than to one turn.
flashcards.detail: There is no "system" role among the first messages. Later system-role messages can be added mid-conversation on current models without invalidating a cached prefix.

flashcards.back: The typed pieces that make up a message body, such as text, image, document, tool_use, tool_result and thinking, so a single turn can mix several kinds of content.
flashcards.detail: A response's content is always an array. Loop over it and branch on each block's type instead of assuming the first block is text.

flashcards.back: A required request field that caps how many tokens the model may generate in a reply; if generation reaches the cap, the reply is cut off wherever it stands.
flashcards.detail: It is a ceiling, not a target, and does not count toward output-token rate limits. Thinking tokens count toward it, so leave headroom when thinking is on.

flashcards.back: A field on every successful response that says why generation ended, which decides whether you use the text, run a tool, continue, retry or handle a refusal.
flashcards.detail: Always branch on it. Treating every response as a finished answer is the classic bug, because truncation and tool requests look like normal replies.

flashcards.back: The value meaning the model completed its answer on its own, so the content is whole and ready to use, in contrast to a cutoff or a request to run a tool.
flashcards.detail: It is the normal outcome. An empty reply with this value often follows text added right after a tool result, which teaches the model its turn is over.

flashcards.back: The reply was cut off because it reached the output cap you set, so it may be incomplete, including half-written JSON or an unfinished tool call.
flashcards.detail: Raise the cap or ask the model to continue. Structured output that stopped for this reason may not match the schema.

flashcards.back: The model is asking your application to run one or more tools; execute them and send back matching result blocks in a new user message so it can continue.
flashcards.detail: Every tool_use block needs a tool_result with the same ID, placed first in that user message. Loop while this value is returned.

flashcards.back: A server-side tool loop, such as web search, hit its iteration limit before finishing; send the assistant content back unchanged in a new request so the model can pick up where it stopped.
flashcards.detail: It never appears when a client tool is waiting on you; that case is tool_use. Handle it in any loop that uses server tools.

flashcards.back: The model declined to produce a response for safety reasons; it arrives as a normal HTTP 200 rather than an error, with a stop_details object naming the category, and output may not match a requested schema.
flashcards.detail: Branch on the stop reason, not on message text. Retrying on another Claude model can often succeed. In a batch, a refusal comes back as a succeeded request.

flashcards.back: Generation ended because the model emitted one of the custom strings you listed in the request; a companion field says which string fired.
flashcards.detail: Useful for cutting output at a delimiter such as a closing tag. The response also reports the matched string in its own stop_sequence field.

flashcards.back: Generation ended because input plus output filled the model's context window before the output cap was reached, so the response is valid but truncated.
flashcards.detail: Distinct from hitting the output cap you set. It lets you request a large output without computing the exact input size first.

flashcards.back: A one-way HTTP streaming format in which the server pushes named events as they happen; the Claude API uses it when streaming is on so text can appear token by token.
flashcards.detail: It is server-to-client only, not a WebSocket. Use streaming to cut perceived latency and to avoid timeouts on long outputs.

flashcards.back: The ordered events of a streamed reply: a message start, then for each content block a start, a run of deltas and a stop, then a message delta carrying the stop reason and cumulative usage, and a message stop.
flashcards.detail: Ping events can appear anywhere and unknown event types may be added later, so handle unfamiliar ones gracefully. Usage in the message delta is cumulative.

flashcards.back: A streaming delta type carrying fragments of a tool call's JSON arguments as partial strings, which must be accumulated and parsed only after the block stops, since the final input is a complete object.
flashcards.detail: Parsing a fragment early throws errors. SDK streaming helpers accumulate and parse for you.

flashcards.back: A failure delivered as an event inside a streamed reply that already returned HTTP 200, such as an overloaded error, so streaming code needs its own handling beyond checking the status code.
flashcards.detail: Keep the partial text you received. The overloaded error here corresponds to the 529 status in non-streaming calls.

flashcards.back: An SDK convenience that consumes the event stream internally and hands back the complete message object, giving streaming's protection against long-request timeouts without per-event handling.
flashcards.detail: In Python it is get_final_message on the stream object. It is the right tool for very large max_tokens when you do not need incremental output.

flashcards.back: Pre-filling the opening words of the model's reply in the final assistant message to steer format; current models from the 4.6 generation reject it with a 400 error.
flashcards.detail: Replace it with structured outputs for guaranteed JSON, or with clear instructions in the system prompt. Old code that relies on it breaks on migration.

flashcards.back: A feature that constrains decoding to a JSON Schema you supply in output_config.format, so the reply text parses and matches the schema, apart from cases such as refusals or truncation.
flashcards.detail: It is GA with no beta header. Limits: no recursive schemas, additionalProperties must be false, numeric and string-length constraints are unsupported, and it cannot be combined with citations.

flashcards.back: A tool-definition flag that applies schema-constrained decoding to the arguments of tool calls, so inputs always have the right field names and types before your code runs.
flashcards.detail: It guarantees shape, not truth: a valid argument can still be a wrong one. Reserve it for tools where a schema violation causes real harm, since there are per-request complexity limits.

flashcards.back: Treating model output as untrusted data: check the stop reason, catch parse failures, validate against the schema and business rules, and keep a retry or fallback path even when constrained decoding makes bad output unlikely.
flashcards.detail: Validation catches what schemas cannot, such as an invalid order number or a plausible but wrong value. Never execute or store output unchecked.

flashcards.back: The part of a response that reports input and output token counts, plus cache creation and cache read counts, for that call; the basis of cost tracking and capacity planning.
flashcards.detail: Log it per request. When caching is on, input_tokens covers only the tokens after the last breakpoint, so add the cache counts to get the total.

flashcards.back: An endpoint that returns the estimated input token count for a prospective request, covering system prompt, tools, images and PDFs, without generating a reply.
flashcards.detail: It is POST /v1/messages/count_tokens. The number is an estimate, and the tokenizer on Claude 4.7 and later produces roughly 30 percent more tokens for the same text, so recount for the model you will use.

flashcards.back: A content block that supplies a picture to the model from a base64 string, a URL or an uploaded file ID, in JPEG, PNG, GIF or WebP format; placing it before the text question tends to work best.
flashcards.detail: Large images are downscaled and cost visual tokens by area. For many images or multi-turn chats, file IDs keep request payloads small.

flashcards.back: A content block for PDFs and plain text that can be supplied as base64, a URL or a file ID; each PDF page is converted to an image and its extracted text is supplied alongside, so charts and tables are understood.
flashcards.detail: Requests are capped at 32 MB and a page limit. Word and Excel files must be converted to text or PDF first.

flashcards.back: Endpoints for uploading a file once and referencing it by ID in later requests instead of resending its bytes; files are stored per workspace, up to 500 MB each, and the operations themselves are free.
flashcards.detail: Content used in a request is billed as input tokens. Files you upload cannot be downloaded back; only files generated by tools or skills can.

flashcards.back: Uploaded files are visible to every key in the workspace rather than to one end user, so a multi-tenant app keeps its own user-to-file mapping, never accepts file IDs from users, and can give each tenant its own workspace.
flashcards.detail: A user-supplied file ID would let one customer read another's upload. The workspace is the isolation boundary.

flashcards.back: An asynchronous endpoint that accepts up to 100,000 requests or 256 MB at half the standard price, processes them independently within 24 hours (most finish within an hour), and returns results you poll for.
flashcards.detail: It suits overnight evals, bulk classification and content generation. It does not support streaming, and results are kept for 29 days after creation.

flashcards.back: A caller-chosen unique string of 1 to 64 letters, digits, hyphens or underscores on each batch request, needed because results can return in any order and are matched back by it.
flashcards.detail: Use meaningful IDs such as a document key, so retries and joins to your own data are trivial.

flashcards.back: The four per-request outcomes in a finished batch: succeeded, errored, canceled and expired; the last three are not billed.
flashcards.detail: Handle each: fix and resubmit invalid-request errors, retry server errors and expired items, and expect a refusal to show up under succeeded.

flashcards.back: The tradeoff between synchronous calls, which answer in seconds for interactive features, and batch jobs, which are cheaper and higher-throughput but promise only completion within a 24-hour window.
flashcards.detail: Choose by who is waiting. A user watching a screen needs realtime; an overnight report or evaluation run is a batch job.

flashcards.back: A marker on a content block, or a top-level field for automatic caching, telling the API to cache the whole prompt prefix up to that point so later requests that reuse it pay a fraction of the input price.
flashcards.detail: The prefix is tools, then system, then messages. Entries last about five minutes by default and refresh on use; a longer lifetime costs more to write.

flashcards.back: Two counts in the usage object, one for tokens written to the cache and one for tokens read from it, that show whether caching works; total input is those plus the tokens after the last breakpoint.
flashcards.detail: The names are cache_creation_input_tokens and cache_read_input_tokens. A read count of zero on repeated requests means the prefix is changing.

flashcards.back: An encrypted field on each thinking content block that must be returned unchanged on later turns, especially in tool-use conversations; edited, reordered or dropped thinking blocks cause a 400 error.
flashcards.detail: If your code filters blocks by type before resending history, keep both thinking and redacted thinking blocks.

flashcards.back: A unique identifier returned in the response header and in error bodies that you log and quote to Anthropic support to trace one specific call.
flashcards.detail: The header is request-id and the field in errors is request_id. SDKs expose it as _request_id on response objects.

flashcards.back: A required request header, currently 2023-06-01, that pins the API contract version; the SDKs send it automatically.
flashcards.detail: Within a version, new fields, values and event types can still appear, so clients should ignore what they do not recognise.

flashcards.back: Using Claude through a cloud provider's endpoint, with that provider's IAM and billing, instead of the direct Claude API; the request shape is similar but features, model IDs, limits and timing differ by platform.
flashcards.detail: Choose it for existing cloud commitments, consolidated billing or compliance needs. Choose the direct API for the newest features first.

flashcards.back: An Anthropic-operated offering inside AWS that is billed through AWS Marketplace and authenticated with AWS credentials, exposing the Claude API with typically same-day feature access.
flashcards.detail: Contrast with Amazon Bedrock, which is operated by the partner. Responses carry both an AWS request ID and the Anthropic request ID.

flashcards.front: Claude on Google Cloud request format
flashcards.back: On Google Cloud's Agent Platform the model is named in the endpoint URL instead of the request body, and the body carries an anthropic_version value of vertex-2023-10-16 rather than a header.
flashcards.detail: Bedrock and Google Cloud also accept only base64 image and document sources, so a URL or file ID source fails there.

flashcards.back: A per-request field on Claude 4.6 and later models whose values are global (the default) and us, controlling where model inference runs for data residency needs.
flashcards.detail: Workspace geography separately controls where data is stored at rest. On Bedrock and Google Cloud the region comes from the endpoint instead.

flashcards.back: Status returned when a request, input-token or output-token ceiling is exceeded; wait for the retry-after value, then retry. A monthly spend-cap variant carries no retry-after and will not clear by retrying.
flashcards.detail: Short bursts can trip it even when the per-minute total looks fine, because limits are enforced with a token bucket.

flashcards.back: Status signalling the API is temporarily overloaded across all users, not that your own limit was hit; retry with exponential backoff, and note that during streaming it can arrive as an error event.
flashcards.detail: Unlike a 429 it is not caused by your usage. Backoff and a fallback path are the right responses; asking for a higher limit is not.

flashcards.back: Status for a malformed or unsupported request, such as a prefilled final turn on a model that rejects it, an unsupported schema keyword, or a spend limit you set yourself; retrying it unchanged fails again.
flashcards.detail: Fix the request. Many validation errors are 400s with a descriptive message, so log the body and the request ID.

flashcards.back: Status returned when the payload exceeds the endpoint maximum, which is 32 MB for Messages, 256 MB for batches and 500 MB for file uploads; shrink the payload or reference uploaded files by ID.
flashcards.detail: Base64 images and PDFs inflate payloads quickly. Partner platforms have lower limits than the direct API.

flashcards.back: A rejected key or token versus a valid key that is not allowed to use the requested resource; neither is transient, so fix the credential or access settings instead of retrying.
flashcards.detail: Rotate or reconfigure the key, check the workspace, and never loop on these. A retry storm on a revoked key only adds noise.

flashcards.back: The split behind error handling: transient failures such as 429, 5xx, 529, timeouts and dropped connections are retried with backoff, while client errors like 400, 401, 403 and 404 need a code or configuration change.
flashcards.detail: A truncated reply (max_tokens) and a refusal are not errors at all; they are successful responses that need their own handling.

flashcards.back: A retry schedule whose waits grow by a multiplier after each failure, with random variation added so many clients do not retry in lockstep and overload the service again.
flashcards.detail: Cap the number of attempts and the maximum wait, and prefer the server's retry-after value when it is present.

flashcards.back: A response header giving the number of seconds to wait before retrying a rate-limited request; earlier retries will fail, and the SDKs honor it automatically.
flashcards.detail: Not every 429 carries it. The monthly spend-cap 429 never does, which is how you tell the two apart.

flashcards.back: Built-in behavior of the official clients: connection errors, timeouts, conflict, rate-limit and server errors are retried twice by default with a short exponential backoff, configurable per client or per request.
flashcards.detail: The setting is max_retries. Layering your own retry loop on top multiplies attempts, so configure one layer deliberately.

flashcards.back: The three per-model ceilings enforced for an organization: requests per minute, input tokens per minute and output tokens per minute, replenished continuously rather than reset on a clock tick.
flashcards.detail: Exceeding any one yields a 429 that names which. Workspaces can have lower limits than the organization.

flashcards.back: The algorithm behind the API's rate limiting: capacity refills steadily up to a maximum, so a burst above the average rate can be rejected even though the minute total looks fine.
flashcards.detail: Smooth traffic with a queue or bounded concurrency rather than firing everything at the top of the minute.

flashcards.back: For most models, tokens read from the prompt cache do not count against the input-tokens-per-minute ceiling; only uncached input and cache writes do, so effective throughput rises with the cache hit rate.
flashcards.detail: This makes caching a throughput tool as well as a cost tool for apps that repeat a long prefix.

flashcards.back: A rate limit error that can appear when an organization's usage rises sharply in a short time; ramping traffic up gradually and keeping usage patterns consistent avoids it.
flashcards.detail: Typical trigger: a launch or a new batch job that goes from zero to full volume in seconds.

flashcards.back: Monthly dollar ceilings on API use: a tier cap plus any lower limit you set. Hitting your own limit returns a 400, while hitting the tier cap returns a 429 with an enforced_spend_limit_reached code until the next month.
flashcards.detail: Retries cannot fix either. Raise the limit or move up a tier, and alert on spend before it is reached.

flashcards.back: Practices for calls that may run many minutes: the SDK default timeout is 10 minutes and it rejects non-streaming calls expected to take longer, so large outputs should stream or go through the batch endpoint.
flashcards.detail: Networks may drop idle connections. Streaming keeps the connection active, and the final-message helper hides the event handling.

flashcards.back: An operation that has the same effect whether performed once or many times, which makes a retry after a timeout safe; tools that charge cards or send email need explicit duplicate protection.
flashcards.detail: Pass an idempotency key to the downstream system so a replayed tool call does not repeat the side effect.

flashcards.back: A resilience pattern that stops calling a failing dependency for a cool-down period after repeated failures, failing fast or using a fallback instead of piling up slow retries.
flashcards.detail: It protects your threads and your rate limit, and gives an overloaded service room to recover.

flashcards.back: A planned alternative when a request is declined by the model's safety classifiers, most often retrying the same request on another Claude model, either server-side where available or in your own client.
flashcards.detail: Refusals are normal 200 responses, so detect them through the stop reason, not through exception handling.

flashcards.back: An HTTP interface organized around resources identified by URLs and manipulated with standard methods and status codes; the Claude API is one, and the SDKs are typed wrappers over it.
flashcards.detail: You can call it with plain HTTP and three headers: the API key, the version and the content type. SDKs add retries, typed errors and streaming helpers.

flashcards.back: A text data format built from objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans and null, used for API request and response bodies and for tool arguments.
flashcards.detail: Parse it strictly, validate shape and ranges after parsing, and never assume model-produced text is valid unless structured outputs guarantee it.

flashcards.back: A concurrency style where waiting on a network call does not block the thread, letting one process overlap many model requests; the Python SDK offers a separate async client for it.
flashcards.detail: Model calls are slow and I/O-bound, so async raises throughput. Combine it with a cap on concurrent requests.

flashcards.back: Capping how many requests are in flight at once, for example with a semaphore or worker pool, so parallel model calls stay inside rate limits and memory.
flashcards.detail: Unbounded fan-out is the usual way a batch script triggers a wall of 429 errors.

flashcards.back: Repeatedly asking a service whether work has finished, as when checking a batch's processing status until it reads ended; simple and robust, but wasteful compared with being called back.
flashcards.detail: Poll at a sensible interval such as a minute for batches, not in a tight loop. Managed Agents can instead notify you with webhooks.

flashcards.back: Recording every change to code, prompts and configuration in a shared history, with work done on branches and merged through reviewed pull requests, so any version can be traced and rolled back.
flashcards.detail: Prompts, schemas, tool definitions and CLAUDE.md files belong in it just like source code.

flashcards.back: Peer inspection of a change before it merges, to catch defects, security issues and design problems; for model-generated changes it is the human checkpoint that passing tests alone do not replace.
flashcards.detail: Review for what tests miss: hidden coupling, security, unneeded complexity and plausible but wrong logic.

flashcards.back: Restructuring existing code without changing its externally visible behavior, in small tested steps, to improve readability, remove duplication or prepare for a new feature.
flashcards.detail: Keep tests green after each step. Do not mix refactoring with feature changes in one commit.

flashcards.back: A large-scale refactoring approach that replaces a legacy system piece by piece behind a stable interface, routing traffic to new components gradually until the old code can be retired.
flashcards.detail: It beats a big-bang rewrite because each step ships, is testable and can be rolled back.

flashcards.back: Automation that builds, tests and deploys every change; for a Claude app it also runs evals when a prompt or model changes, and can run Claude Code non-interactively as a step.
flashcards.detail: Gate merges on eval scores as well as unit tests, and keep the API key in the pipeline's secret store.

flashcards.back: Running Claude Code non-interactively from a script or pipeline by passing a prompt with the print flag, optionally with JSON output and pre-approved tools, exiting non-zero on failure.
flashcards.detail: The command is claude -p. A bare mode skips auto-discovery of hooks, plugins, MCP servers and CLAUDE.md so every machine behaves the same.

flashcards.back: A MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH scheme whose ranges such as ^2.0 or ~2.1.0 let consumers accept compatible updates while blocking breaking ones.
flashcards.detail: Plugin dependencies use these ranges to decide which release is installed.

flashcards.back: A runtime switch that turns a code path, such as a new prompt or model, on for a share of traffic without redeploying, enabling gradual rollout and instant rollback.
flashcards.detail: Pair it with monitoring so a regression is noticed while only a small share of users is affected.

flashcards.back: A statement of what the system must do, such as summarise a support ticket, extract fields from an invoice or call a refund tool.
flashcards.detail: Testable as pass or fail on behavior. Contrast with quality targets such as latency or cost.

flashcards.back: A quality target for how well the system behaves, such as latency, throughput, availability, cost per request, data residency or compliance, which drives model, platform and architecture choices.
flashcards.detail: In Claude apps these decide realtime versus batch, model tier, caching, region and which cloud platform to use.

flashcards.back: The staged lifespan of a software system from requirements and design through build, test, deploy, operate and maintain to retirement; each stage has Claude-specific work such as evals, prompt versions and model migrations.
flashcards.detail: Operations is not the end: models get deprecated, prompts drift and costs change, so maintenance continues for as long as the app runs.

flashcards.back: The states a model passes through: active, legacy, deprecated with a replacement and retirement date, and retired, after which requests fail; Anthropic gives at least 60 days' notice for publicly released models.
flashcards.detail: Audit which models you call (the Console usage export breaks it down by key and model) and test replacements well before the date.

flashcards.back: Returning production to the last known-good prompt, configuration or model version after a bad release; it works only when those artifacts are versioned and pinned.
flashcards.detail: If the model is an alias that moved, there is nothing to roll back to. Pinning is what makes rollback possible.

flashcards.back: Claude's behavior depends on what wraps it: claude.ai and the mobile apps add an Anthropic-written system prompt, the raw API sends only what you supply, and Claude Code adds its own instructions plus your CLAUDE.md files.
flashcards.detail: The consumer apps' prompt updates do not apply to the API. A prompt that works in a chat window must be rebuilt, including date and formatting rules, when moved into your app.

flashcards.back: A clear separation between your trusted instructions and untrusted material such as documents, web pages or tool output, using structure like tags, distinct blocks and tool results so the model treats the latter as data.
flashcards.detail: It lowers the chance that text inside a document is read as a command. It is a design aid, not a guarantee, so pair it with least-privilege tools and hooks.

flashcards.back: Shaping the JSON Schema behind tool inputs and structured outputs: descriptive names and field descriptions, required fields, closed sets as enums, shallow structure and no extra properties.
flashcards.detail: A clear schema is also documentation for the model. Fewer optional fields means less ambiguity and a simpler compiled grammar.

flashcards.back: A schema keyword limiting a field to a fixed list of allowed values, which narrows what the model can emit and makes downstream branching safe.
flashcards.detail: Structured outputs do not guarantee capitalization of enum values, so compare case-insensitively and avoid values that differ only by case.

flashcards.back: Habits that keep an interactive coding session's context useful: clearing between unrelated tasks, restarting with a sharper prompt after repeated corrections, compacting with instructions, and delegating research to subagents.
flashcards.detail: A long session full of failed attempts performs worse than a fresh one with a better prompt. Name and resume sessions that span several sittings.

flashcards.back: A directory of skills, subagents, hooks and MCP servers installed together as one versioned unit from a marketplace, described by a manifest file named plugin.json.
flashcards.detail: Use one when several components should ship together. A single skill or hook works fine standalone.

flashcards.back: Where an installed plugin is enabled: for you in every project, for everyone in a repository through committed settings, or for you in one repository only.
flashcards.detail: The three scopes are user, project and local. A project-scope plugin still has to be installed on each teammate's machine.

flashcards.back: A semantic-version range declared in a plugin's manifest for each plugin it relies on; without one the dependency floats to every new release, which can silently break the dependent plugin.
flashcards.detail: Constrain with a range you have tested, such as ~2.1.0, and widen it deliberately after testing a newer release.

flashcards.back: Every enabled plugin adds the names and descriptions of its skills and agents to context on every turn, so unused plugins cost tokens and attention even when nothing from them runs.
flashcards.detail: Check the footprint before installing, and disable plugins that are not used recently. A plugin also runs code with your privileges, so review it.

flashcards.back: The layered locations of persistent project instructions: organization-managed, user-level, project-level shared through source control, and a personal local file; all found files are concatenated into context rather than overriding each other.
flashcards.detail: Files in directories above the working directory load at launch, subdirectory files load on demand, and a target of under 200 lines per file keeps adherence high.

flashcards.back: The ordering for Claude Code settings: managed settings win, then the command line, then project-local, then shared project, then user settings; list-type keys such as permission allow rules merge across scopes.
flashcards.detail: Shared team policy goes in the committed project file, personal overrides in the local file, and non-negotiable rules in managed settings.

flashcards.back: Specifying an exact model ID, or fixing the variable that an alias resolves through, so behavior does not change when an alias moves to a newer release.
flashcards.detail: Aliases such as sonnet or opus follow the newest version. Production should pin, run evals, and then migrate on purpose.

flashcards.back: Giving every revision of a prompt an identifier, a changelog entry and linked eval results, and recording which revision produced each response, so a regression can be traced to one edit and rolled back.
flashcards.detail: Store the prompt version with each logged response. Changing a prompt is a release, not a quick edit in a dashboard.

flashcards.front: Data access patterns for Claude calls
flashcards.back: The three ways an application puts data in front of the model: inline in the request for small or one-off content, by reference through an uploaded file ID for content reused across calls, and on demand through a tool the model calls to fetch just what it needs.
flashcards.detail: Inline suits a short input, file IDs suit a document reused across turns, and a lookup tool suits a large or fast-changing database that would not fit in a prompt or would go stale.

flashcards.back: A way of building software in short cycles that each end with a working increment and feedback, instead of one long sequential plan; it suits Claude applications because prompt and model behavior must be measured and adjusted repeatedly.
flashcards.detail: Contrast with a strictly sequential, plan-everything-first approach. Each cycle should end with evals, not just a demo.

flashcards.back: The places Claude Code runs: the terminal, IDE extensions, the desktop app and the browser. The local ones read the same settings files on one machine, but a cloud session does not load the plugins in your local settings.
flashcards.detail: A plugin installed at user scope in the terminal also appears in the desktop app's local sessions and the VS Code extension on that computer, but not in a cloud session.

flashcards.back: The small chunk of text, often a word fragment, that a model reads and writes; context limits, prices and rate limits are all measured in this unit, and the count for identical text depends on the model generation's text-splitting scheme.
flashcards.detail: Budgets, max_tokens and cost estimates all use it. On older models one unit is about 3.5 English characters; Claude 4.7 and later models produce roughly 30 percent more units for the same text.

flashcards.back: The maximum material a model can hold in view for one request: the system prompt, every message, tool definitions and results, images and documents, plus the reply it generates, thinking included. It works like working memory, and filling it is not automatically better.
flashcards.detail: All current Claude models offer 1M tokens (Haiku 5.5 charges more above 100,000). Accuracy and recall can degrade as the window fills, so curate what goes in.

flashcards.back: How a language model writes text: given everything so far it scores every possible continuation, selects one small piece, appends it and repeats, so a reply is built one unit at a time and each earlier choice shapes the later ones.
flashcards.detail: This is why long replies take longer and cost more, why a reply can be cut off mid-sentence, and why early wording choices can steer everything after them.

flashcards.back: Request settings that control how randomly the next piece of text is picked from the model's probability scores: one reshapes the distribution, another keeps only the most probable options up to a cumulative share, a third keeps a fixed number of top options. The newest Claude models reject any non-default value with a 400 error.
flashcards.detail: On Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5 and Fable 5.1 do not send them; steer behavior with prompts, examples, effort and structured outputs. Old advice to set temperature to 0 no longer applies.

flashcards.back: The property that identical requests can return different replies from one call to the next; reducing randomness settings does not make output fully repeatable, so tests and pipelines must tolerate variation instead of expecting byte-identical text.
flashcards.detail: Grade with rubrics, thresholds or schema checks rather than string equality, and validate outputs in code. Anthropic notes that even temperature 0 is not fully deterministic.

flashcards.back: Asking the model to perform a task from instructions alone, with no worked examples included in the prompt.
flashcards.detail: Often enough for clear tasks on current models. Add examples when the output format or edge-case handling keeps going wrong.

flashcards.back: Including exactly one demonstration of an input and its desired output in the prompt, to show the expected format or style before the real input is given.
flashcards.detail: One example can fix format, but the model may copy its quirks. If answers come in several shapes, vary the examples.

flashcards.back: Supplying several varied, relevant demonstrations, typically three to five, of an input and its ideal output, each wrapped in its own tags, so the model infers the pattern, format and edge-case handling.
flashcards.detail: One of the most reliable ways to steer format, tone and structure. The examples must be diverse, otherwise the model picks up accidental patterns.

flashcards.back: A mode in which the model itself decides whether and for how long to reason before answering, based on how hard the request is and on the effort setting. On the newest Opus and Fable models it is always on and cannot be turned off.
flashcards.detail: It replaced manual budgets. Control depth with effort; thinking is billed as output. Sending thinking type disabled returns 400 on Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1.

flashcards.back: The older way to enable reasoning, where a request sets thinking type enabled with a fixed budget_tokens allowance. It is deprecated on the 4.6 generation and rejected with a 400 error on current models, which use the adaptive approach instead.
flashcards.detail: Migration trap: code that sends budget_tokens fails after a model upgrade. Remove it, choose an effort level, and use max_tokens as the hard ceiling.

flashcards.back: A request setting with five levels from low to max that scales how much work the model puts into the whole reply, including its reasoning, the number and verbosity of tool calls and the answer text. It is a behavioral signal, not a hard token limit.
flashcards.detail: Default is high on most models and medium on Opus 5.5 and Haiku 5.5. Tuning it is often a better lever than switching models; changing it mid-conversation invalidates the prompt cache.

flashcards.back: The rule that reasoning produced before the answer is billed as output, counts against the response ceiling and takes up context space, even when the reasoning text is hidden from the application.
flashcards.detail: Leave room in max_tokens at higher effort levels. A stop_reason of max_tokens with a short visible answer usually means thinking used up the budget.

flashcards.back: A research-preview option on some Opus models that serves the same model weights with a faster inference setup, giving up to about 2.5 times the output speed at premium pricing; it speeds up generation, not the wait before the first output appears.
flashcards.detail: Set speed to fast with the beta header. It is not available with the Batch API or on partner clouds, and switching speeds invalidates the prompt cache.

flashcards.back: The delay between sending a request and receiving the first piece of generated output; the measure that makes streaming interfaces feel responsive, driven by prompt length, model choice and any up-front reasoning.
flashcards.detail: Long prompts raise it; shorter prompts and prompt caching lower it; fast mode does not. Total time is roughly this delay plus output length divided by generation speed.

flashcards.back: Anthropic's lowest-latency, lowest-price model tier, aimed at high-volume work such as classification, extraction, routing and sub-agent tasks where speed and cost dominate but reasoning quality still matters.
flashcards.detail: The natural starting point for efficiency-first selection. Haiku 5.5 defaults to medium effort; confirm on your own evals before trusting it with harder steps.

flashcards.back: The balanced model tier: fast and capable enough for everyday coding, data analysis, content creation and agentic tool use, priced well below the top tiers, and a common default for production workloads.
flashcards.detail: Pick it when the small tier falls short but the highest capability is not needed. Sonnet 5.5 defaults to high effort.

flashcards.back: The tier built for complex, long-running agentic coding and knowledge work, and the documentation's suggested starting point for most workloads; moderate latency, with higher capability and cost than the balanced tier.
flashcards.detail: Opus 5.5 always uses adaptive thinking and defaults to medium effort; fast mode is offered on some Opus models.

flashcards.back: The highest-capability tier open to all customers, meant for demanding reasoning and long-horizon agentic work such as multi-hour agent sessions and deep research; it is slower and the most expensive, and it is a Covered Model that requires 30-day data retention.
flashcards.detail: Move up to it when evals on Opus at xhigh or max effort still fall short. A sibling model with the same capabilities is limited to verified organizations.

flashcards.back: Starting with the smallest, cheapest tier that might work, testing it thoroughly on your own tasks, and moving up a tier only for the capability gaps those tests expose.
flashcards.detail: Best for prototypes, tight latency and high-volume straightforward work. The opposite approach is capability-first.

flashcards.back: Starting with a strong model so the task is solved at all, tuning prompts for it, then trading down in effort or tier for as long as the evals still pass.
flashcards.detail: Best for complex reasoning, high-stakes accuracy and long-horizon agents: the savings come after you know what quality is achievable.

flashcards.back: The comparison measure that divides total spend, including retries, extra turns and verbose output, by the number of tasks actually solved, instead of comparing per-million-token prices.
flashcards.detail: A pricier model can be cheaper if it finishes in fewer turns, and a tokenizer change makes per-token comparisons misleading.

flashcards.back: A multi-model pattern in which a smaller executor model runs the loop and consults a stronger model through an advisor tool only at hard decisions; it helps only when the executor actually asks for advice.
flashcards.detail: Measure the consult rate and compare against simply raising effort. The advisor tool definition itself adds roughly a thousand prompt tokens to every request.

flashcards.back: A difference between model generations that makes unchanged code fail or behave differently, such as removed parameters, new defaults or a different tokenizer, found by reading the migration guide and re-running your evals before switching.
flashcards.detail: Examples: sampling parameters, prefill, manual thinking budgets and forced tool_choice are rejected on newer models, and the default effort changed on Opus 5.5.

flashcards.back: The shift in which Claude 4.7 and later models split the same text into roughly 30 percent more pieces than earlier models, so counts, limits and bills measured on an older model must be re-baselined for the target model.
flashcards.detail: Recount with the token counting endpoint and the new model ID; revisit max_tokens, compaction triggers and any client-side size estimates.

flashcards.back: A listing endpoint that returns each available model's id, maximum input and output sizes and a capabilities object, so code can check support, such as whether thinking may be disabled, instead of hard-coding assumptions.
flashcards.detail: Read capabilities rather than inferring them from a model name. It also reports which line a model belongs to, useful for model pickers.

flashcards.back: The designation for the most capable model families (Fable and Mythos) that require 30-day data retention, which means zero data retention is not available for them unless Anthropic expressly authorizes it.
flashcards.detail: A model-selection constraint for regulated workloads: an organization without the required retention setting can have requests rejected with a 400 error. Check it before choosing the top tier.

flashcards.back: The pricing shape of caching: writing a prefix costs more than ordinary input (about 1.25 times for the five-minute lifetime, 2 times for one hour), while later reads cost only a small fraction (a tenth or less), so it pays off when a prefix is reused soon and often.
flashcards.detail: At the standard read rate break-even is one read for the five-minute lifetime and two for the one-hour lifetime. Output pricing is unaffected, and batch discounts stack with it.

flashcards.back: How long a cached prefix stays available: five minutes by default, refreshed at no charge each time it is read, or one hour at a higher write price. Pick it from the gaps between requests in a conversation.
flashcards.detail: Turns seconds apart suit the default; a person pausing between five minutes and an hour suits the longer lifetime. A miss rewrites the whole prefix at the write price.

flashcards.back: Placing breakpoints at the end of each stable section (tool definitions, system instructions, a large reference document, the conversation so far) so each part is reused independently; up to four, each on the last block that is identical across requests.
flashcards.detail: Never mark a block that changes per request, such as a timestamp or the newest user message. Because the lookback is 20 blocks, long conversations may need an extra checkpoint.

flashcards.back: What happens when anything at or before a breakpoint changes: the prefix no longer matches, so the next request misses and pays the write price again. Editing tool definitions clears everything; editing the system prompt clears it and later messages; changes to tool_choice, images, thinking or effort clear the message layer.
flashcards.detail: Keep volatile data after the last breakpoint, and make unavoidable changes at natural breaks, such as right after a compaction.

flashcards.back: The shortest prefix the API will cache (512 tokens on the current models, more on older ones). Shorter prompts are processed normally with no error and no caching, which shows up as zero in both cache fields of the usage object.
flashcards.detail: If a prompt sits just under the minimum, adding stable content to reach it can lower cost. Always confirm caching happened by reading the usage fields.

flashcards.back: The pricing asymmetry in which generated text costs several times more per unit than input text (five times on the current models), and in an agent loop each generated unit is re-read as input on later turns, so concise replies save more than shorter prompts.
flashcards.detail: Ask for the answer you will read, not the one that looks thorough: in one measured agent a long memo format cost far more than a one-line answer with no gain in accuracy.

flashcards.back: Deciding in advance how much each request, agent turn or session may consume across input, reasoning, tool results and output, and enforcing it with ceilings and alerts rather than hoping usage stays reasonable.
flashcards.detail: Tools include max_tokens per response, effort, task budgets, session budgets in Managed Agents, and workspace spend limits as the final backstop.

flashcards.back: A beta output setting that gives the model an advisory total allowance for a whole agentic loop, shown to it as a running countdown so it paces itself and wraps up gracefully; unlike a hard ceiling, the model can see it.
flashcards.detail: It complements effort (thoroughness per step) and max_tokens (a hard cap on one response). The API does not report the remaining amount back to you.

flashcards.back: Estimating spend before launch by multiplying expected request volume by input, output and reasoning volumes at their different prices, then adjusting for cache hits, batch discounts and tool overhead, and validating the estimate against real usage data.
flashcards.detail: Include the resent conversation history, tool definitions and thinking, and recount tokens for the target model.

flashcards.back: An administrative reporting interface that returns token usage and cost in time buckets, filterable and groupable by model, workspace, API key, service tier and more, for attribution, chargeback and cache-efficiency analysis; it needs an Admin-level credential, not a workspace key.
flashcards.detail: Data appears within minutes, and the Console shows similar Usage and Cost pages. Separate workspaces per feature or environment make attribution simple.

flashcards.back: A language library that wraps the HTTP interface so code calls typed functions instead of crafting requests by hand, adding authentication, required headers, retries, timeouts, streaming helpers and error classes.
flashcards.detail: Official SDKs exist for Python, TypeScript, C#, Go, Java, PHP and Ruby, and read ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment. Hand-written HTTP must send the version header and implement retries itself.

flashcards.back: A protocol that upgrades an HTTP connection into a persistent two-way channel, unlike a plain request/response call or a one-way event stream; Claude's streaming replies do not use it.
flashcards.detail: The Messages API streams over server-sent events. A WebSocket can still make sense between your own backend and a browser when the user must send messages while a reply streams, but that layer is yours, not the API's.

flashcards.back: Stating the task, audience, success criteria, format and constraints explicitly, as if briefing a capable new colleague who has no background, because the model cannot infer unstated norms or intentions.
flashcards.detail: Golden-rule test: if a colleague with minimal context would be confused by the prompt, the model will be too. "Above and beyond" behavior has to be requested, not assumed.

flashcards.back: Adding the purpose behind a rule, for example that the text will be read aloud by a speech engine, so the model can apply the intent to cases the rule never listed instead of obeying a bare prohibition mechanically.
flashcards.detail: A bare "never use ellipses" is weaker than saying why. Explanations generalize; shouting in capitals does not.

flashcards.back: Wrapping each kind of prompt content (instructions, context, examples, variable input, documents) in its own consistently named tags, nested when the content is hierarchical, so the model separates them without ambiguity.
flashcards.detail: It also works for output: ask for the answer inside a named tag so code can extract it reliably.

flashcards.back: Choosing demonstrations that are relevant to the real task, diverse enough to cover edge cases and every label without teaching accidental patterns, and enclosed in their own tags so they are not mistaken for instructions.
flashcards.detail: Three to five is a good range. A set of all-positive examples biases a classifier; near-duplicates add nothing.

flashcards.back: Setting a persona or area of expertise in the system prompt, even in a single sentence, to focus the model's tone, vocabulary and behavior for the application.
flashcards.detail: A system prompt works best as a role plus durable policies; per-request data belongs in the user turn.

flashcards.back: The rule of thumb for where text goes: the stable role, policies and output rules that apply to every turn live in the system prompt, while the specific task and the data to work on arrive in the user turn.
flashcards.detail: Untrusted material does not belong in the system prompt, which carries the highest authority. Long documents go in the user turn, ahead of the question.

flashcards.back: Placing long reference material, tens of thousands of units and more, near the top of the prompt and the question or instructions after it, which tests showed can raise answer quality, especially with many documents.
flashcards.detail: Wrap each document with its source in tags, and consider asking for relevant quotes before the answer.

flashcards.back: Asking the model to extract word-for-word quotes from the supplied documents first and then answer using only those quotes, which focuses it on the relevant passages and cuts down on invented claims.
flashcards.detail: Pair it with permission to say the answer is not in the documents. A claim with no supporting quote should be withdrawn.

flashcards.back: Phrasing guidance as the behavior you want (write in flowing paragraphs) rather than the behavior you forbid (do not use lists), which steers more reliably and avoids drawing attention to the unwanted pattern.
flashcards.detail: Match the prompt's own style to the desired output: a prompt full of markdown tends to produce markdown.

flashcards.back: Explicit limits on the shape of a reply: required format or schema, structure, tone and length. For length, sentence or paragraph limits work better than word counts, because the model works in pieces of text rather than words.
flashcards.detail: A hard max_tokens cut-off truncates mid-sentence, so treat it as a safety net rather than the length control. Use structured outputs when the shape must be guaranteed.

flashcards.back: A disciplined loop: write a first prompt, run it against a fixed set of test cases, inspect the failures, change one thing, re-run everything and repeat until the criteria are met, instead of tuning on the latest complaint.
flashcards.detail: Keep the test set and record each revision. Fixing three anecdotes can silently break others.

flashcards.back: Re-reading existing prompts, tool descriptions and instruction files after a model change and deleting text written for an older model, such as emphatic warnings, "verify twice" rules and hand-built scratchpads, because newer models obey such text literally.
flashcards.detail: Over-obeyed instructions cost money through extra tool rounds; stale settings and contradictions cost accuracy. Claude Code offers /doctor prompt-audit for a first pass.

flashcards.back: Replacing shouted wording such as CRITICAL or MUST ALWAYS with ordinary phrasing like "use this tool when...", because newer models respond strongly to the system prompt and tend to over-apply rules that are emphasized.
flashcards.detail: Symptom: a tool or skill that used to under-trigger is now called constantly. Fix the prompt before reaching for lower effort.

flashcards.back: Cleaning and bounding untrusted text before it enters a prompt: escaping or removing delimiter sequences that could close your data section, limiting length, normalizing encoding and rejecting inputs that match known attack patterns.
flashcards.detail: A first line of defense, not a complete one; combine it with structural separation, least privilege and output checks.

flashcards.back: Choosing the layer that should hold each instruction: the system prompt for durable role and policy, the user turn for the task and its data, a tool description for per-tool usage, CLAUDE.md for always-on project facts, a skill for occasional procedures, and a hook or code for rules that must never be missed.
flashcards.detail: The wrong layer is a common root cause: a must-always rule in a prompt is a wish, and a rare procedure in an always-loaded file is waste.

flashcards.back: The decline in accuracy and recall as a context fills with more material, which is why a huge window does not remove the need to choose carefully what goes into it.
flashcards.detail: Curate: retrieve only what is relevant, trim stale tool output, summarize, or delegate side work.

flashcards.back: The gradual loss of early goals, constraints or decisions in a long session, as newer material crowds them out or older turns are summarized away, so the model starts ignoring rules it followed earlier.
flashcards.detail: Counter with durable instructions in the system prompt or CLAUDE.md, periodic restatement, state files and fresh sessions between unrelated tasks.

flashcards.back: Replacing the older turns of a long conversation with a model-written summary so work can continue inside the window; recent turns can be kept verbatim, but detail from the summarized part may be lost.
flashcards.detail: Server-side compaction is the primary strategy for long agent runs. Rules that must persist belong in the system prompt or CLAUDE.md, not only in early messages.

flashcards.back: An API feature (beta) that applies rules to the history before the prompt reaches the model, such as clearing the oldest tool results or earlier thinking blocks once a threshold is passed and leaving a placeholder behind.
flashcards.detail: Use it for tool-heavy loops where old results no longer matter. Unlike compaction it deletes by rule instead of summarizing.

flashcards.back: Keeping tool results small: returning only the fields the next step needs, truncating or paginating large payloads, and replacing stale bulky results with a one-line extract at task boundaries.
flashcards.detail: The cheapest context lever is not producing the bulk in the first place; tool search and programmatic tool calling attack other sources of bloat.

flashcards.back: Giving the agent lightweight handles such as file paths, queries or links, plus tools to open them, so it loads detail only when needed instead of stuffing everything into the prompt up front.
flashcards.detail: It keeps the window focused and lets an agent explore a huge repository or knowledge base.

flashcards.back: Keeping noisy side work out of the main conversation by giving it its own window, through a delegated subagent or a separate fresh model call in a multi-step workflow, and carrying forward only the conclusions.
flashcards.detail: Pass structured results, not transcripts, between steps. It also stops one step's chatter from steering the next.

flashcards.back: Durable artifacts that let a fresh context window resume long work: a structured status file such as tests.json, free-form progress notes and the git history, which the new session reads before continuing.
flashcards.detail: When a task spans many windows, starting fresh and reading these files is often better than relying on a lossy summary.

flashcards.back: Pulling relevant passages from an external knowledge base at question time and placing them in the prompt, so answers rest on current, specific evidence rather than on what the model memorized; quality depends on the quality of the retrieval.
flashcards.detail: Choose it when knowledge is large or changes often. Cite the sources and let the model say when nothing relevant was found.

flashcards.back: Plausible-sounding output that is wrong or unsupported by the supplied sources, produced because the model predicts likely text rather than looking facts up.
flashcards.detail: Reduce it with permission to say "I do not know", quote-first grounding, citations, restriction to the provided documents and external checks. It can be lowered, never eliminated.

flashcards.back: The engineering habit of treating a fluent, assured answer as unverified until it is checked against a source, a test, a schema or a second opinion, particularly before the output triggers an action or reaches users.
flashcards.detail: Confidence in tone is not evidence. Scale verification to the stakes: tests for code, citations for facts, human review for irreversible actions.

flashcards.back: Checking each reply in code against the schema and business rules and, on failure, re-prompting with the specific error for a bounded number of attempts before escalating to a fallback or a person.
flashcards.detail: Feeding the exact violation back usually fixes it, while unbounded retries burn money. Constrained decoding reduces, but does not remove, the need.

flashcards.back: Running the same prompt several times and comparing the answers; disagreement between runs flags content that is likely unreliable and worth verifying.
flashcards.detail: A cheap signal for factual claims, but agreement does not prove correctness, and it costs N times as much.

flashcards.back: An API option on document blocks that returns, alongside the text, pointers to the exact passages in your supplied sources that support each claim, making answers auditable instead of relying on the model's own account of where facts came from.
flashcards.detail: More dependable than asking in the prompt for sources. Cache the document block; the option cannot be combined with structured outputs.

flashcards.back: The detailed plain-language text attached to a tool definition that tells the model what the tool does, when to use it and when not to, what each parameter means and what the result contains; the biggest single factor in whether tools are chosen and called correctly.
flashcards.detail: Aim for several sentences, not a phrase. Differentiate similar tools by WHEN to use each one, not only by what they do.

flashcards.back: An optional list of sample argument objects, each valid against the schema, shipped with a tool definition to show how complex, nested or format-sensitive inputs should look; invalid samples are rejected and each adds a little prompt cost.
flashcards.detail: Use it when the description alone leaves optional fields or formats ambiguous. Not supported on server-executed tools.

flashcards.back: A request field that governs whether the model may or must call tools: automatic choice, any one tool, one named tool, or none. The forcing options are rejected on the newest models, which expect automatic choice plus strict schemas.
flashcards.detail: Changing it between requests invalidates cached message content. A forced call skips thinking and suppresses preamble text.

flashcards.back: Merging closely related operations into one tool with an action argument, rather than exposing many near-identical tools, so the model faces fewer, clearer choices and the tool list stays short.
flashcards.detail: The trade-off is that a merged tool needs a precise description of every action. Pair it with namespacing.

flashcards.back: Prefixing tool names with the service or resource they belong to, such as github_list_prs or slack_send_message, so similar tools from different systems stay unambiguous as the catalog grows.
flashcards.detail: It matters most with tool search and with several MCP servers; clients that aggregate servers should prefix names to avoid collisions.

flashcards.back: Designing tool results to return only the fields the next decision needs, with stable, meaningful identifiers instead of opaque internal references, and keeping payloads small, because bulky results waste context and bury what matters.
flashcards.detail: Paginate or summarize large lists. Bloated results are a main source of context rot in agents.

flashcards.back: Failure results returned with is_error set whose message states what went wrong and what to try next, so the model can fix a parameter or wait and retry instead of guessing.
flashcards.detail: "failed" teaches nothing; "date must be in the future, today is 2026-10-15" does. An invalid call is normally retried by the model two or three times.

flashcards.back: Any tool whose code runs inside your own application: the model emits a request, your harness runs it and returns a result block. It covers your own functions and Anthropic-schema tools such as bash, text editor, memory and computer use.
flashcards.detail: You own execution, permissions, logging and the loop. The contrast is a tool that Anthropic runs for you.

flashcards.back: A tool that Anthropic runs on your behalf, such as web search, web fetch, code execution or tool search; you enable it and read the results instead of building a result block, except when the loop pauses or a client tool is called alongside it.
flashcards.detail: Look for server_tool_use blocks. If the iteration limit is hit the stop reason is pause_turn, and you re-send the conversation to continue.

flashcards.back: A tool whose definition Anthropic publishes and the models were trained on, such as bash, text editor, memory, computer or browser use; Claude calls it more reliably than a home-made equivalent, but your application still executes it.
flashcards.detail: Choose these for standard developer operations and define your own for business logic.

flashcards.back: The harness code that maps each incoming tool request's name to a handler, validates the arguments, runs it with the right permissions, and returns a result, or an error result, for every request id.
flashcards.detail: The right place for authorization, input validation, rate limits, logging and approval checks, because it runs no matter what the model decides.

flashcards.back: A server-side tool that lets the model search a large catalog and load only the definitions it needs; tools marked defer_loading stay out of the prompt until discovered, cutting context cost and improving selection among dozens of tools.
flashcards.detail: About 55k tokens of definitions in a five-server setup shrink by over 85 percent. Consider it past roughly 20 tools; the search tool itself is never deferred.

flashcards.back: Letting the model write code that runs in the code execution sandbox and calls your tools from there, so loops and filtering happen in code and only the final, trimmed result enters the conversation.
flashcards.detail: Good for many repetitive lookups, such as checking 20 employees with one script instead of 20 round trips. The tool must allow code execution as a caller.

flashcards.back: An open standard, built on JSON-RPC, for connecting AI applications to external tools and data through one common interface, so a capability built once can be used by many compliant clients; often compared to a USB-C port for AI.
flashcards.detail: It is not Claude-specific. The current specification, dated 2026-07-28, uses stateless, self-contained requests with capabilities negotiated on each request.

flashcards.back: A program that exposes tools, resources and prompts over the protocol so any compliant client can use them, built, deployed and maintained independently of the applications that connect to it.
flashcards.detail: Local servers usually run as subprocesses; shared or remote ones run over HTTP. Treat third-party servers as untrusted code.

flashcards.back: The consuming-side roles: the host is the AI application that starts connections and talks to the model, and a client is the connector inside the host that maintains the link to exactly one server.
flashcards.detail: Claude Code and Claude Desktop are hosts; each configured server gets its own client connection.
