options: Sort the results file alphabetically by message ID before matching it to the inputs
Match every result back to its input by the custom_id that was set on each request
Submit exactly one request per batch so that the order of results cannot change
Assume the order matches whenever the batch finishes quickly enough to be trusted
questions.explanation: Batch results can return in any order, so the unique custom_id on each request is the only reliable key. Sorting by message ID or relying on timing does not recover the original order, and one request per batch defeats the purpose of batching.
questions.whyTested: Batch API use.

questions.question: A finished batch reports most requests succeeded, 3 percent errored with invalid_request_error and 1 percent expired. What is the BEST handling?
options: Retry the invalid requests again unchanged until they eventually start to succeed
Keep the successes, fix the invalid requests, and resubmit those and the expired ones
Resubmit the entire batch from the beginning so that all of the results are consistent
Treat the batch as successful overall and ignore the errored and expired requests
questions.explanation: Each request is processed independently, and errored, canceled or expired requests are not billed. Repair what was malformed and resubmit only the failed or expired items. Resubmitting everything wastes money, ignoring failures loses data, and an invalid request fails again if sent unchanged.
questions.whyTested: Batch results handling.

questions.question: A batch of 50,000 requests ended, and 40 percent errored because of the same mistake in how the request body was built. Nobody noticed until the whole batch had finished. What would have prevented this?
options: Testing one request of each shape on the Messages API before submitting the batch
Turning on streaming for the batch so that errors show up while it is still running
Waiting for the full 24-hour expiry window to pass before reading any of the results
Splitting the same malformed requests across a larger number of smaller batches
questions.explanation: Request validation inside a batch happens asynchronously and shows up in the results, so a quick dry run of each request shape on the Messages API catches shape mistakes cheaply. Streaming is not supported for batches, splitting identical bad requests changes nothing, and waiting only delays the discovery.
questions.whyTested: Batch API use and testing.

questions.question: An app sends images by URL to the direct Claude API successfully. After the team moves to Amazon Bedrock, the same requests fail. What is the likely reason and fix?
options: Bedrock accepts only base64-encoded image sources, so download and encode the images
URL sources need an extra header on Bedrock that carries the host name of the image
Bedrock does not support vision at all, so the images have to be removed from requests
Images must first be uploaded through the Files API before they can be used on Bedrock
questions.explanation: On Amazon Bedrock and Google Cloud only base64 sources are currently available for images and documents, whereas the direct API also accepts URLs and file IDs. Vision itself is supported, there is no host header, and the Files API is not the route on those platforms.
questions.whyTested: Invoking Claude through third-party vendors: features differ by platform.

questions.question: A tool-using app with thinking enabled starts returning 400 errors on the second turn. The developer rebuilds each assistant message from only its text and tool_use blocks before resending. What is the cause and fix?
options: The tool_use blocks should have been removed from the history instead of thinking blocks
The thinking blocks were dropped: pass them back unchanged, even ones with empty text
Thinking cannot be combined with tools at all, so thinking has to be turned off
The signature field should be regenerated by the client application before resending it
questions.explanation: Thinking blocks carry an encrypted signature and, in tool-use conversations, must be returned exactly as received; filtering or editing them in the latest assistant turn is rejected. Removing tool_use blocks would break pairing with results, clients cannot regenerate signatures, and thinking works with tools.
questions.whyTested: Thinking in the Messages API.

questions.question: A developer enabled prompt caching on a long system prompt but every response shows cache_creation_input_tokens above zero and cache_read_input_tokens at zero. Which cause is MOST likely?
options: Prompt caching is only available when requests are submitted through the batch endpoint
The prefix changes on each call, such as a timestamp near the start, so nothing matches
Cache reads are reported only in the response headers and never in the usage object
The model ignores cache breakpoints whenever they are placed on a system prompt
questions.explanation: A cache read requires the prompt prefix up to the breakpoint to be identical to an earlier request (tools, then system, then messages). A varying value early in the prompt makes each call write a new entry. Read counts appear in the usage object, system prompts can be cached, and caching works on the Messages API.
questions.whyTested: Caching mechanics at the API level.

questions.question: Before sending a 300-page contract, a developer wants to know whether it fits the model's context and roughly what it will cost, without generating an answer. Which approach is BEST?
options: Estimate the count by dividing the size of the file in bytes by a fixed factor of four
Ask Claude in an ordinary chat message how many tokens the attached file is going to use
Send the real request with a large max_tokens value and read the usage object afterwards
Call the token counting endpoint with the same system prompt, tools and document
questions.explanation: The token counting endpoint accepts the same structure as a message, including system prompt, tools and PDFs, and returns an estimated input count without generating output. Sending the real request spends tokens, a byte-based guess ignores images and tokenizer differences, and the model has no reliable way to count its own input.
questions.whyTested: Token usage tracking and cost modeling.

questions.question: An intermittent server error needs investigation with Anthropic support. Which piece of information should the application have logged for each failing call?
options: The complete API key that was used to authenticate the failing call
Only the time of day at which each failing call happened to be made
The request ID returned in the response header and in the error body
A full copy of the whole conversation text written into every single log line
questions.explanation: Every response carries a unique request ID that support can use to trace the exact call, and error bodies repeat it as request_id. Logging keys is a security risk, timestamps alone are ambiguous, and copying full conversations into logs creates a privacy problem without helping the trace.
questions.whyTested: Debugging at the integration layer.

questions.question: A non-streaming call that asks for a 100,000-token report makes the SDK raise an error about the expected duration. What is the BEST resolution?
options: Raise the number of automatic retries that the client performs for each request
Switch to a model that offers a larger context window than the current one
Catch the error and retry the same non-streaming call again until it finally passes
Stream the response, using the final-message helper if events need no handling
questions.explanation: The SDK refuses non-streaming requests expected to run beyond about ten minutes because idle connections can be dropped. Streaming keeps the connection active, and the final-message helper returns the complete message. Retrying, a bigger context window and extra retries do not change the expected duration.
questions.whyTested: Long requests and streaming.

questions.question: While streaming, a developer needs to know why generation ended so the UI can show a "continue" button after truncation. Where does the stop reason arrive?
options: Only in a response header that is read after the stream has been closed
In a message_delta event near the end; the first event carries it as null
In the message_start event, which is the very first event of the stream
In every content_block_delta event, as a running value that is updated
questions.explanation: The initial message object has a null stop_reason, and the real value is delivered in a message_delta event shortly before message_stop. Content block deltas carry content, not the stop reason, and it is part of the event data rather than a header.
questions.whyTested: Streaming event flow.

questions.question: A nightly job receives a 429 response that includes a retry-after value of 30. What is the BEST way to handle it?
options: Retry immediately on ten parallel threads to get through before the limit resets
Switch to a second API key from the same organization and continue at full speed
Treat the 429 as a permanent failure and fail the whole nightly job immediately
Wait at least 30 seconds, retry a bounded number of times and lower concurrency
questions.explanation: The retry-after value says when capacity returns; earlier retries will fail. Waiting, limiting attempts and reducing concurrency respects the limit. Parallel immediate retries make the burst worse, a 429 is transient rather than permanent, and keys in the same organization share its limits.
questions.whyTested: Error recovery for rate limits.

questions.question: Starting mid-month, every request returns 429 with no retry-after header and a message that the organization crossed its monthly usage threshold. SDK retries keep failing. What is the right conclusion and action?
options: A monthly spend cap was reached; retries cannot help, so raise the limit or tier
It is an ordinary burst limit, so add jitter to the retry schedule and try again
The API key was revoked, so create a new key and update the deployment
The API is overloaded for everyone, so wait for the incident to clear and retry
questions.explanation: A tier spend-cap 429 has no retry-after header and persists until access resumes at the start of the next month or the limit is raised. Burst limits and overload clear on their own, and a revoked key returns an authentication error rather than a rate-limit error.
questions.whyTested: Distinguishing error types before choosing a recovery strategy.

questions.question: Monitoring shows bursts of 529 overloaded_error responses across many customers' calls, while your own usage is far below every limit. Which response is MOST appropriate?
options: Rotate to a new API key in order to get away from the overloaded server
Request a higher rate limit from support, because the current limit is clearly too low
Retry with exponential backoff and jitter, and keep a degraded or fallback path ready
Fail fast and show an error page, since overload errors cannot be handled in code
questions.explanation: A 529 reflects temporary capacity pressure across the service, not your quota. Backoff with jitter and a fallback keep the product working. A higher limit or a new key address problems that are not present, and giving up immediately throws away a request that would succeed moments later.
questions.whyTested: Matching the recovery strategy to the error.

questions.question: A team wrapped every SDK call in its own five-attempt retry loop, not realizing the SDK already retries twice by default. During an incident, traffic to the API triples. What is the BEST correction?
options: Retry only after a user has clicked a button to confirm that retrying is wanted
Remove every retry from the system so that all errors surface immediately
Treat the layers as one retry budget and set the SDK count or your loop on purpose
Add a third retry layer around the first two for an extra margin of safety
questions.explanation: Stacked retries multiply attempts (here up to 15 per call), amplifying load exactly when the service is stressed. Decide where retrying lives, cap it and back off. More layers make it worse, no retries throws away transient-failure protection, and a manual button is a poor default.
questions.whyTested: Retry design and rate limits.

questions.question: An agent's charge_card tool is wrapped in a timeout-and-retry helper. After a slow response the helper retried, and several customers were charged twice. What is the BEST fix?
options: Tell the agent in its prompt never to call the charge tool twice for one order
Remove the retry helper from every tool, whatever the tool does or costs
Increase the timeout far enough that retries practically never happen any more
Make the charge idempotent by sending an idempotency key with each logical payment
questions.explanation: When a call can be repeated, the downstream service must be able to recognise duplicates; an idempotency key makes the repeated request safe. Longer timeouts only reduce the frequency, prompt instructions do not control a helper outside the model, and removing retries trades one failure for another.
questions.whyTested: Idempotency in integrations.

questions.question: A script processes 5,000 documents and launches every call at once with a gather over all tasks. The result is a wall of 429 errors. Which change is BEST?
options: Increase max_tokens so that each call does a larger amount of work than before
Split the 5,000 calls across 5,000 separate processes so that they run independently
Switch the script to plain synchronous calls and remove all of the retry handling
Cap in-flight requests with a semaphore or worker pool sized to the limits, plus backoff
questions.explanation: Asynchronous code makes unbounded fan-out easy, so bound concurrency and add backoff to stay within limits. If no one is waiting, the batch endpoint is another good option. More processes only fire more requests, and max_tokens does not reduce request volume.
questions.whyTested: Asynchronous programming with rate limits.

questions.question: An app crashes with an index error when reading content[0].text for certain inputs, although the HTTP status is 200. Which cause and fix are MOST likely?
options: The server dropped the connection partway through, so retry the same request
The API key lacks permission for this model, so ask an admin to change its role
The reply was a refusal with no content: check stop_reason first and use a fallback
The text block is always the last block in the array, so read the final element
questions.explanation: A refusal is a normal 200 response whose stop reason is refusal, and the content can be empty. Branch on stop_reason before touching content, and decide on a fallback such as another model. Connection and permission problems would produce errors rather than a 200, and block order is not guaranteed.
questions.whyTested: Defensive handling of responses.

questions.question: Which failure should an HTTP client NOT retry automatically?
options: A 401 authentication error returned after the API key was revoked
A 500 internal error returned by the service on a single request
A 529 overloaded response during a busy period for the whole service
A dropped connection before any response bytes were received at all
questions.explanation: Authentication failures are not transient; retrying the same revoked key just repeats the failure, so surface the problem and fix the credential. Overload, connection drops and 5xx errors are the classic transient cases suited to retry with backoff.
questions.whyTested: Retryable versus non-retryable errors.

questions.question: Claude Code produced a 900-line refactor of a payment module, and every existing test passes. What is the BEST step before merging?
options: Discard the whole change and rewrite the payment module by hand from scratch
Merge it immediately, because every one of the existing tests is already green
Ask the same Claude session that wrote the change to approve its own work
Split it into small commits and have an engineer review the diff before merging
questions.explanation: Passing tests show only that covered behavior is unchanged. Human code review catches hidden coupling, security problems and logic the tests do not exercise, and smaller commits make that review realistic. Self-approval is not independent, and discarding useful work is wasteful.
questions.whyTested: Code review and refactoring discipline.

questions.question: A team must move a 400,000-line service from one HTTP library to another over six months while still shipping features. Which approach is BEST?
options: Leave both libraries in the codebase permanently and let each team choose its own
Freeze all feature work and rewrite the entire service in one long-lived branch
Ask Claude to replace every call site in the codebase in a single huge pull request
Add an interface, migrate module by module with tests, then retire the old library
questions.explanation: A strangler-style incremental migration keeps the system shippable, limits each change so it can be reviewed and rolled back, and ends with the old code removed. A big-bang rewrite is risky and blocks delivery, one enormous pull request cannot be reviewed well, and permanent duplication is technical debt.
questions.whyTested: Small- and large-scale refactoring.

questions.question: A team wants Claude Code to review every pull request in CI. Runs must behave the same on every runner, and no secrets may be committed. Which setup is BEST?
options: Run the CLI with every permission check bypassed, on the shared developer laptops used for CI
Run the CLI non-interactively in bare mode with read-only tools and a key from the secret store
Run the interactive CLI and answer its permission prompts through a screen-scraping script
Commit the API key to a file in a private repository for convenience across all runners
questions.explanation: Print mode with bare startup skips auto-discovery of local hooks, plugins, MCP servers and CLAUDE.md so each runner behaves the same, pre-approved tools avoid prompts, and the key belongs in a secret store. Scraping an interactive session is fragile, committed keys leak, and bypassing permissions on laptops is unsafe.
questions.whyTested: SDLC integration with Claude Code in CI.

questions.question: A developer hand-writes an HTTP call to /v1/messages instead of using an SDK and gets a 400 about a missing version. Which request headers does the call need?
options: Only an authorization header, because the API infers the version on its own
A custom header naming the model, plus the API key header and nothing else
An API key header, the anthropic-version header and a JSON content type
A session cookie copied from a signed-in Claude Console browser tab
questions.explanation: Direct REST calls need the API key, an anthropic-version value such as 2023-06-01, and content-type application/json; the SDKs add these automatically. The model is specified in the JSON body, and Console cookies are not used for API authentication.
questions.whyTested: REST APIs and SDK usage.

questions.question: A new engineer asks why the team wraps the Anthropic SDK behind its own small interface instead of calling it throughout the codebase. Which reason is MOST sound?
options: The API rejects calls that arrive from more than one module in the same process
Wrapping the SDK reduces the number of tokens that each individual request uses
One boundary makes retries, logging, model IDs and test fakes easy to change in one place
The SDK is deprecated, so application code is no longer permitted to call it directly
questions.explanation: A thin adapter centralises cross-cutting concerns and lets tests substitute a fake, which also eases model migrations. The SDK is supported, a wrapper does not change token counts, and the API has no concept of calling modules.
questions.whyTested: Software engineering foundations around SDK integration.

questions.question: A prompt produced neat formatting and knew today's date when tried in the claude.ai chat window, but through the API in the team's app it answers in plain text and gets the date wrong. What explains this?
options: The API ignores every formatting instruction and always answers in plain text only
claude.ai adds an Anthropic system prompt that the API lacks, so the app must add its own
The current date is stored on the user account and is sent along with API keys
The model behind the API is a weaker version than the one that is used in claude.ai
questions.explanation: Consumer apps add their own system prompt (current date, formatting habits and more), whereas the API sends only what you provide. To reproduce the behavior, state the date, format and style rules in your own system prompt. The model is not weaker, formatting instructions are honored, and keys do not carry dates.
questions.whyTested: How Claude interprets instructions across interfaces.

questions.question: An app summarizes web pages submitted by users. How should the request be structured to keep the page text from being treated as instructions?
options: Paste the instructions and the page text together in one continuous paragraph
Append the page text to the system prompt so that it carries the highest priority
Ask the authors of the pages not to include anything that looks like a command
Put the instructions in the system prompt and wrap the page in a delimited data block
questions.explanation: A content boundary separates trusted instructions from untrusted material using structure the model can follow, such as tagged blocks labelled as input data. It is a design aid that works best with least-privilege tools. Putting untrusted text into the system prompt gives it more authority, a blended paragraph hides the boundary, and you cannot control page authors.
questions.whyTested: Content boundaries in application design.

questions.question: A tool schema has a free-text type field whose valid values are described only in prose, and about 30 optional parameters. The model often supplies unexpected values. Which redesign helps MOST?
options: Remove the field descriptions altogether in order to reduce the number of input tokens
Use enums for closed sets, describe each field, and make parameters required where possible
Add a much longer system prompt that repeats all of the valid values for the field
Allow additionalProperties so that the model can add whatever extra fields it likes
questions.explanation: A schema is both a contract and documentation: enums narrow choices, descriptions explain intent and fewer optional fields reduce ambiguity. A repeated prompt is weaker than a constraint in the schema, extra properties make output less predictable, and removing descriptions removes guidance.
questions.whyTested: Schema design.

questions.question: After adding dozens of optional fields and several union types to a strict schema, requests fail with a 400 saying the schema is too complex to compile. Which response is BEST?
options: Retry the same request several times with exponential backoff between the attempts
Remove the schema and parse the prose that comes back with regular expressions
Raise the max_tokens value on the request so the grammar has more room to fit
Simplify it: fewer optional parameters, flatter nesting, strict mode only where needed
questions.explanation: Complexity limits are about the compiled grammar, so reduce optional parameters and unions, flatten nesting, and reserve strict mode for tools where violations matter. Retrying an unchanged invalid schema fails again, output caps are unrelated, and regex parsing of prose is the brittle approach schemas replace.
questions.whyTested: Schema design limits.

questions.question: A developer has corrected Claude Code three times on the same bug in one long session, and answers are getting worse. Which step is BEST?
options: Switch the project over to a different programming language for the fix
Clear the session and restart with a sharper prompt that includes what was learned
Keep correcting the same mistake, since the model will eventually learn from it
Paste the entire transcript of the session back in again as a new message
questions.explanation: Repeated failed corrections fill context with dead ends. A clean session with a better prompt almost always beats a long cluttered one. More corrections add to the clutter, pasting the transcript recreates it, and changing languages is unrelated.
questions.whyTested: Session hygiene.

questions.question: An engineer wants to understand how a large legacy module works before editing it. Reading it directly would flood the working session with file contents. Which approach is BEST?
options: Run the research in a separate, unrelated project directory on the same machine
Delegate the research to a subagent that returns a summary, sparing the main context
Read every file in the main session and compact the conversation afterwards
Skip the research entirely and make the edit based only on the file names
questions.explanation: Subagents explore in their own context window and return only a concise report, which protects the main session. Reading everything into the main context costs space and attention, guessing from names risks errors, and a separate project loses the repository context.
questions.whyTested: Managing context across sessions.

questions.question: A team installed fourteen Claude Code plugins. Sessions feel slower and token usage creeps up, yet most plugins are rarely invoked. What is the MOST appropriate action?
options: Disable unused plugins, because their skill descriptions occupy context on every turn
Ignore the problem, because plugins that are not being used cannot add any cost
Rename the plugins so that their skill descriptions end up a good deal shorter
Install additional plugins whose job is to compress the output of the other plugins
questions.explanation: An enabled plugin places the names and descriptions of its skills and agents in context on every turn, and its hooks and servers run alongside sessions, so unused ones carry a cost. Disabling or removing them is the fix. They are not free, and renaming does not remove the overhead.
questions.whyTested: Plugin management.

questions.question: A team lead wants every contributor to a repository to have the same code-review plugin enabled by default. Which install scope is BEST?
options: Project scope, which records the plugin as enabled in the committed project settings
User scope on the lead's own machine, so it follows the lead into every project
No install scope at all; just email the teammates the manual installation steps
Local scope, so the plugin applies only to the lead and only in this repository
questions.explanation: Project scope writes the enabled plugin into the shared settings file that is committed, so contributors get the same setup (each still installs it on their own machine). User and local scopes affect only one person, and informal instructions drift.
questions.whyTested: Plugin management and configuration scope.

questions.question: A developer is about to install a plugin from a marketplace that nobody on the team has reviewed. What is the BEST precaution?
options: Install it straight away and delete it again if anything looks odd afterwards
Install it at user scope, because that scope sandboxes it from the rest of the machine
Trust it, because every plugin marketplace is operated and reviewed by Anthropic itself
Review its hooks, commands and MCP servers first, because it runs with your privileges
questions.explanation: A plugin can run code, hooks and servers as you, whichever marketplace it comes from, so review the contents before installing. Scope does not sandbox anything, third-party marketplaces exist, and damage from a malicious plugin may happen before you notice anything.
questions.whyTested: Plugin management and trust.

questions.question: An agent fetches web pages with a client tool. Where should the application place the fetched page text when it replies to Claude?
options: Inside the tool_result block that answers that particular tool call
In the system prompt, so the model fully trusts the fetched content
In an assistant message that the application writes on the model's behalf
As a new user text block placed ahead of the tool result block
questions.explanation: Untrusted material returned by tools belongs in tool_result content, which keeps it separate from your instructions and keeps the required pairing with the tool_use block. System text is treated as trusted instructions, text before the result breaks the ordering rule, and assistant messages are for the model's own output.
questions.whyTested: Content boundaries for tool output.

questions.question: A team shares Claude Code settings that select the sonnet alias. After a new Sonnet release, behavior changes for everyone overnight. What is the BEST way to prevent surprise changes?
options: Switch to the opus alias instead, because that alias never moves to a new version
Disable automatic updates to the Claude Code application for the whole team
Keep the alias and ask everyone on the team to re-check their prompts every week
Pin the full model name in shared settings and migrate deliberately after running evals
questions.explanation: Aliases point at the recommended newest version and move over time, so shared configurations that want stability should pin an explicit model. Weekly manual checks are unreliable, application updates are not what changed, and every family alias moves.
questions.whyTested: Model version pinning.

questions.question: A developer wants sandbox URLs and personal test data available to Claude in one repository without committing them. Which approach is BEST?
options: Use a local instructions file at the project root and add it to the ignore list
Place them in the organization-managed policy file so they apply to every developer
Paste them into the very first prompt of every session by hand each time
Add them to the shared project CLAUDE.md so that every teammate benefits as well
questions.explanation: A local instructions file loads alongside the project CLAUDE.md for this repository only, and ignoring it keeps personal data out of source control. The shared file and managed policy expose the data to others, and retyping it every session is tedious and error-prone.
questions.whyTested: CLAUDE.md hierarchy.

questions.question: An organization requires that no developer ever runs Claude Code with permission checks bypassed, even if individuals set it in their own settings. Where should the rule be placed?
options: In the project's local settings file kept next to the shared project settings
In every developer's own user settings file under their home directory
In managed settings, which take precedence over every other settings scope
In the shared project CLAUDE.md, written down as a clearly worded policy
questions.explanation: Managed settings sit at the top of the precedence order, above the command line, local, project and user settings, so individuals cannot override them. The other locations are overridable or are guidance rather than enforced configuration.
questions.whyTested: settings.json precedence.

questions.question: A project's CLAUDE.md has grown to 900 lines and Claude Code seems to ignore some rules. What is the MOST effective improvement?
options: Trim it to concise, specific instructions and move situational guidance to skills
Add more rules so that each of the rules that are being missed is repeated again
Split it into twenty imported files, because imported files do not load at launch
Add bold and capital-letter emphasis to the important rules so they stand out more
questions.explanation: Long files consume context and reduce adherence, and contradictions make behavior unpredictable. Keep the file short and specific, and load situational guidance on demand. Imported files are still loaded at launch, so splitting does not help, and adding rules makes it longer.
questions.whyTested: Configuration management of CLAUDE.md.

questions.question: The authors of a plugin depend on another plugin, secrets-vault, with no version constraint. A new release of secrets-vault renamed a tool, and the dependent plugin broke for everyone who updated. What is the BEST fix?
options: Declare a version range such as ~2.1.0 on the dependency, widening it only after testing
Remove the dependency and ask each user to install that other plugin by hand
Tell all of the users never to update any plugin they have installed, at any time
Copy the dependency's code into the plugin permanently so that it can never change
questions.explanation: An unconstrained dependency moves to every new release. A tested range keeps users on compatible patches until the author deliberately widens it. Freezing all updates blocks fixes, copying code forks it, and manual installation reintroduces drift.
questions.whyTested: Plugin dependencies.

questions.question: An app has separate development, staging and production deployments. An engineer hard-codes one API key in a config file in the repository. What is the BEST correction?
options: Encode the key in base64 inside the config file so that it is no longer readable
Keep the key in the repository but make the repository private to the team
Share the production key with every environment so that all of them stay identical
Read keys from the environment or a secret manager, with a workspace per environment
questions.explanation: Keys belong outside source control, supplied per environment, with workspaces separating environments and their limits and spend. A private repository still leaks to everyone with access and to history, a shared production key widens the blast radius, and base64 is not encryption.
questions.whyTested: Configuration management for secrets and environments.

questions.question: Which TWO of the following are non-functional requirements for a Claude-powered support assistant? (Choose two.)
options: The assistant must summarize each ticket in three sentences
The assistant must call the refund tool for eligible orders
Model inference for EU customers must stay in an approved geography
Ninety-five percent of replies must begin streaming within three seconds
questions.explanation: Non-functional requirements describe qualities such as latency, throughput, availability, cost and data residency. Summarizing tickets and calling a refund tool describe what the system does, so they are functional.
questions.whyTested: Functional and infrastructure requirements.

questions.question: Which TWO workloads are good candidates for the Message Batches API? (Choose two.)
options: Answering a customer typing in a live chat window
Completing the next line of code as a developer types
Re-tagging an archive of 200,000 documents with a new taxonomy by next week
Scoring a 20,000-prompt evaluation set overnight
questions.explanation: Batches are cheaper and high-throughput but promise results only within 24 hours, so they fit latency-tolerant bulk work. Live chat and as-you-type completion have a person waiting and need synchronous calls.
questions.whyTested: Realtime versus batch selection.

questions.question: A team wants safe, repeatable changes to prompts and model versions. Which TWO practices support that? (Choose two.)
options: Store prompts in version control and release them through review
Switch the production model alias whenever a new release appears
Edit the live prompt directly during an incident without recording the change
Run an evaluation suite in CI and gate merges on its scores
questions.explanation: Versioned, reviewed prompts and automated evals make changes traceable, testable and reversible. Untracked live edits and automatic alias changes remove that safety and make regressions hard to trace.
questions.whyTested: Systems life cycle management for Claude applications.

questions.question: A client consumes a streamed Messages API response. Which THREE behaviors make it robust? (Choose three.)
options: Ignore ping events and keep reading
Parse every partial JSON fragment of a tool call as soon as it arrives
Read the final stop reason from the first event in the stream
Handle an error event that arrives after the HTTP 200
Skip event types it does not recognise instead of crashing
questions.explanation: Streams can contain ping events, mid-stream error events, and new event types added over time, so a robust client tolerates all three. The stop reason is null at the start and arrives in a later message_delta, and partial JSON is valid only after the block finishes.
questions.whyTested: Streaming and error handling.

questions.question: A reply arrives with stop_reason tool_use. Which TWO things must the next request contain? (Choose two.)
options: The tool_result blocks placed before any other content in the user message
A new anthropic-version value reserved for tool turns
An assistant message restating the tool output in the model's voice
A tool_result for every tool_use ID in the previous reply
questions.explanation: Each tool_use needs a matching result in a user message that follows the assistant turn, with the results first. Results are never sent as assistant text, and the version header does not change per turn.
questions.whyTested: Mechanics of the tool-use round trip.

questions.question: Which THREE are valid ways to supply an image to the Messages API on the direct Claude API? (Choose three.)
options: A path to a file on the application server
Raw bytes placed inside a text block
A file ID from the Files API
A URL that points to the image
A base64-encoded string with a media type
questions.explanation: Image blocks accept base64, URL and file sources. The API cannot read a path on your server, and image bytes in a text block are not interpreted as an image.
questions.whyTested: Vision inputs.

questions.question: Which TWO statements about the Message Batches API are accurate? (Choose two.)
options: Results are guaranteed within five minutes
Results can come back in a different order from the requests
It is charged at half the standard price
It supports streaming so results arrive token by token
questions.explanation: Batch usage costs 50 percent of standard prices and results are matched by custom_id because order is not guaranteed. Streaming is not supported, and processing can take up to 24 hours, although most batches finish within an hour.
questions.whyTested: Batch API use.

questions.question: Which TWO errors are normally worth retrying with exponential backoff? (Choose two.)
options: A 429 response that includes a retry-after header
A 401 authentication_error for a revoked key
A 400 invalid_request_error caused by an unsupported parameter
A 529 overloaded_error response
questions.explanation: Overload and burst rate limits are transient and clear with time. A malformed request or a bad credential stays wrong until you change it, so retrying only adds noise.
questions.whyTested: Error type identification and recovery strategy selection.

questions.question: A bulk job keeps hitting 429 errors. Which THREE changes help? (Choose three.)
options: Raise max_tokens so each call does more
Bound the number of in-flight requests
Retry every failed call immediately with no delay
Honor the retry-after value before retrying
Ramp traffic up gradually instead of starting at full volume
questions.explanation: Limiting concurrency, waiting as instructed and avoiding sudden jumps respect token-bucket and acceleration limits. Instant retries worsen the burst, and max_tokens does not affect request counts.
questions.whyTested: Rate limit handling.

questions.question: A team uses Claude Code to help with a large refactoring. Which TWO practices reduce risk? (Choose two.)
options: Keep refactoring commits separate from feature changes
Make small steps and keep the test suite green after each one
Skip human review because the changes were written by a model
Land the whole change as a single enormous pull request
questions.explanation: Small, tested, single-purpose steps are easier to review, bisect and revert. One giant change and skipped review remove those safeguards.
questions.whyTested: Small- and large-scale refactoring.

questions.question: Why do model-generated changes still need human code review even when all tests pass? (Choose two.)
options: Plausible but wrong logic and design problems can pass tests
Tests do not cover every behavior or security property
Model-generated code cannot be syntactically valid
The hosting platform refuses to merge any unreviewed pull request
questions.explanation: Green tests only prove the covered behavior, so review is where hidden coupling, security flaws and subtly wrong logic are caught. Generated code is usually valid syntax, and merge rules are a team policy rather than a platform fact.
questions.whyTested: Code review in the SDLC.

questions.question: Which TWO are good practices when designing JSON Schemas for tool inputs and structured outputs? (Choose two.)
options: Make most parameters optional so the model has flexibility
Allow arbitrary extra properties to avoid validation failures
Write clear descriptions for fields whose meaning is not obvious
Use enums for fields with a closed set of valid values
questions.explanation: Enums constrain choices and descriptions tell the model what each field means. Many optional parameters and open-ended extra properties increase ambiguity and compile complexity.
questions.whyTested: Schema design.

questions.question: Which THREE habits keep an interactive Claude Code session effective? (Choose three.)
options: Delegating broad codebase research to a subagent
Restarting with a sharper prompt after repeated failed corrections
Keeping one session open forever so it learns everything
Pasting the full output of every command into the chat
Clearing the session between unrelated tasks
questions.explanation: Context is the scarce resource: reset it between tasks, avoid carrying dead ends, and keep exploration in separate contexts. A permanent session and pasting everything fill the window with irrelevant material.
questions.whyTested: Session hygiene.

questions.question: Which TWO statements about CLAUDE.md files are accurate? (Choose two.)
options: Block-level HTML comments in them are sent to the model with the rest of the text
They are loaded as context, not as enforced configuration
A project file always replaces the user-level file
Files found at different levels are concatenated into context rather than overriding each other
questions.explanation: All discovered files are combined, with instructions closer to the working directory read last, and Claude treats them as guidance, so use hooks or permission rules to enforce. HTML block comments are stripped before injection, and project files do not replace user files.
questions.whyTested: Configuration management: CLAUDE.md files.

questions.question: A team will migrate from one Claude model to a newer one. Which TWO practices support a safe migration? (Choose two.)
options: Run your own eval suite on the candidate and compare results to the current model
Pin the exact model ID in production while the candidate is evaluated
Wait for the retirement date, then pick a replacement
Change the alias in production first and watch what breaks
questions.explanation: Pinning keeps production stable while you measure the candidate on your own tasks. Switching blindly or waiting until retirement removes the safety margin that the notice period provides.
questions.whyTested: Model version pinning and breaking changes across releases.

questions.question: The Messages API keeps the conversation on the server between requests, so a client only needs to send the newest user message.
questions.explanation: The API is stateless. The application must send the full history it wants the model to see with every request.

questions.question: A 429 caused by reaching a monthly spend cap will not be fixed by SDK automatic retries.
questions.explanation: That variant has no retry-after header and persists until the limit is raised or the next month begins. Retrying only repeats the failure.

questions.question: A refusal from the model's safety classifiers is returned as an HTTP 4xx error, so exception handling is enough to catch it.
questions.explanation: A refusal is a normal 200 response with stop_reason refusal. Code must check the stop reason, because no exception is raised.

questions.question: An error can arrive inside a streamed response even though the HTTP status was already 200.
questions.explanation: Once streaming starts, the status line has been sent. Failures such as overloaded_error are delivered as error events in the stream, so streaming code needs its own handling.

questions.question: Message Batches API requests cost half of standard prices, and results are matched to requests by custom_id because order is not guaranteed.
questions.explanation: Both statements are correct. Batch usage is charged at 50 percent of standard prices, and results can return in any order.

questions.question: Files you upload through the Files API can be downloaded again later with the download endpoint.
questions.explanation: Only files created by skills or the code execution tool are downloadable. Downloading a file you uploaded returns an error, so keep your own copy.

questions.question: On the direct Claude API, an image block can use a base64 source, a URL source or a file ID source.
questions.explanation: All three source types are supported. Amazon Bedrock and Google Cloud currently accept only base64.

questions.question: Structured outputs guarantee that every value in the returned JSON is factually correct.
questions.explanation: They guarantee the shape (valid JSON that matches the schema), not the truth of the values. Semantic validation and verification are still your job.

questions.question: Assistant prefill remains supported on Claude 4.6 and later models.
questions.explanation: A prefilled final assistant message is rejected with a 400 error on those models. Use structured outputs or system prompt instructions instead.

questions.question: Server-sent events used for Claude streaming allow the browser and server to exchange messages in both directions over the same connection.
questions.explanation: SSE is one-way, server to client. A WebSocket is the bidirectional alternative, and the Claude API streams responses with SSE.

questions.question: The max_tokens parameter is a target length that the model tries to reach.
questions.explanation: It is only a ceiling. The model usually stops sooner, and if it reaches the cap the reply is cut off with stop_reason max_tokens.

questions.question: The official SDKs retry transient failures such as connection errors, 429 and 5xx responses twice by default.
questions.explanation: Automatic retries with short exponential backoff are on by default and can be changed with max_retries per client or per request.

questions.question: Using asynchronous code makes a single model request return faster.
questions.explanation: Async lets one process overlap many requests, which raises throughput. Each individual call still takes as long as the model needs.

questions.question: Prompts, tool schemas and configuration files belong in version control alongside the source code.
questions.explanation: They determine behavior as much as code does, so changes should be reviewed, traceable and reversible.

questions.question: A feature flag can switch traffic back to the previous prompt without redeploying the application.
questions.explanation: Flags are runtime switches, which is what makes gradual rollout and instant rollback possible.

questions.question: A dateless model ID from the Claude 4.6 generation onward, such as claude-sonnet-4-6, is a fixed snapshot rather than a pointer that quietly moves to newer releases.
questions.explanation: Anthropic does not change the weights behind an existing model ID; updated versions ship under new IDs. Convenience aliases that move exist for earlier models and in tools such as Claude Code.

questions.question: After a model's retirement date, requests that name it fail.
questions.explanation: Retired models are no longer available. Anthropic gives at least 60 days' notice for public models, which is the window to migrate.

questions.question: Updates to the system prompt used in claude.ai also change how the Claude API behaves.
questions.explanation: The consumer apps' system prompt is separate. Those updates do not apply to the API, which uses only the instructions you send.

questions.question: Claude Code loads CLAUDE.md files from the working directory and from every directory above it at launch, and combines them.
questions.explanation: Files up the directory tree are concatenated, ordered from the root down to the working directory. Subdirectory files load later, on demand.

questions.question: A plugin dependency declared without a version constraint follows each new release its marketplace publishes.
questions.explanation: That is why authors add a tested range such as ~2.1.0 when a new release could break the dependent plugin.

questions.question: Enabling a plugin at project scope automatically installs it on every teammate's machine with no further action.
questions.explanation: The committed settings record that the plugin should be enabled, but each collaborator still installs it on their own machine.

questions.question: A requirement that 95 percent of replies start within three seconds is a functional requirement.
questions.explanation: Latency targets describe how well the system performs, so they are non-functional requirements. Functional requirements describe what the system does.

questions.question: Usage of the Message Batches API reduces the rate limits available to the synchronous Messages API.
questions.explanation: Batches have their own limits, and using them does not affect Messages API rate limits.

questions.question: The token counting endpoint returns an exact count that will always equal the billed input tokens.
questions.explanation: The count is an estimate and can differ by a small amount from actual usage, so treat it as a planning tool and rely on the usage object for billing.

questions.question: Committing an API key to a private repository is an acceptable way to share it with a team.
questions.explanation: Keys in source control spread to everyone with access and live on in history. Use a secret manager or environment variables, with separate workspaces per environment.

questions.question: A support assistant must answer questions about a 40,000-row order database that changes every minute. The team pastes an export into the system prompt; it barely fits the context window and is minutes out of date. Which approach is BEST?
options: Raise max_tokens so that the model can hold the entire export in its working memory
Upload a fresh export through the Files API every minute and reference the newest file ID
Give the model a read-only lookup tool that queries the live database for the orders it needs
Send the export through the Message Batches API so that it is processed with each question
questions.explanation: For large, fast-changing data, let the model fetch only what it needs on demand through a tool: the answer is current, the prompt stays small, and access can be limited to read-only queries. A minute-by-minute upload still sends stale or oversized data into the context, max_tokens limits output rather than memory, and the batch endpoint is asynchronous and unsuited to live questions.
questions.whyTested: Messages API data access patterns: inline, by reference, on demand.

questions.question: A developer installs a plugin at user scope from the Claude Code terminal. Where will it also be available on the same computer without another installation?
options: In every cloud session run from a browser, because plugins follow the user account
In any teammate's terminal, because user scope shares plugins across the organization
Only in the terminal session where the command was run, until it is restarted
In the desktop app's local sessions and the VS Code extension, but not in cloud sessions
questions.explanation: The local surfaces read the same settings files, so a user-scope plugin is shared among the terminal, the desktop app's local sessions and the VS Code extension on that machine. A cloud session does not load the plugins in your local settings, user scope applies to one person rather than a team, and the install persists beyond a single terminal session.
questions.whyTested: How configuration applies across Claude Code interfaces.

questions.question: Because prompts are plain text, tuning a Claude application can safely be treated as a one-time design phase finished before the first release.
questions.explanation: Model behavior, inputs and models themselves change, so prompts need measured, repeated iteration: evals on each change, monitoring after release, and migrations when models are deprecated.

questions.question: A team upgrades a ticket-classification service to Claude Opus 5.5. Every request now fails with a 400 invalid_request_error, and the only change was the model ID. The request still sets temperature to 0 to keep labels stable. What is the BEST fix?
options: Send the same temperature value inside the output_config object, where newer models expect all of their tuning settings
Replace temperature with top_k set to 1, which forces the single most likely token at every step of the reply
Remove the sampling parameters and get stable labels from clear instructions, varied examples and a constrained output format
Keep the request unchanged and retry each failure, because a 400 on a newly released model is usually transient
questions.explanation: Claude Opus 5.5, like Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5 and Fable 5.1, rejects any non-default temperature, top_p or top_k with a 400, so the parameters have to go. Consistency now comes from prompt design (clear instructions, varied examples), a constrained output such as structured outputs, and the effort setting. top_k is rejected as well, output_config has no sampling section, and a 400 is a request error that retrying cannot fix. Even temperature 0 never gave fully repeatable text, so tests and pipelines should tolerate variation.
questions.whyTested: LLM fundamentals: sampling parameters and breaking changes between model releases.

questions.question: A unit test asks Claude to summarize a fixed support ticket and asserts that the reply equals a stored string. It passes on some runs and fails on others although no code changed. What is the BEST way to fix the test?
options: Call the model twice inside the test and pass only when the two replies come back word for word identical to each other
Re-run the failing test up to ten times and accept the build as soon as one run happens to match the string
Set temperature to 0 so that the stored string is reproduced exactly on every run of the suite
Assert what must hold for any good summary, such as required facts and a length limit, or grade it with a rubric
questions.explanation: Output from a language model varies from call to call, and even temperature 0 does not make it fully repeatable (current models also reject non-default sampling values). Tests should check properties that must hold, such as facts, format, schema and length, or use a rubric grader. Comparing two replies or retrying until one matches still demands identical wording and only hides the flakiness.
questions.whyTested: Non-determinism of LLM outputs and how to test around it.

questions.question: A developer runs Claude Sonnet 5.5 at xhigh effort on a hard analysis task and sets max_tokens to 1,500 to keep answers short. Many responses stop with stop_reason max_tokens and contain little or no answer text, even though the thinking display is set to omitted. What explains this, and what is the BEST fix?
options: Omitted thinking is still generated but billed as input rather than output, so set the display to summarized to release those tokens
Hidden thinking still counts toward max_tokens, so raise the ceiling and control cost with effort and a request for brevity
The xhigh level allocates its own separate token budget, so the truncation must have come from the network layer
Streaming is switched off, so turning streaming on removes the output ceiling for long answers
questions.explanation: Thinking is billed as output and counts against max_tokens whether or not the text is returned; a display of omitted only hides it. At high effort the reasoning can use up a small ceiling before the visible answer starts. Raise max_tokens (the docs suggest large values at high effort levels), and manage spend through effort and by asking for a concise answer. Display settings change what you see, not what is counted; effort is a soft signal, not a separate allowance; streaming does not change the ceiling.
questions.whyTested: Thinking token accounting and the link between effort and max_tokens.

questions.question: Code written for an earlier model enables reasoning with thinking type enabled and budget_tokens set to 10,000. After the team switches to Claude Opus 5.5, the API returns a 400 error for this field. What is the MOST appropriate change?
options: Remove the manual budget, let adaptive thinking run, tune its depth with effort, and keep max_tokens as the hard ceiling
Raise budget_tokens to the largest value the model allows, so that the request is no longer treated as invalid by the validation layer of the API
Send thinking type disabled to switch reasoning off, since the budget field is no longer needed at all
Add the extended-thinking beta header to the request so that the budget field is accepted again by the model
questions.explanation: Manual extended thinking (type enabled with budget_tokens) is not accepted on current models. They use adaptive thinking, which is always on for Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1, and effort is the control for how much it reasons; max_tokens stays the strict ceiling. A larger budget does not make the type valid, Opus 5.5 rejects thinking disabled with a 400 as well, and the old mode has been removed from these models, so no header brings it back.
questions.whyTested: Extended versus adaptive thinking, and migration breaking changes.

questions.question: A team sets effort to low on Claude Opus 5.5 hoping replies never exceed 300 tokens, yet some replies reach 900 tokens. How should the requirement be met?
options: Move effort to max, because the highest level follows length instructions most strictly of all the levels
Turn on fast mode, which limits how many tokens a reply can contain in return for a premium price
Treat effort as a soft signal: ask for the length needed in the prompt and set max_tokens as the hard ceiling
Lower the temperature, since random sampling is what lets some replies run much longer than others
questions.explanation: Effort is a behavioral signal, not a strict token budget: lower levels tend to produce terser output but give no guarantee. For a bound, state the length in the prompt (sentence or paragraph limits work better than word counts) and set max_tokens as the strict ceiling, remembering that a reply cut off at the ceiling may be incomplete. A higher effort level spends more, current models reject non-default temperature, and fast mode speeds up generation without limiting it.
questions.whyTested: Effort levels versus hard limits in token budgeting.

questions.question: A ticket router prompted with instructions only returns labels in inconsistent shapes ('Billing', 'billing issue', 'BILL') and often confuses refunds with billing questions. Which prompting change is MOST likely to fix both problems?
options: Add three to five varied examples in separate tags, with exact labels, including a refund versus billing edge case
Raise effort to max so the model spends much longer deciding which of the labels fits the ticket
Add one example of a billing ticket so that the model has a format to copy for all of the other categories
Put a line in capital letters at the top of the prompt demanding that the exact label is always used, with no variations at all
questions.explanation: Multi-shot prompting with several varied, relevant examples teaches format and edge-case handling at once. One example can fix the format but invites the model to copy its quirks and says nothing about the confusing pair. Capitals add emphasis that newer models tend to over-apply, and more reasoning does not tell the model what the label vocabulary is. (If the labels are a fixed set, a constrained output format also guarantees the shape.)
questions.whyTested: Zero-shot, single-shot and multi-shot prompting.

questions.question: Last quarter a team estimated costs by assuming about 3.5 characters per token. After moving the same prompts to Claude Opus 5.5, bills run roughly 30 percent above that estimate, although request volume and prompt text are unchanged. What is the MOST likely explanation and best next step?
options: Output tokens are billed at the input rate on newer models, so the cost model should drop its output term entirely and count input tokens only
The newer tokenizer produces more tokens for the same text, so recount with the token counting endpoint on the target model
Opus 5.5 silently adds a hidden system prompt to every API request, so ask support to remove it from the account
Prompt caching was switched off during the upgrade, so enable it again to restore last quarter's bill
questions.explanation: Claude 4.7 and later models use a tokenizer that yields roughly 30 percent more tokens for the same text, so counts, limits and bills measured on an older model must be re-baselined. The token counting endpoint takes the target model ID. The API adds no hidden system prompt, output tokens are still priced well above input tokens, and an upgrade never switches caching off.
questions.whyTested: Tokens, tokenizer changes and cost estimation.

questions.question: A voice assistant on Claude Opus 5.5 streams its answers. Profiling shows the first token arrives after about 400 ms, but a 600-token answer then takes about 12 seconds to finish. The team can pay a premium for speed. Which option addresses the actual bottleneck?
options: Raise max_tokens so that the model has room to finish the long answer more quickly
Add prompt caching to the system prompt, which shortens the wait before the first token appears
Enable fast mode on a model that supports it, which raises output tokens per second at premium pricing
Submit the requests through the Message Batches API, which gives higher throughput for large volumes
questions.explanation: Latency has two parts: time to first token, driven by prompt length, model and any up-front reasoning, and generation speed in output tokens per second. The first token is already quick here, so generation speed is the bottleneck. Fast mode (a research preview on some Opus models) serves the same model at up to about 2.5 times the output speed for a higher price; it does not shorten the wait before the first token. Caching targets that first part, batch processing trades speed for a discount and cannot be combined with fast mode, and max_tokens is only a ceiling.
questions.whyTested: Fast mode, and the difference between time to first token and output speed.

questions.question: A summarization endpoint takes about 9 seconds per call. Each prompt has around 2,000 tokens, but the model writes about 1,500 tokens and the product needs only a three-sentence summary. Which change gives the BIGGEST latency improvement?
options: Instruct the model to answer in three sentences, because output is generated token by token and its length drives the wait
Switch the call to the Message Batches API so the work is handled by a more efficient queue
Place a cache breakpoint on the prompt, because cache reads make every generated token arrive faster
Cut the 2,000-token prompt in half, because input and output tokens take the same time to process and the prompt is the larger of the two
questions.explanation: Generation is autoregressive: the model produces one token after another, so after the first token, response time grows with output length. Asking for the short form (sentence or paragraph limits work better than word counts) removes about 1,400 generated tokens. Input is processed before the first token and mostly affects the time to first token, so halving it saves little. Caching reduces input cost and the first-token wait but not generation, and batch processing is for latency-tolerant work, not for faster answers.
questions.whyTested: Next-token generation: why output length dominates latency.

questions.question: A Node service calls the Messages API with hand-built HTTP requests. Engineers have repeatedly fixed missing version headers, absent retries on 429 and 5xx responses, and inconsistent timeouts. What is the MOST maintainable improvement?
options: Send every request through the Message Batches API, which handles retries on the server side for the caller
Write a shared helper around the raw HTTP calls and ask engineers to use it for every new call from now on, checked in code review
Move the calls onto a WebSocket connection, which keeps the session open and avoids the need for retry logic
Adopt the official SDK, which sets the headers, retries transient errors with backoff and provides timeouts and typed errors
questions.explanation: Client SDKs are thin wrappers around the REST API that already supply authentication, the required anthropic-version header, retries for connection errors, 429 and 5xx responses (two by default, honoring retry-after), timeouts, streaming helpers and error classes. A homemade helper recreates all of that and tends to drift. The Messages API is not a WebSocket interface, and the Batches API is asynchronous bulk processing rather than a reliability layer.
questions.whyTested: Technical fundamentals: SDKs that wrap REST APIs.

questions.question: A chat web app must let users keep typing and cancel while a reply is still streaming. A developer proposes connecting the browser straight to the Claude API over a WebSocket. Which architecture is the BEST fit?
options: Browser polling of the Messages API every second to fetch the partial text of the reply that is in progress
One non-streaming request held open until the full reply is ready, with cancellation handled by closing the tab
A WebSocket from the browser directly to the Claude API itself, with the API key stored in the page's JavaScript
A WebSocket between the browser and your own backend, which streams from the Messages API and relays the text
questions.explanation: The Messages API streams over server-sent events on an ordinary HTTP response and has no WebSocket endpoint, and a browser must never hold the API key. A two-way channel between the browser and your own backend lets the user send messages and cancel while the backend consumes the event stream with the SDK and relays the text. There is no endpoint for polling a partial reply, and a non-streaming call returns only when it is complete.
questions.whyTested: Technical fundamentals: where WebSockets fit and how Claude streams.

questions.question: A platform lets customers choose any Claude model. Some models accept thinking set to disabled and others return 400, and the lineup changes every few months. How should the code decide whether to send that setting?
options: Keep a hard-coded table of model names and their settings in the code and update it by hand after every new release
Always send the setting, catch the 400 and retry without it on every single request
Assume each new model accepts exactly the settings of its predecessor and test only when users complain
Read the capabilities from the Models API and check whether disabling thinking is supported, rather than matching names
questions.explanation: The Models API reports each model's capabilities, including whether thinking can be disabled, along with its maximum input and output sizes, so code can check support at runtime. A hand-maintained table goes stale, catching a 400 on every call wastes requests and hides the design flaw, and assuming parity is exactly what breaks across releases, as when disabling thinking is accepted on one model and rejected on another.
questions.whyTested: Model capabilities and breaking behavior changes across releases.

questions.question: A legal-research tool sends whole case files to Claude. The largest files, over a million tokens, now fail with a 400 'prompt is too long', while smaller files work. Prompt caching is already enabled. What is the BEST way to handle the oversized files?
options: Send only the relevant parts, using retrieval or summarization, because input beyond the window is rejected however it is cached
Add more cache breakpoints, because cached tokens do not count against the context window of the model
Set the thinking display to omitted so that reasoning tokens are removed from the window before the call
Raise max_tokens so that the response budget leaves enough space for the very long input in the window, which is shared with the reply
questions.explanation: The context window is a hard limit on what a request can hold, and input alone beyond it is rejected with a 400. Prompt caching changes the price of repeated prefixes, not whether those tokens occupy the window. max_tokens only limits the output, and hiding thinking changes what you see, not how much input you send. Reduce the input: retrieve relevant passages, summarize or compact, or split the job across calls.
questions.whyTested: Context windows: capacity, and why caching does not extend it.

questions.question: A fintech routes 40 million short support messages a month into twelve categories and needs a decision in well under a second. A prototype exists, but quality has not been measured. Which approach to model selection is BEST?
options: Start with Claude Haiku 5.5, measure accuracy on a labeled sample of real messages, and move up only if the evals show a gap
Choose Claude Sonnet 5.5 for every message, because the middle tier is the safest default for any workload
Start with Claude Fable 5.1 so that accuracy is as high as possible, then see whether the bill is acceptable
Start with Claude Opus 5.5 at max effort and lower the effort only if finance complains about the cost
questions.explanation: High-volume, latency-sensitive, well-defined work such as classification and routing is the case for efficiency-first selection: begin with the fastest, cheapest tier (Haiku 5.5), test on your own data and upgrade only for capability gaps the tests expose. Starting at the top is the capability-first path, suited to complex reasoning and high-stakes accuracy, and at this volume it would burn cost and latency before anything is known. A default tier chosen without measurement is a guess.
questions.whyTested: Opus versus Sonnet versus Haiku use cases, and efficiency-first selection.

questions.question: A research team's multi-hour agent reads hundreds of filings and writes a cited memo. On their eval set, Claude Opus 5.5 at xhigh effort passes 71 percent of tasks against a 90 percent target, and prompt improvements have stalled. What is the BEST next step?
options: Run the same eval set on Claude Fable 5.1, built for long-horizon work, and compare pass rate and cost per completed task
Lower effort to low on Opus 5.5 so that the model becomes more decisive about which filings to cite
Reduce the target to the 71 percent that the current model achieves and ship the agent as it stands
Switch to Claude Haiku 5.5, because the fastest tier lets the team iterate on the stalled prompt more quickly and run many more experiments
questions.explanation: This is the documented capability-first path: start strong, optimize prompts, and if evals at xhigh or max effort still fall short on demanding reasoning or long-horizon agentic work, move to Claude Fable 5.1, then confirm the gain and its cost on your own evals (and check its data-retention requirements). A smaller model or lower effort cuts capability on a task that is already failing, and lowering the target is not an engineering fix.
questions.whyTested: Capability-first selection and when to move up a tier.

questions.question: A document-analysis feature runs on Claude Opus 5.5 and meets its quality bar, but spend is 40 percent over budget. Engineers want to move all traffic to Claude Haiku 5.5 right away. What should the team do FIRST?
options: Route a tenth of live traffic to Haiku 5.5 with no evals and watch the complaint rate for a week
Halve max_tokens so that every response is shorter and therefore cheaper to produce
Delete the system prompt to cut input tokens and keep the model and everything else unchanged
Run an effort sweep on the existing eval set, lowering effort step by step on Opus 5.5 while the pass rate holds
questions.explanation: The docs note that tuning effort is often a better lever than switching models: lower effort cuts thinking, tool calls and answer length while the model stays familiar, and a sweep on your own evals shows the cheapest level that still passes. Testing on customers instead of evals is risky; max_tokens only truncates a response and does not make the model economize (truncated output is still billed); deleting the system prompt would destroy the behavior the evals confirm.
questions.whyTested: Tuning effort before switching models: quality, latency and cost tradeoffs.

questions.question: A team wants to move a contract-clause extraction pipeline from Claude Sonnet 5.5 to a cheaper tier. Which evidence BEST supports the decision?
options: A third party's published ranking of the model tiers on general coding benchmarks
Pass rates and cost per completed task for both models on an evaluation set of the team's own contracts and edge cases
The list price per million tokens of each model, since the cheaper one is cheaper for any pipeline, however many retries it needs
A manual check of five short, clean contracts that the engineers picked themselves
questions.explanation: Anthropic's guidance: build benchmark tests specific to your use case (a good evaluation set is the most important step), test with your actual prompts and data, compare accuracy, quality and edge-case handling, then weigh cost. Per-token price ignores retries and extra turns, generic benchmarks may not resemble your contracts, and five hand-picked clean examples cannot reveal edge-case failures.
questions.whyTested: Model selection tradeoffs decided with your own evals.

questions.question: On a team's eval set, a smaller-tier model costs $0.30 per attempt and passes 40 percent of tasks; a larger-tier model costs $0.60 per attempt and passes 90 percent. Failed attempts are discarded and the task is attempted again until one passes. Which statement about expected cost per completed task is correct?
options: The smaller tier is cheaper at about $0.12 per task against $0.54, because cost scales with the pass rate
The two tiers cost the same, because the higher price of the larger tier is exactly offset by its pass rate
The larger tier is cheaper: about $0.67 per completed task against $0.75 for the smaller tier
The smaller tier is cheaper, because $0.30 is half of $0.60 whatever the pass rates turn out to be
questions.explanation: Expected attempts per solved task are 1 divided by the pass rate, so cost per completed task is cost per attempt divided by pass rate: 0.30 / 0.40 = $0.75 for the smaller tier and 0.60 / 0.90, about $0.67, for the larger. Comparing per-token or per-attempt prices ignores failures and retries, and multiplying cost by the pass rate gets the relationship backwards.
questions.whyTested: Cost per completed task rather than price per token.

questions.question: After switching an extraction service to Claude Sonnet 5.5, every request that forces a specific tool through tool_choice returns a 400, although it worked on the previous model. The team still needs tool inputs that always match the schema. What is the BEST change?
options: Use tool_choice auto and turn on strict tool use for the tool, or request a JSON schema through structured outputs
Keep forcing the tool and wrap the call in a retry loop until the 400 stops appearing
Add a prefilled assistant turn that begins the tool call, so that the model has to continue it and cannot choose another tool
Set temperature to 0 so that the model reliably picks the only tool that is available to it
questions.explanation: Forced tool use (tool_choice of type any or tool) is rejected on Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1. The supported route is tool_choice auto, which the API accepts, combined with strict tool use so that tool inputs are schema-valid, or structured outputs when the reply itself must follow a schema. Prefill is rejected on Claude 4.6 and later, non-default temperature is rejected on the current models, and a 400 is a request error that retries cannot cure.
questions.whyTested: Breaking behavior changes across releases (forced tool use).

questions.question: A healthcare analytics company has a zero-data-retention arrangement with Anthropic. Its evals show only Claude Fable 5.1 meeting the quality bar on a hard reasoning workload. What should the team do BEFORE building on it?
options: Rule out Fable 5.1 and drop to Haiku 5.5 so that the retention arrangement stays untouched
Check with compliance and Anthropic, because Fable models require 30-day retention and zero retention is unavailable for them
Enable Fable 5.1 as is, because zero data retention applies automatically to every model on the account, so no further check is needed
Route the requests through the Message Batches API, which never stores any request data on the server
questions.explanation: Fable and Mythos models are Covered Models: they require 30-day data retention, so zero data retention is not available for them unless Anthropic expressly authorizes it, and an organization without the required setting can see requests rejected with a 400. This is a model-selection constraint to resolve first, by accepting the retention terms, seeking an exception, or tuning a model that fits the arrangement. The Batch API is stateful and not zero-retention eligible, and dropping to a much weaker tier ignores the quality bar the evals established.
questions.whyTested: Model selection constraints beyond capability, such as data retention.

questions.question: A team runs a coding agent on a smaller executor model and gives it an advisor tool backed by a stronger model, hoping to cut cost while keeping quality on hard decisions. After a week, cost is down but hard-case quality has not improved. What should they check FIRST?
options: Whether the advisor model's temperature is lower than the executor's on each consultation
How many cache breakpoints the executor's system prompt contains and where they are placed
How often the executor actually calls the advisor at hard decisions, which is the consult rate
Whether the advisor's context window is larger than the context window of the executor
questions.explanation: The advisor pattern helps only when the executor consults the stronger model at the moments that matter. If it rarely does, the team pays for the extra tool definition (roughly a thousand prompt tokens on every request) and gets the smaller model's quality. Measure the consult rate, adjust the instructions, and compare the result with simply raising effort on one model. Sampling temperature is not adjustable on current models, and caching or window size does not decide whether the executor asks for help.
