questions.whyTested: Multi-model strategies (executor and advisor) and how to evaluate them.

questions.question: A support assistant sends the same 10,000-token policy prefix with every request, and it is sent 11 times within one five-minute window. Assume a five-minute cache write costs 1.25 times the base input price and a cache read costs 0.1 times it. How does the cost of the prefix compare with sending it uncached each time?
options: About one and a quarter times as much, since every request pays the write price
About one tenth as much, since all 11 requests are billed as cache reads
About one fifth as much, since one write is followed by ten cheap reads
About nine tenths as much, since a cache read saves only ten percent
questions.explanation: Uncached: 11 x 10,000 = 110,000 token-equivalents. Cached: one write at 1.25 x 10,000 = 12,500 plus ten reads at 0.1 x 10,000 = 1,000 each, so 10,000, for a total of 22,500, about 20 percent. Only the first request pays the write premium, and it does pay it, so not every request is a read; the later requests are not charged the write price; and a read costs a tenth of the base price, a 90 percent saving per read.
questions.whyTested: Cost modeling with prompt caching multipliers.

questions.question: A tax-advice assistant caches a 30,000-token regulation excerpt. Users typically pause between 8 and 40 minutes between questions. The default five-minute cache lifetime is in use and cache reads are usually zero. What is the BEST change?
options: Move the excerpt below the user's message so that the cache treats it as the newest content
Keep the five-minute lifetime and send a dummy request every four minutes, around the clock, to refresh each idle user's entry
Use the one-hour cache lifetime, accepting its higher write price, so that the prefix survives the users' pauses
Remove cache_control completely, since caching is never worthwhile when users pause between questions
questions.explanation: A cache entry lives for five minutes from its last use, and each read refreshes it. With pauses of 8 to 40 minutes the entry has expired before the next turn, so every turn rewrites the prefix at the write price. The one-hour lifetime (written at twice the base input price, and paying off after two reads at the standard read rate) fits gaps between five minutes and an hour. Keep-alive pings add paid traffic for every idle user, moving content after the user message breaks the required prefix order of tools, system, then messages, and caching stays worthwhile whenever reuse within the lifetime is likely.
questions.whyTested: Prompt caching lifetimes and cache check-pointing.

questions.question: An assistant keeps one long conversation per user. To save money, the team sets effort to low on simple turns and high on complex ones, changing the top-level value from turn to turn. Cache reads fall sharply and spend rises. What is the MOST likely cause and best remedy?
options: Cache entries are keyed to the exact wording of each user message, so normalize every message before it is sent
Each effort level is billed as a separate product, so the extra spend is simply the price of using two levels
Low effort disables prompt caching on that turn, so raise the minimum effort to medium for every turn of every conversation in the product
Changing effort invalidates the cached messages; keep it fixed per conversation or use per-message effort, which keeps the cache
questions.explanation: Effort, like the thinking configuration, speed, tool_choice and images, is rendered into the prompt, so changing the top-level value starts a new cache prefix at the message layer and forces the conversation to be rewritten at the write price. Hold it constant, change it at a natural break such as right after a compaction, or use per-message effort (beta), which carries the change in a system message and leaves the cached prefix intact. Low effort does not disable caching, entries match on exact prefix content rather than on wording, and effort levels are not separate billing products.
questions.whyTested: Cache invalidation and its interaction with effort.

questions.question: A team picks Claude Haiku 5.5 as the cheapest model for summarizing long reports; each request carries about 300,000 tokens of input. Before projecting costs, what should they check?
options: That requests above 200,000 tokens are rejected on Haiku 5.5, so the reports must be split in advance
That Haiku 5.5 charges more once a prompt passes 100,000 tokens, so compare cost per completed task with Sonnet 5.5 at this length
That thinking on Haiku 5.5 is billed as input, which changes the arithmetic for very long prompts
Nothing, because every current model bills a 1M-token request at the same per-token rate as a short one, so the lowest list price decides
questions.explanation: Current models offer a 1M-token window, and most bill a long request at the same per-token rate as a short one. Claude Haiku 5.5 is the exception: it is priced by prompt length, and a prompt over 100,000 tokens (counting cache reads and writes) pays higher prices. A lower list price therefore does not guarantee the lowest cost at this size; compare cost per completed task at the real prompt length. The window applies to Haiku as well, and thinking is billed as output on every model.
questions.whyTested: Cost modeling: long-context pricing and model tradeoffs.

questions.question: Finance wants monthly spend broken down by product feature and by environment, and engineering wants to see cache efficiency per model. Which setup BEST supports this?
options: Separate workspaces per feature and environment, queried through the Usage and Cost API with an admin credential, grouped by workspace and model
One organization-wide key shared by every service, with each developer recording token counts by hand in a spreadsheet
Parsing the monthly invoice and dividing its total by the number of requests that each team believes it sent
Character-count estimates stored next to every request and summed per feature at the end of each month
questions.explanation: The Usage and Cost API reports token usage and cost in time buckets that can be filtered and grouped by model, workspace, API key and service tier, which also supports cache-efficiency analysis; it needs an admin-level credential rather than a normal workspace key. Giving each feature and environment its own workspace makes attribution a simple group-by (and isolates limits and caches). Hand-kept counts, invoice splitting and character-based estimates are inaccurate and cannot show cache or model differences.
questions.whyTested: Token usage tracking and cost attribution.

questions.question: An autonomous agent makes dozens of tool calls. It sometimes exhausts its output allowance in the middle of a step and leaves work half done. The team wants the model to pace itself and wrap up gracefully within a total allowance for the whole loop. Which control fits BEST?
options: A larger context window, because running out of window is the only way a loop can end early
A smaller max_tokens, so that the model notices the limit and economizes as it works
A higher effort level, because thorough models always finish before they reach any limit
A task budget, an advisory allowance for the whole agentic loop that the model sees as a running countdown
questions.explanation: max_tokens caps a single response and is invisible to the model, so reaching it truncates the work mid-step (and the discarded turn is still billed). A task budget (beta) is advisory: the model sees a countdown across the whole loop and can prioritize and finish cleanly. Effort scales thoroughness per step rather than total length, and the window size is unrelated to the allowance.
questions.whyTested: Token budgeting for agentic loops.

questions.question: An internal tool resends a 15,000-token style guide and tool list with every request, thousands of times a day, to a model that already meets its quality targets. Which optimization saves the MOST with NO quality tradeoff?
options: Move to the next smaller model tier and accept the small drop in accuracy that the team measured on its own evals
Cap max_tokens at a small number so that responses are cut off early
Enable prompt caching on the stable prefix so that repeated reads cost a fraction of the normal input price
Lower effort one level for every request, regardless of how hard each one is, and accept some loss
questions.explanation: Caching cuts the cost and latency of repeated input without changing what the model produces, so the docs count it among the free wins and it is usually the largest. A smaller tier, a lower effort and output caps are tradeoffs: each can cost quality, and a tight max_tokens truncates replies, wasting the tokens already generated.
questions.whyTested: Cost optimization levers: caching versus tradeoffs.

questions.question: Which TWO statements about getting consistent output from Claude Opus 5.5 are accurate? (Choose two.)
options: Raising top_k widens the pool of candidate tokens, which makes repeated runs of one request more alike
Prefilling the opening words of the reply is the recommended way to lock its wording
A JSON schema supplied through structured outputs removes variation in the shape of the reply, though not in its wording
Non-default temperature, top_p and top_k are rejected with a 400, so consistency comes from prompts, examples and output constraints
Setting temperature to 0 makes repeated identical requests return byte-identical text on every run
questions.explanation: Current models reject non-default sampling parameters, so consistency is engineered through clear instructions, varied examples, structured outputs (a schema-guaranteed shape) and effort. Structured outputs fix the form, not the wording. Temperature 0 never guaranteed identical text, a wider top_k would increase variety rather than reduce it (and is rejected anyway), and prefill is rejected with a 400 on Claude 4.6 and later models.
questions.whyTested: Sampling, non-determinism and output consistency.

questions.question: Which TWO statements about thinking tokens on current Claude models are accurate? (Choose two.)
options: Setting the display to omitted removes the cost of the reasoning from the bill
They are free whenever the prompt prefix was served from the cache
They are billed as output tokens even when the response omits the thinking text
They count toward max_tokens, so a low ceiling at high effort can leave no room for the visible answer
A summarized display is billed at the length of the summary rather than the reasoning that was generated
questions.explanation: Thinking is billed as output and counts against max_tokens whether or not the text is returned. A summarized display is a readable summary produced separately; you are charged for the full thinking tokens, not the summary. Caching affects input pricing only, and omitting the display changes only what is returned (it can improve time to first text token when streaming), not what is billed.
questions.whyTested: Thinking token accounting.

questions.question: Which THREE changes between two requests invalidate a cached prefix that covers the tools, the system prompt and the conversation so far? (Choose three.)
options: Appending a new user message after the last cache breakpoint of the conversation
Changing the top-level effort value between the two requests
Sending the next request 90 seconds after the last one, inside the five-minute lifetime
Inserting a per-request timestamp into the system prompt
Editing the wording of one tool's description
questions.explanation: The cache is a prefix in the order tools, system, messages, matched exactly, and a change at one level invalidates that level and everything after it. Tool edits clear everything, a system edit clears the system and messages layers, and effort, thinking, speed, tool_choice or image changes clear the messages layer. New content after the last breakpoint is simply new input, and a read inside the lifetime refreshes the entry rather than invalidating it.
questions.whyTested: Cache invalidation and check-pointing.

questions.question: A team wants to cut the bill of a stable workload without lowering answer quality. Which TWO measures qualify? (Choose two.)
options: Set max_tokens to a small value so that replies stop early
Move every request to the next smaller model tier
Lower effort one level across the board without running evals
Send non-urgent work, such as a nightly evaluation run, through the Message Batches API
Cache the large prefix that repeats across requests
questions.explanation: Caching repeated input and batching work that can wait up to 24 hours (half price on input and output) cut cost without changing what the model produces. Moving to a smaller tier, lowering effort and capping output are tradeoffs that may reduce quality, so they need evals first; a tight max_tokens truncates replies and wastes the tokens already generated.
questions.whyTested: Cost optimization: free wins versus tradeoffs.

questions.question: A team is building a pre-launch cost model for a multi-turn assistant that calls tools. Which THREE items belong in the estimate? (Choose three.)
options: Only the length of the user's visible messages, since everything else is free
A flat fee per request that does not depend on the number of tokens
Tool definitions and the tool-use overhead added to every request
Thinking tokens, which are billed at the output rate
The conversation history that is resent as input on every turn
questions.explanation: The Messages API is stateless, so the whole history is sent again each turn and input grows with conversation length; tool definitions, tool_use and tool_result blocks and the special tool-use system prompt all count as input tokens; reasoning is billed as output. Then adjust for cache hits and batch discounts, and recount for the target model's tokenizer. Charging is per token rather than a flat fee, and history, system prompts and tool results are far from free.
questions.whyTested: Cost modeling and token budgeting.

questions.question: A team is moving production code from an older model to Claude Opus 5.5. Which THREE changes should they expect to make? (Choose three.)
options: Add a prefilled assistant message so that the reply is forced to start with an opening brace
Recount prompts with the token counting endpoint, because the tokenizer yields more tokens for the same text
Remove non-default temperature, top_p and top_k values
Send thinking disabled to cut cost on simple requests
Replace manual thinking budgets with adaptive thinking and an effort setting
questions.explanation: Opus 5.5 rejects non-default sampling parameters and the manual budget_tokens mode, and the tokenizer introduced with Claude 4.7 produces roughly 30 percent more tokens for the same text, so counts and cost estimates must be redone. Prefill is rejected on Claude 4.6 and later, and thinking cannot be disabled on Opus 5.5, so both of those would return a 400.
questions.whyTested: Breaking behavior changes across model releases.

questions.question: A nightly job scores 40,000 documents against the same 12,000-token rubric, and the results are needed by morning. Which TWO measures together lower the cost MOST? (Choose two.)
options: Submit the work through the Message Batches API for the half-price discount on input and output
Lower max_tokens to one token for every document in the job
Send the requests synchronously in parallel so that the cache is warm for all of them at once
Put the rubric in a cached prefix with the one-hour lifetime, because the batch and caching discounts stack
Request fast mode for the job so that it finishes earlier, at premium prices
questions.explanation: Batch processing is 50 percent off both input and output and suits work that can wait up to 24 hours; caching a shared prefix stacks with that discount (cache hits inside a batch are best-effort, so the one-hour lifetime is recommended). Parallel synchronous calls get no batch discount, and a cache entry becomes available only after the first response begins, so simultaneous requests may all miss. Fast mode costs a premium and is not available with the Batch API, and a one-token output cannot score anything.
questions.whyTested: Combining batch processing and caching.

questions.question: Setting temperature to 0 guarantees that Claude returns identical text for identical requests.
questions.explanation: Output can vary between calls even with low randomness settings, and current models reject non-default temperature anyway. Tests and pipelines should tolerate variation and validate outputs in code.
questions.whyTested: Non-determinism of LLM outputs.

questions.question: Claude Opus 5.5 accepts thinking type disabled as a way to switch reasoning off for simple requests.
questions.explanation: Adaptive thinking is always on for Opus 5.5 (and Fable 5.1), and sending disabled returns a 400. Lower the effort level to reduce reasoning. Some other models do accept disabling it, which is why code should read capabilities from the Models API.
questions.whyTested: Adaptive thinking support by model.

questions.question: Fast mode raises output speed in tokens per second but does not shorten the wait before the first token appears.
questions.explanation: Fast mode serves the same model with a faster inference setup, up to about 2.5 times the output speed at premium pricing, on some Opus models. Time to first token is driven by prompt length, model choice and up-front reasoning, so shorter prompts and caching address that part.
questions.whyTested: Fast mode and latency components.

questions.question: Prompt caching lowers the price of a repeated prefix, but the cached tokens still count toward the context window.
questions.explanation: Caching changes what you pay and how fast the prefix is processed, not whether the tokens occupy the window. A request whose input exceeds the window is rejected however much of it is cached.
questions.whyTested: Context windows and caching.

questions.question: Writing a prefix to the five-minute cache costs more than sending it uncached, so caching a prompt that is never reused within five minutes raises the bill.
questions.explanation: A five-minute write costs about 1.25 times the base input price and the saving comes only from later reads, at a tenth of the price or less. Without reuse inside the lifetime there are no reads, so you only pay the premium. Check the cache usage fields to confirm hits.
questions.whyTested: Prompt caching economics.

questions.question: On Claude Sonnet 5.5, a 900,000-token request is billed at the same per-token rate as a 9,000-token request.
questions.explanation: The 1M-token window is included at standard pricing on Claude 4.6 and later models. Claude Haiku 5.5 is the exception, because it is priced higher for prompts over 100,000 tokens.
questions.whyTested: Long-context pricing.

questions.question: A smaller model tier always costs less per completed task than a larger tier.
questions.explanation: Cost per completed task includes retries, extra turns and failed attempts. A pricier model that passes more often or finishes in fewer turns can be cheaper per solved task, so measure on your own evals instead of comparing price lists.
questions.whyTested: Cost per completed task.

questions.question: The effort setting also influences tool use: at lower levels Claude tends to make fewer and terser tool calls.
questions.explanation: Effort affects all tokens in a reply, including text, tool calls with their arguments, and thinking when it is active. Lower effort saves cost and time, but on long agent tasks it can mean skipped searches or checks, so validate on evals.
questions.whyTested: Effort levels.

questions.question: All current Claude models share the same default effort level.
questions.explanation: The default is high on most models but medium on Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Haiku 5.5, and setting the default explicitly is the same as omitting the parameter. Set effort explicitly when moving between models and sweep it on your evals.
questions.whyTested: Effort defaults differ by model.

questions.question: A cache breakpoint belongs on the last block that stays identical across the requests meant to share a cache, not on content that changes with every request.
questions.explanation: Cache writes happen only at breakpoints and the prefix up to the breakpoint must match exactly. A breakpoint on a timestamp or on per-request context never matches, so every request pays a fresh write and never reads.
questions.whyTested: Cache check-pointing.

questions.question: A prompt shorter than the minimum cacheable length that carries a cache_control marker is rejected with an error.
questions.explanation: It is processed normally without caching and no error is returned; both cache counts in the usage object show zero. The minimum is 512 tokens on the current models, and padding a prompt that sits just under it with stable content can lower the cost of frequently reused prompts.
questions.whyTested: Minimum cacheable prompt length.

questions.question: Output tokens cost several times more than input tokens on the current models, so asking for a concise reply can save more than trimming the prompt by the same number of tokens.
questions.explanation: Output is priced at five times input on the current models, and in an agent loop the generated text is re-read as input on later turns. Asking for the answer you will actually read is a cheap, effective lever.
questions.whyTested: Output token premium and token budgeting.

questions.question: A support bot gives wrong refund-policy answers in production, but the same prompt text run by hand in the Console workbench gives correct ones. Logs show 200 responses with normal stop reasons. What is the BEST first step to find the cause?
options: Raise max_tokens, since truncated policy text could explain wrong answers even with a normal stop reason
Move to a stronger model tier, since a more capable model answers correctly whatever the request contains and whatever the system prompt says
Capture the exact request body the app sent, replay it unchanged outside the app, and compare it with the hand-built one
Rewrite the system prompt with stricter wording and redeploy it to see whether the answers improve
questions.explanation: When the same words behave differently in two places, suspect what differs in the request, not the model: an application may send a stale or truncated history, drop the system prompt, omit retrieved policy text or name another model. Replaying the logged request verbatim isolates the origin. If the replay reproduces the bad answer, the fault lies in the request content or the model's behavior; if it answers correctly, the integration layer is assembling or handling something differently. A bigger model, more tokens or new wording treat a symptom without evidence, and the normal stop reason already rules out truncation.
questions.whyTested: Problem origin isolation between the integration layer and model output.

questions.question: A research agent sometimes ends a run by saying it could not find an answer. Aggregate dashboards show normal latency, token use and error rates. Which evidence will MOST directly explain why one specific failed run went wrong?
options: The text of the agent's closing message on its own, read without any of the steps that produced it
The average number of output tokens per request across the last thirty days of production traffic
The run's trace, showing each model request, tool call, tool input and tool result in order
The daily count of HTTP 200 responses returned by the model endpoint across all of the customers
questions.explanation: Aggregates hide what happened inside one run. A trace records each step with its inputs, results, timing and status, so you can see a search returning nothing, the same query repeated, a result the model misread, or a handoff missing context, then group runs into failure modes and fix the right layer (tool description, tool output, prompt or context). Averages and success counts cannot localize a failure, and the final text shows only the symptom.
questions.whyTested: Trace analysis to identify failure modes.

questions.question: A pipeline extracts the invoice total, due date and vendor ID from 5,000 test invoices whose correct values are known. The team needs a fast, repeatable score after every prompt change. Which grading approach is BEST?
options: Code-based grading that compares each extracted field with its known value after normalizing formats
An LLM judge that reads each extraction and rates how good it looks on a scale of 1 to 5 for every field
Embedding similarity between the extracted text and the full text of the invoice
Human reviewers who read all 5,000 outputs after every prompt change
questions.explanation: When the right answer has a checkable form, code-based grading is the fastest, most reliable and most scalable method, and exact values call for exact comparison. A rating judge adds cost, variance and fuzziness where none is needed, human review is slow and expensive, and similarity scores cannot tell a correct total from a close-looking wrong one. Keep LLM grading for open-ended qualities such as tone, and use humans to validate graders on samples.
questions.whyTested: Choosing a grading method when designing evals.

questions.question: A developer edits the system prompt to fix a complaint and checks three conversations by hand before releasing. The next week another behavior is found broken, and nobody can say when it broke. Which practice would have caught this?
options: Running the full evaluation set on every prompt change and comparing its scores with the stored baseline before merging
Freezing the prompt permanently so that later edits cannot introduce side effects
Asking the model after each edit whether its behavior is still correct for all of the earlier cases, and trusting its own answer
Waiting for support tickets to arrive and treating the ticket volume as the quality measure
questions.explanation: A prompt change can fix one case and break others. A regression run over a fixed, representative set, wired into the delivery pipeline and gated on scores, catches such side effects before release and shows which edit caused them. The model's own assurance is not a measurement, freezing the prompt blocks improvement, and tickets are a lagging indicator (though real failures should be added to the set as new cases).
questions.whyTested: Regression evaluation and monitoring production quality.

questions.question: In a long conversation, cache_read_input_tokens falls to zero on turn 6 although the team believes it only appends messages. They pass the previous response's ID in the diagnostics field, and the reply reports that the system prompt differed from the previous request. What is the MOST likely cause and fix?
options: A timestamp or request ID is inserted into the system prompt; make it constant and put dynamic data after the breakpoint
The five-minute lifetime expired between turns, so the one-hour lifetime has to be enabled from the first turn of the conversation
The conversation grew past the context window, so the oldest messages have to be compacted or dropped
Cache reads are billed separately and are left out of the usage object, so the zero is only a reporting quirk
questions.explanation: Cache diagnostics compares consecutive requests and reports the first place they diverged. A system-prompt difference means the system parameter changed between turns, typically because a timestamp, request ID or other per-request value was interpolated into it, so the prefix misses every time. Make the system prompt a constant and move dynamic data into a user message after the breakpoint. An expired entry would show no divergence reason with low reads, exceeding the window produces a 400 rather than a cache miss, and cache reads are reported in the usage object.
questions.whyTested: Debugging cache misses with cache diagnostics.

questions.question: A pipeline's replies suddenly fail schema validation after a deploy that changed only application code. Which TWO checks BEST help decide whether the integration layer or the model's output is at fault? (Choose two.)
options: Add more instructions about valid JSON to the prompt and redeploy immediately
Inspect the stop_reason and the raw response body of the failing calls before any parsing step runs
Switch the pipeline to a different model tier to see whether the failures disappear
Replay a logged request from before the deploy and one from after it, and compare the two request bodies field by field
Raise the sampling temperature to see whether the failures become random
questions.explanation: Comparing request bodies from before and after the deploy shows whether the application now sends something different (history, system prompt, max_tokens, schema), and the raw response with its stop_reason shows whether the output was truncated or refused before your code touched it. Together they separate integration faults from model behavior. Changing temperature is not supported on current models and tells you nothing, rewriting the prompt treats a symptom before the cause is known, and switching tiers changes two things at once.
questions.whyTested: Problem origin isolation and error type identification.

questions.question: Before an LLM-based grader is trusted at scale, its verdicts should be checked against human judgments on a sample.
questions.explanation: LLM grading is fast and flexible, but the docs advise testing its reliability first and then scaling: write a detailed rubric, constrain the output (for example correct or incorrect, or a 1 to 5 scale), and compare with human labels on a sample.
questions.whyTested: LLM-based grading in evals.

questions.question: An evaluation set should contain only typical, well-formed inputs so that its scores stay stable between runs.
questions.explanation: Evals should mirror the real task distribution and include edge cases such as irrelevant, overlong, ambiguous or harmful inputs. A set without them reports comfortable scores while real traffic fails.
questions.whyTested: Designing evals.

questions.question: A repository has test files named *.test.ts spread across forty folders. The team wants Claude Code to follow specific testing conventions whenever it works with those files, without loading them for unrelated work. What is the BEST setup?
options: A custom slash command that developers must remember to run before any test-related task
A rule file in .claude/rules with a paths pattern of **/*.test.ts, so it loads only when a matching file is used
A paragraph in the root CLAUDE.md, which loads at the start of every session whatever the task, and costs context each time
A copy of the testing conventions in a CLAUDE.md inside each of the forty folders
questions.explanation: Rules in .claude/rules can carry paths frontmatter with glob patterns; such a rule loads when Claude reads or edits a matching file, so the conventions arrive when relevant and cost nothing otherwise. Forty copies of a CLAUDE.md drift apart and load only per folder, a root paragraph loads in every session, and a manual command depends on people remembering it. If a convention must be enforced rather than followed, use a hook or a permission rule.
questions.whyTested: Claude Code components: rules and the CLAUDE.md hierarchy.

questions.question: A CI step runs Claude Code non-interactively to review a diff, and a later script must read a list of issues as a field it can parse and validate. Which invocation is BEST?
options: claude -p with --output-format stream-json, then wait for the process to exit and parse its first line
claude -p with --output-format json and a --json-schema describing the list, then read the structured_output field
claude -p with default text output, then extract the issues from the prose with regular expressions
An interactive session whose terminal output is recorded and parsed after the review finishes
questions.explanation: In print mode, --output-format json returns a single JSON object with the result, session ID and usage, and adding --json-schema places a conforming answer in the structured_output field, which a script can parse and validate. Regular expressions over prose are brittle. stream-json emits one event per line with the result at the end, so its first line is not the answer and it suits live progress rather than a single parse, and interactive capture is not a pipeline interface.
questions.whyTested: Headless mode and output formats.

questions.question: A developer works in a disposable dev container and is tired of approving every test run and file edit, but the organization still wants a safeguard against actions that stray from the request. Which permission mode fits BEST?
options: Plan mode, which lets Claude edit files and run commands freely while it drafts a plan
bypassPermissions, which skips the prompts but keeps a safety classifier reviewing each action
acceptEdits, which approves every shell command and network call automatically as well as file edits, whatever the command or its target
Auto mode, where a background classifier reviews actions like shell commands and network requests against the request
questions.explanation: Auto mode removes routine prompts while a separate classifier checks that actions such as shell commands and network requests align with the request, which fits a team that wants fewer prompts and still a guard. It reduces prompts but does not guarantee safety, and administrators can disable it in managed settings. bypassPermissions skips prompts with no such review and belongs only in isolated environments, acceptEdits approves file edits and common filesystem commands only, and plan mode is read-only exploration without source edits.
questions.whyTested: Claude Code features: auto mode and permission modes.

questions.question: Midway through a long Claude Code session, a developer wants to try a risky alternative design while keeping the current conversation intact to return to. What is the BEST approach?
options: Run /branch, or resume with --fork-session, to copy the conversation into a new session and experiment there
Run /compact so the history becomes a summary, then carry on with the new design in the same session
Resume the same session in a second terminal and try the alternative there, which gets its own copy
Run /clear and re-explain the task, relying on the session picker to bring back the old context later
questions.explanation: /branch (or --continue or --resume combined with --fork-session) copies the transcript into a new session with its own ID; the original stays unchanged on disk and can be resumed later with /resume. Resuming one session in two terminals without forking interleaves both into a single transcript, /compact replaces the history with a summary inside the same session, and /clear starts with an empty context, so the experiment would lose the history it is meant to branch from.
questions.whyTested: Session management in Claude Code.

questions.question: A team wants a code-review helper that keeps its own notes about recurring defects in this repository across sessions, with those notes shared with teammates through version control. What is the BEST setup?
options: A sentence in the root CLAUDE.md asking the main agent to remember recurring defects
A subagent file with memory set to user, so the notes follow each developer across all projects and repositories on their machine
A subagent file with memory set to local, which keeps the notes out of version control
A subagent file in .claude/agents with memory set to project, whose notes go to the committed .claude/agent-memory folder
questions.explanation: The memory field of a subagent has three scopes: user (a folder under the home directory, shared across all of a developer's projects), project (.claude/agent-memory, meant to be committed and shared with the team) and local (.claude/agent-memory-local, kept out of version control). Only project scope matches notes for this repository shared through git. CLAUDE.md holds instructions you write, not learnings a subagent accumulates.
questions.whyTested: Agents and agent memory as Claude Code components.

questions.question: A team is deciding where each kind of guidance should live in Claude Code. Which TWO placements are sound? (Choose two.)
options: A developer's private sandbox URL is committed in the shared project settings file so it is always available
Instructions that matter only when editing one subfolder are placed at the top of the root CLAUDE.md
The rule that deployments must never touch the production database is enforced by one sentence in CLAUDE.md
A reusable multi-step release procedure goes in a command or skill file in the repository so anyone can invoke it
The build and test commands and the code style conventions go in the committed project CLAUDE.md
questions.explanation: CLAUDE.md is the place for always-relevant project facts such as commands and conventions, and a command or skill file packages a procedure that is loaded when invoked. A sentence in CLAUDE.md is context, not enforcement, so a rule that must hold needs a hook or a permission rule; a private value belongs in CLAUDE.local.md or the local settings file, which stay out of version control; and instructions that matter for one folder belong in a path-scoped rule or a CLAUDE.md in that folder, so they load only when relevant.
questions.whyTested: Placing guidance in CLAUDE.md, commands, skills, hooks and settings.

questions.question: Running /init in a project that already has a CLAUDE.md replaces the file with a newly generated one.
questions.explanation: When a CLAUDE.md already exists, /init suggests improvements instead of overwriting it. On a fresh project it analyzes the codebase and drafts build commands, test instructions and conventions, which you should then review and trim.
questions.whyTested: Repository initialization.

questions.question: Claude Code's auto memory notes are stored in the repository and reach teammates through version control.
questions.explanation: Auto memory is machine-local: the notes live under the user's own .claude/projects folder (shared by the worktrees of one repository on that machine). The shareable file is the committed CLAUDE.md, which you write yourself.
questions.whyTested: Auto memory versus CLAUDE.md.

questions.question: A triage tool sends each support ticket to Claude with the prompt "Summarize this ticket." Summaries range from one line to a full page, and the routing code that reads them cannot rely on any structure. Which change is BEST?
options: Add the word IMPORTANT in capital letters and ask the model to be consistent every time
Run each ticket three times and keep whichever of the summaries turns out to be the shortest
Name the reader and purpose, and fix the fields and length: symptom, component and impact in three sentences
Truncate every summary to its first 200 characters before it is passed to the routing code
questions.explanation: The prompt leaves the audience, content and shape to guesswork, so a capable colleague without context would have to guess as well. Naming the reader and fixing the fields and length removes the variance at its source. Capital letters add pressure but no information, picking the shortest of three runs triples the cost and still guesses the structure, and truncation cuts content arbitrarily.
questions.whyTested: Prompt engineering: instruction clarity.

questions.question: A sentiment classifier prompt contains four worked examples, all labelled positive, written inside the paragraph of instructions. In production it labels nearly every review positive and sometimes copies phrasing from the examples. What is the BEST fix?
options: Replace the examples with a longer written description of positive reviews and leave the negative cases to general knowledge
Provide varied examples that cover every label and the tricky edge cases, each in its own example tags
Repeat the same four examples a second time so that the model gives them more weight
Strip the labels from the examples so that the model has to infer the answers itself
questions.explanation: Examples teach by pattern, so a one-sided set teaches a one-sided habit. Varied examples that span every label and the hard cases, kept in tags that separate them from the instructions, fix both the bias and the copying. A prose description does not show the boundary between labels, duplicating a biased set amplifies it, and unlabeled examples remove the very thing they were meant to demonstrate.
questions.whyTested: Prompt engineering: few-shot examples.

questions.question: An HR assistant answers questions from about 60 policy documents, roughly 150,000 tokens in all. The prompt begins with the employee's question and then pastes the documents with no markers, and answers often miss details buried in the middle. Which restructure is BEST?
options: Put the documents first in source-labeled tags, the question last, and ask for relevant quotes before the answer
Move the question into the middle of the documents so that it sits as close as possible to the relevant text, wherever that is
Compress every document to a fifty-word summary first and send only the summaries to keep the prompt short
Repeat the employee's question at the start of every document so that the model never loses track of it
questions.explanation: For long inputs, put the documents near the top and the question or instructions at the end. Tagging each document with its source lets the model point to it, and asking for word-for-word quotes first focuses attention on the relevant passages. Hiding the question inside the text, over-compressing the documents and repeating the question dozens of times all add noise or throw detail away.
questions.whyTested: Prompt engineering: prompt and instruction placement.

questions.question: A chat widget needs short answers. The prompt asks for "no more than 120 words" and max_tokens is set to 160, yet many replies still run long and some stop in the middle of a sentence. What is the BEST approach?
options: Lower max_tokens to 80 so that every reply is forced to stay inside the widget
Raise the temperature so that the model is less likely to keep repeating itself at length
Ask the model to count its words after writing and to rewrite any answer that is over the limit
Ask for two to three sentences in the prompt and keep max_tokens as a safety ceiling well above that
questions.explanation: The model works in pieces of text rather than words, so sentence or paragraph limits are followed more closely than word counts. max_tokens is a hard ceiling that cuts text off wherever it falls, so it belongs behind the prompt as a safety net, not in front of it as the length control. Lowering it makes truncation worse, randomness settings do not govern length, and a count-and-rewrite pass spends extra output tokens on an unreliable check.
questions.whyTested: Prompt engineering: output constraints.

questions.question: A prompt says: "Do not use markdown. Do not use bullet points. Never use headings." The system prompt itself is full of markdown headings and lists, and replies still arrive as bullet lists. Which change is MOST likely to fix this?
options: Repeat the three prohibitions in capital letters at the very end of the user message
Rewrite the prompt in plain prose and state the target, such as "write in flowing paragraphs, like a short email"
Start the assistant turn with a plain-text sentence so that the reply continues in that style instead of switching to lists
Remove the bullet characters from every reply with a regular expression before display
questions.explanation: Saying what to do steers more reliably than listing what to avoid, and the style of a prompt tends to leak into the style of the output, so a markdown-heavy prompt invites markdown. Capital letters add pressure rather than information, prefilling the assistant turn is rejected on Claude 4.6 and later models, and stripping bullets treats the symptom and can mangle legitimate text.
questions.whyTested: Prompt engineering: positive instructions and format control.

questions.question: A team moves from an older model to Claude Sonnet 5.5. Their prompt says: "CRITICAL: you MUST ALWAYS call search_docs before answering anything." Now the agent calls search_docs for greetings and arithmetic, adding latency and cost. What is the BEST first step?
options: Restate the rule with its condition in plain words, such as "use search_docs for questions about company documents"
Set the effort level to its minimum so that the model has less room to over-apply the rule
Add a second CRITICAL rule telling the model never to search when the user is only greeting
Pin the application to the older model so that the previous behavior comes back unchanged, and postpone any prompt changes
questions.explanation: Newer models follow system prompts closely, so wording that was needed to overcome under-triggering in older models now causes over-application. Restating the rule with its condition in plain language and re-testing is the first fix. Lowering effort changes how hard the model works, not what it was told; a second shouted rule piles on emphasis; pinning an old model skips the prompt audit that every model change deserves.
questions.whyTested: Prompt adjustment after a model change.

questions.question: A voice assistant's replies are read aloud by a text-to-speech engine that stumbles over symbols. The prompt says "Never use ellipses." Replies now avoid ellipses but include emoji, slashes and parenthetical asides that the engine also mispronounces. Which prompt change is BEST?
options: Add each symbol that has caused trouble so far to a growing list of banned characters
Warn the model that any reply containing a symbol will be penalized and thrown away
Say that replies are spoken aloud by a speech engine, and ask for short natural sentences without symbols
Ask the model to scan each finished reply for symbols and to fix any it finds before sending, as a last pass
questions.explanation: A rule with no reason is applied only to the case it names; giving the purpose lets the model generalize to symbols nobody listed. A ban list always lags behind the next failure, threats add pressure but no information, and a self-scan costs tokens and still depends on the model knowing what to look for.
questions.whyTested: Prompt engineering: instruction clarity and motivation.

questions.question: A prompt template places customer feedback between <feedback> and </feedback> tags. A tester submits text that begins with </feedback> followed by new instructions, and the model starts obeying them. Which step addresses this break-out MOST directly?
options: Neutralize the closing-tag sequence in the submitted text and cap its length before inserting it
Rename the tags to an unusual word and keep the new name out of all documentation
Add a note on the feedback form asking customers not to type anything that looks like a tag or an instruction
End every reply with a statement that only the original instructions were followed
questions.explanation: The attack works because the data section can be closed by the data itself. Escaping or removing the delimiter sequence, bounding the length and normalizing the text keeps untrusted input inside its section. It is one layer, not a cure, so pair it with least-privilege tools and output checks. A secret tag name is obscurity, a polite request to attackers is not a control, and a closing statement changes nothing about what the model has already read.
questions.whyTested: Prompt engineering: input sanitization.

questions.question: A legal team sends its entire 600,000-token contract archive with every question because the model's window can hold it. Answers are slow and expensive, and sometimes worse than when a developer pasted just the relevant clauses by hand. What is the BEST redesign?
options: Move to a larger model tier so that the extra context is handled without any loss of accuracy
Tell the model in the prompt to pay equal attention to every document in the archive
Cache the archive and keep sending all of it, since caching removes the accuracy penalty of length
Retrieve the few passages that are relevant to each question and send only those, with their sources
questions.explanation: A large window is a ceiling, not a target: accuracy and recall tend to fall as irrelevant material piles up (context rot), and every extra token adds latency and cost. Retrieval keeps the prompt focused on evidence that matters. A bigger tier does not remove the effect, an instruction cannot make attention uniform, and caching lowers the price of repeated tokens while they still occupy the window.
questions.whyTested: Context engineering: context window management.

questions.question: A research agent runs for hours. Its history is dominated by old web-page tool results that are no longer needed, while its own findings and decisions must stay word for word. Which feature fits BEST?
options: Compaction, replacing all older turns with a model-written summary of the whole session
Context editing, clearing the oldest tool results by rule and leaving placeholders behind
Prompt caching on the full history so that the old results cost less to resend each turn
A lower max_tokens value so that fewer tokens are carried over into later turns
questions.explanation: Tool result clearing targets exactly the stale bulk and leaves everything else untouched. Compaction summarizes the older turns, so findings and decisions would be paraphrased and details lost. Caching changes the price of the repeated prefix, not the space it occupies, and max_tokens caps one reply, not the history.
questions.whyTested: Context engineering: tool output pruning versus compaction.

questions.question: A migration agent works through 300 database tables over several hours, and its context is compacted twice. Afterwards it repeats tables it already converted and skips others. What is the MOST reliable improvement?
options: Ask the model to remember the finished tables more carefully after each compaction
Turn compaction off so that the early messages stay in context however long the run lasts
Keep a structured progress file of finished tables that the agent updates and re-reads as it works
Process fewer tables per session and let the compaction summary carry the rest of the list between sessions
questions.explanation: Exact state is a poor fit for a model-written summary, which is lossy by design. A small structured file, ideally alongside version control, is durable, cheap to re-read and precise, and it survives compaction or a fresh session. Asking the model to try harder cannot restore details that were summarized away, switching compaction off eventually overflows the window, and leaning on the summary repeats the original weakness.
questions.whyTested: Context engineering: preventing context drift with durable state.

questions.question: One long prompt asks Claude to read 30 vendor contracts, extract every termination clause, draft a risk memo and then critique its own memo. Quality drops in the later steps, and the critique tends to repeat the memo's mistakes. Which redesign is BEST?
options: Split it into separate calls: extract per contract, draft the memo from the structured clauses, review in a fresh context
Keep the single prompt but add an instruction to think carefully, double-check each step and critique the memo as harshly as possible
Run the identical prompt five times and keep the memo that most of the runs agree with
Switch to a model with a larger context window so that every contract and all four steps can stay in one call
questions.explanation: A multi-step workflow gives each step a clean context: extraction runs per contract (and can run in parallel), only structured results move forward, and the reviewer sees the memo without the author's reasoning, so it can catch errors instead of inheriting them. Added caution, voting among identical runs and a bigger window all leave one crowded context in place.
questions.whyTested: Context engineering: context isolation through multi-step workflows.

questions.question: A coding agent must work in a monorepo with millions of lines. A proposal is to generate a summary of every directory and load all of it into the system prompt at the start of each session. What is the BEST alternative?
options: Split the repository into chunks and send the chunks on a rotating schedule over successive turns
Paste the whole repository into the first user message and rely on prompt caching to keep the cost of later turns down
Ask the model to memorize the directory summaries and then drop them from the prompt after turn one
Give the agent search and file-reading tools plus path conventions, so it loads detail only when a task needs it
questions.explanation: Lightweight handles such as paths and queries, plus tools to open them, let an agent explore the way an engineer does: find what matters, read it, move on. Preloading everything fills the window with mostly irrelevant material that also goes stale. Rotating chunks or a cached giant paste still occupy the window, and a model cannot memorize text it no longer sees.
questions.whyTested: Context engineering: just-in-time retrieval.

questions.question: A support chatbot keeps only the last ten messages of each conversation to control cost. After a long chat it forgets the account number and the problem the customer described at the start. What is the BEST improvement?
options: Keep a running summary of older turns plus a pinned block of durable facts, such as the account number
Raise the cutoff to the last forty messages and accept the higher cost for every conversation
Ask customers to repeat their account number whenever the assistant seems to have forgotten it
Store the full transcript in a database and expect the model to recall it from there on its own when it needs it
questions.explanation: Dropping old turns loses exactly the facts that were set early. A summary of older turns plus a pinned block of durable facts is cheap and survives trimming. A longer cutoff only postpones the problem, asking customers to repeat themselves pushes the work onto them, and a database helps only if the application actually puts the content into the request, because the model sees nothing else.
questions.whyTested: Context engineering: context drift in long conversations.

questions.question: An invoice extractor uses structured outputs, so every reply parses. Still, about 2 percent of results have a total that does not equal the sum of the line items. What is the BEST way to handle this?
options: Add "be careful with arithmetic" to the prompt and treat the problem as solved
Check the totals in code, re-prompt once with the exact discrepancy on a mismatch, then escalate to a person
Turn structured outputs off, since constrained decoding is what introduces the arithmetic errors, and parse free text instead
Resend the same request unchanged until the totals happen to match
questions.explanation: A schema guarantees shape, not truth. Business rules such as lines summing to the total belong in code, and feeding the exact violation back usually fixes the reply. Capping the attempts and escalating keeps failures visible and cost bounded. A reminder in the prompt is a wish, constrained decoding does not cause arithmetic errors, and blind retries burn money without adding information.
questions.whyTested: Output handling: response validation and validate-and-retry.

questions.question: A policy Q&A bot sometimes invents rules that are not in the 200-page handbook it is given. Which prompt design reduces this MOST?
options: Ask it to state a confidence percentage and show a warning to users when the number is low
Tell it to avoid expressing doubt and to always give a definite answer so that users trust the bot
Restrict it to the handbook, make it quote supporting passages first, and let it say when the handbook is silent
Let it use general knowledge when the handbook is silent, marking those answers with the word "estimate" so that users can judge them
questions.explanation: Grounding techniques cut invented claims: limit the model to the supplied text, make it extract quotes before it answers, and give it explicit permission to say the answer is not there. A self-reported percentage is not calibrated evidence, forcing a definite answer pushes toward invention, and licensing general knowledge reopens the gap. These techniques reduce hallucination but cannot eliminate it, so critical answers still need checks.
questions.whyTested: Output handling: reducing hallucination.

questions.question: A research assistant answers with quoted passages from uploaded reports. A reviewer finds a quote that appears nowhere in the report it is attributed to. Which safeguard is MOST effective against this?
options: Ask the model, at the end of each answer, to confirm that every quote is accurate and appears in the report
Add "never fabricate quotes" to the system prompt in emphatic wording
Ask for longer answers with more quotes so that errors become easier to spot by eye
Check in code that each quote occurs in the cited source, and withdraw any claim whose quote does not
questions.explanation: A mechanical check against the source is independent of the model's confidence: a quote that cannot be found is rejected. The citations feature, which returns pointers to the exact supporting passages in your documents, serves the same purpose. A confirmation from the same model shares its blind spots, a prohibition is still only a request, and more quotes mean more to verify.
questions.whyTested: Output handling: skepticism toward confident output and source grounding.

questions.question: A contracts tool must return a parseable verdict (approve, review or reject) and also ground its statements with citations to the supplied contract. A single request with both citations and structured outputs enabled returns a 400 error. Which design BEST works within this limit?
options: Keep both features on and retry the request with exponential backoff until it succeeds
Call once with citations for the grounded analysis, then again to convert that analysis into the verdict schema
Drop citations and ask for sources in free text, which the code extracts with a regular expression before storing the verdict
Keep structured outputs and add an optional string field in the schema where the model writes its citations
questions.explanation: The two features cannot be combined in one request, and a 400 is a request error that retrying will not fix. Splitting the work lets each feature do what it is good at: verifiable pointers to the source passages in one step, a schema-conforming verdict in the next. Free-text sources and a schema field of model-written strings lose the verifiable pointers that citations provide.
questions.whyTested: Output handling: structured output patterns and their limits.

questions.question: An approval workflow asks Claude to rate its confidence from 0 to 100 and automatically approves anything above 90. A later audit finds several confident approvals that were wrong. What is the BEST correction?
options: Raise the approval threshold to 99 so that only the most confident answers pass automatically
Ask the model to rate its confidence twice and average the two numbers before applying the threshold, so one noisy rating matters less
Rely on checks you can verify, such as rules and tests in code and sampled human review, not self-rating alone
Instruct the model to be more humble so that its confidence numbers become better calibrated
questions.explanation: A fluent, assured answer and a high self-rating are not evidence of correctness. Anchor decisions on independent verification and scale the review to the stakes. A higher threshold or an average only rescales an unreliable signal, and telling the model to be humble does not calibrate it.
questions.whyTested: Output handling: skepticism toward confident output.

questions.question: Which TWO items belong in the system prompt of a customer-support assistant rather than in the user turn? (Choose two.)
options: The text of the customer's current message, which changes on every turn
The assistant's role and the escalation policy that apply to every conversation
The contents of the order record retrieved for this particular customer
The tone and formatting rules that every reply must follow
The specific question to be answered about that order today
questions.explanation: The system prompt carries what is stable across turns: the role, the policies and the output rules. The current message, the retrieved record and today's question change per request and belong in the user turn, where untrusted customer text also gets less authority than the system prompt. A fixed system prompt is also easier to cache.
questions.whyTested: Prompt engineering: system versus user placement.

questions.question: A team moves its prompts to a newer model. Which TWO edits belong in a sensible prompt audit? (Choose two.)
options: Remove hand-built scratchpad steps and "verify everything twice" rules that compensated for an older model
Add a prefilled assistant opening so that the output format stays steady
Replace shouted MUST and CRITICAL wording with plain statements of when to act
Add more capital-letter emphasis so that the old behavior is preserved exactly
Delete every example, since newer models never benefit from demonstrations
questions.explanation: Newer models follow instructions more literally and bring their own reasoning, so compensating text now causes extra work or over-application. The audit removes it and re-runs the evaluation set. Prefill is rejected on Claude 4.6 and later models, extra emphasis worsens over-triggering, and examples remain one of the strongest tools for fixing format.
questions.whyTested: Prompt adjustment and iterative refinement.

questions.question: Which THREE practices keep the context of a tool-heavy agent from filling with stale bulk? (Choose three.)
options: Return only the fields the next step needs from each tool, and paginate large lists
Keep every raw tool response in the history in case the model wants to re-read it later
Clear the oldest tool results by rule once the history passes a size threshold
Delegate noisy side investigations to a subagent that returns a short conclusion
Raise max_tokens so that the window is counted as having more room
questions.explanation: Lean tool outputs, rule-based clearing and isolating side work all keep the working context small, and the cheapest fix is not producing the bulk in the first place. Keeping every raw response is the problem itself, and max_tokens bounds one reply, not the accumulated history.
questions.whyTested: Context engineering: preventing context bloat.

questions.question: A bot answers questions about supplied technical manuals. Which TWO prompt changes reduce unsupported claims? (Choose two.)
options: Ask for a confident, authoritative tone so that users trust the result
Allow the explicit answer that the manual does not contain the information
Tell it to fill gaps from general knowledge whenever a manual is silent
Have it extract word-for-word quotes from the manuals first and answer using only those quotes
Put the question before the manuals so that it is not influenced by the long documents
questions.explanation: Permission to say the answer is not in the manuals removes the pressure to invent, and quote-first answering ties each claim to text that exists. A confident tone encourages bluffing, filling gaps from general knowledge reopens the gap, and for long documents the stronger structure puts the manuals first and the question last.
questions.whyTested: Output handling: reducing hallucination.

questions.question: Explaining why a rule exists, for example that replies will be read aloud by a speech engine, helps the model apply the rule sensibly to cases the prompt never listed.
questions.explanation: A reason conveys the intent behind the rule, so the model can generalize. A bare prohibition tends to be applied to the case it names and little else.

questions.question: Stripping the phrase "ignore previous instructions" from user input is enough on its own to stop prompt injection.
questions.explanation: Blocklists of known phrases are easy to evade by rewording, translating or encoding the attack. Input sanitization, such as escaping delimiters and bounding length, is one layer to combine with structural separation of untrusted content, least-privilege tools and checks in code.

questions.question: Because a very large context window can hold the material, adding more documents to a prompt never lowers the quality of the answer.
questions.explanation: Accuracy and recall tend to degrade as the window fills with material (context rot), and more tokens add latency and cost. Curate what goes in: retrieve what is relevant and trim what is stale.

questions.question: Prompt caching reduces how many tokens of the context window a prompt occupies.
questions.explanation: Caching changes the price and speed of reprocessing a repeated prefix. Cached tokens still count toward the window, so it does nothing for a conversation that is about to overflow; use compaction, context editing or smaller inputs for that.

questions.question: Context editing removes older tool results by rule before the prompt reaches the model and leaves a short marker where the content was.
questions.explanation: Tool result clearing is applied oldest first once a configured threshold is passed, and the marker tells the model that something was removed. Clearing changes the cached prefix, so clear enough tokens each time to make the cache invalidation worthwhile.

questions.question: If several runs of the same prompt give the same answer, that answer is guaranteed to be correct.
questions.explanation: Disagreement between runs is a useful flag for unreliable content, but agreement only shows consistency: the runs share the same blind spots and can repeat the same mistake. Verify important claims against a source, a test or a person.

questions.question: Giving the model explicit permission to say that it does not know is one way to reduce hallucination.
questions.explanation: Without that permission the model is pushed toward producing some answer. Pair it with quote-first grounding and restriction to the supplied documents; none of these techniques eliminates hallucination.

questions.question: Compaction and context editing are the same feature: both replace older content with a model-written summary.
questions.explanation: Compaction summarizes the older turns of a conversation, which keeps the thread alive but loses detail. Context editing deletes specified content, such as old tool results or thinking blocks, by rule and leaves placeholders; nothing is summarized.

questions.question: An inventory assistant has two tools: lookup_item (finds one item by SKU and returns stock and location) and search_items (full-text search over names, returning up to 20 matches with their SKUs). Both are described only as "Gets inventory information," and the model often calls the wrong one. What is the BEST fix?
options: Merge them into one tool named inventory that accepts a single free-text query parameter
Force one tool on every request with tool_choice and let application code decide which one to use
Rewrite each description: what the tool does, when to use it instead of the other, its parameters and its result
Add a paragraph to the system prompt listing which tool to prefer for each kind of question
questions.explanation: The description is the most influential input to tool selection. Differentiating the two by when to use each, with parameters and results spelled out, resolves the ambiguity where the model reads it. A free-text merge hides a real difference between the tools, forced tool choice removes the model's judgment (and is rejected on the newest models), and prompt-level guidance duplicates what belongs with the tool and drifts away from it.
questions.whyTested: Tool implementation: tool description writing.

questions.question: A booking tool returns the text "error" when it is given a date in the past. The model retries the same call three times and then apologizes to the user. Which change to the tool is BEST?
options: Flag the result as an error with a message such as "start_date must be in the future; today is 2026-10-15"
Raise an exception in the harness so that the whole conversation ends and the user can start again with a new request
Return an empty result that looks successful so that the model is not distracted by a failure
Increase the SDK's automatic retry count so that more attempts are made before giving up
questions.explanation: A failed call should come back with the error flag set and say what went wrong and what to try, so the model can correct the argument itself. Ending the run wastes the chance to recover, an empty success misreports the outcome, and SDK retries address transient network and server failures, not invalid arguments.
questions.whyTested: Tool implementation: error handling.

questions.question: In a manual tool loop, Claude requests a send_email tool call. The harness shows the draft to a manager, who declines it. What should the harness send back to the model?
options: Nothing at all: end the conversation, because a call that was declined cannot be answered and the user already knows
A new assistant message that apologizes to the user on the model's behalf
An ordinary user text message with no tool_result, since the tool never ran
A tool_result for that tool_use ID flagged as an error, saying that the person declined and why
questions.explanation: Every tool_use block needs a matching tool_result in the next user message, even when the action is refused. An error result that says the person declined lets the model change course or explain. Ending the run, writing assistant text on the model's behalf, or omitting the result leaves the exchange malformed or the model without information.
questions.whyTested: Tool implementation: approval patterns.

questions.question: A product assistant needs live web lookups and must also read order totals from the company's internal billing service. The team wants to write as little integration code as possible. Which tool setup is BEST?
options: The web search server tool for both needs, configured with the billing service's internal URL
The web search server tool for lookups, plus a custom client tool whose handler calls the billing service
Custom client tools for both, with a web scraping library and a result parser that you write and maintain for lookups
No tools: paste the billing totals into the system prompt and rely on training data for the web
questions.explanation: Server-executed tools run on Anthropic's infrastructure, which cannot reach your private network, but they spare you from building web search. Internal systems need a client tool (or an MCP server) whose handler you own. Rebuilding search adds code for no benefit, and pasted totals go stale while training data is not live.
questions.whyTested: Tool implementation: client-side versus server-side tools.

questions.question: An agent is connected to five MCP servers and sees about 60 tool definitions that together use tens of thousands of tokens on every request. Most tasks need only three or four of them, and the model sometimes picks the wrong one. What is the BEST change?
options: Shorten every description to a few words so that all 60 definitions take up much less space
Set tool_choice to any so that the model must commit to a tool at the first step
Use tool search with deferred loading, so definitions are loaded only when the model discovers them
Cache the tool definitions so that they no longer count against the window when the model chooses between tools
questions.explanation: Tool search keeps most definitions out of the prompt until the model searches for them, which cuts context cost and improves selection in large catalogs (worth considering from roughly 20 tools). Terse descriptions make choosing harder, forcing a tool call does not help pick the right one, and caching lowers the price without reducing the number of choices the model must weigh.
questions.whyTested: Tool implementation: tool set construction.

questions.question: An expense agent must check 150 receipts against a vendor API. Each call returns about 2,000 tokens, the model makes 150 round trips, and the conversation soon overflows. Which technique BEST addresses the cause?
options: Programmatic tool calling, so a script loops over the receipts and returns only a short summary
Tool search, so that the vendor tool's definition is loaded only when it is needed and not on every request
Prompt caching, so that the repeated results are billed at the lower cache rate
A larger max_tokens value so that the model can finish writing out all 150 calls
questions.explanation: The bulk comes from intermediate tool results and round trips. Running the loop in code inside the code execution sandbox keeps those results out of the model's context and returns only what the next decision needs. Tool search targets large catalogs of definitions, caching changes the price rather than the space used, and max_tokens caps a single reply.
questions.whyTested: Tool implementation: tool usage patterns.

questions.question: A classification service sets tool_choice to force a call to classify_ticket. After the team switches to Claude Sonnet 5.5, every request fails with a 400 error, yet the service still needs a label from a fixed set on every call. What is the BEST fix?
options: Retry each failed request until the API accepts the forced tool choice
Request the label with structured outputs, using a schema whose field is an enum of the allowed labels
Drop the schema and parse the label out of the model's prose answer with a regular expression and a table of synonyms
Move back to an older model generation solely to keep the forced tool choice working
questions.explanation: Forced tool choice is not supported on the newest models, so retrying cannot succeed. Structured outputs constrain the reply to a schema, so the label comes from your closed set without forcing a tool (compare labels case-insensitively, because the capitalization of enum values is not guaranteed). Regex over prose is the fragile pattern a schema replaces, and a downgrade trades current capabilities away to avoid a design change.
questions.whyTested: Tool implementation: tool use and function calling configuration.

questions.question: A project's CLAUDE.md includes a 400-word quarterly-close procedure that matters for a few tasks a month. It loads into every session and makes the file long. Where should this procedure move?
options: A hook that prints the whole procedure at the start of every session
The system prompt of every API call the team makes, so that it is applied consistently
A skill, so that only its short description stays in context and the steps load when the task matches
An MCP server that serves the procedure through a tool the model calls at the start of every task
questions.explanation: A skill uses progressive disclosure: its name and description are always available, the body loads when the task matches, and supporting files load on demand. CLAUDE.md is for facts that apply to nearly every session. A hook that prints the text, a system prompt and an MCP tool called on every task would each put the procedure back in context all the time, or add moving parts for no gain.
questions.whyTested: Agentic customization: CLAUDE.md versus skills.

questions.question: A team connected an MCP server for its issue tracker. Claude can now create and update issues, but it applies labels and templates inconsistently with the team's conventions. What addition is BEST?
options: A skill that documents the team's labeling and template conventions and when to use each tool
A second MCP server that exposes the same issue-tracker tools under different names
A hook that prints a reminder after every tool call, whether or not it concerns issues
A larger model tier, since inconsistent behavior means the current model lacks capability
questions.explanation: The server supplies the connection; what is missing is know-how about the team's way of using it, which is what a skill packages and loads when relevant. Another server duplicates the capability, a reminder after every call is noise, and the model is not the problem when the conventions were never written down.
questions.whyTested: Agentic customization: combining skills and MCP servers.

questions.question: One internal web app needs Claude to call a small function that computes shipping quotes from the app's own database. No other application will use it. Which approach is BEST?
options: A standalone MCP server with its own deployment, authentication and release process
A skill that explains the quote formula so that the model can work the quotes out itself
A built-in tool, since built-in tools can query any application's database
A custom tool in the app's tool list, whose handler calls the function in the same codebase
questions.explanation: For logic that belongs to one application, a custom tool is the simplest and cheapest option: a schema plus a handler. A protocol server pays off when several clients need the capability or it must be maintained independently, so building one here adds operations work for no reuse. A skill cannot read the database, and built-in tools do not reach arbitrary application data.
questions.whyTested: Agentic customization: custom tools versus MCP servers.

questions.question: A team plans to give Claude Code thirty skills for different procedures and worries that they will consume the context window in every session. Which statement is accurate?
options: All thirty skill bodies load at session start, so the team should keep the total under a few hundred words and drop the rest
Only each skill's short name and description stays in context, and a skill's full instructions load when it is used
Skills load only when a person types their slash command, so the model can never use one on its own
Each skill runs as a background process whose output is appended to every reply
questions.explanation: Skills use progressive disclosure, which is why a large library is cheap: descriptions are always visible so the model knows what exists, bodies load on demand, and supporting files load only when referenced. Skills can also be invoked by the model when a task matches (unless that is switched off for a skill), and they are instructions, not background processes.
questions.whyTested: Agentic customization: how skills use context.

questions.question: Three teams each copied the same two skills, a formatting hook and an MCP server entry into their repositories, and the copies are drifting apart. Which approach is BEST?
options: Merge the three repositories into one monorepo so that there is only a single copy to keep
Move all of the content into each repository's CLAUDE.md, which every session loads automatically
Package it as a plugin in a marketplace and have each repository install it and update it deliberately
Ask each team to compare its copy with the others at the start of every quarter
questions.explanation: A plugin bundles skills, hooks, subagents and MCP configuration into one versioned unit that can be installed in many repositories.
