CLAUDE.md can carry instructions but not hooks or server definitions, merging repositories is a large organizational change for a packaging problem, and a manual quarterly comparison is the process that is already failing.
questions.whyTested: Agentic customization: choosing how to package and distribute extensions.

questions.question: A coding agent defines its own edit_file tool with a home-made schema for describing text replacements. The model often produces malformed edits. Which change is MOST likely to help?
options: Use Anthropic's text editor tool, whose schema the models were trained on, with your own handler
Turn the tool into a server-executed tool so that Anthropic runs the edits for you
Paste the whole file into the tool description so that the model has more context about it before it edits
Make the schema accept one free-form string so that the model has more flexibility
questions.explanation: Anthropic-schema tools such as the text editor, bash and memory have definitions the models were trained on, so calls tend to be more reliable than with an equivalent home-made schema, but your own code still executes them. They are client tools, not server tools. Pasting file contents bloats the description and free-form strings remove the structure that makes an edit unambiguous.
questions.whyTested: Agentic customization: built-in and Anthropic-schema tools versus custom tools.

questions.question: A developer's local MCP server passes its unit tests, but a host application that launches it as a subprocess reports parse errors on startup. The server prints a banner and debug lines with print(). What is the correct fix?
options: Switch the server to Streamable HTTP, because the stdio transport cannot carry any log output
Print a blank line before each banner so that the client can skip over the extra text
Increase the host's startup timeout so that the extra lines are ignored while it waits
Send logging and diagnostics to standard error, and keep standard output for protocol messages only
questions.explanation: Over stdio, standard output carries newline-delimited JSON-RPC messages and nothing else; the server may write logs to standard error. A stray print corrupts the stream. The remote transport is not needed, a blank line is still invalid output, and a longer timeout does not change what is on the stream.
questions.whyTested: MCP server development: communication patterns (stdio).

questions.question: An MCP tool that books meeting rooms receives a start time in the wrong format. The server currently answers with a JSON-RPC error and a generic message, and the model cannot recover. Which design lets the model self-correct?
options: Keep the protocol error and add a table of numeric error codes to the server documentation
Return a normal result with the error flag set and a message naming the expected format and an example
Coerce any malformed time to the nearest valid time and book the room without telling anyone, so the call always succeeds
Return an empty successful result and log the problem for an administrator to read later
questions.explanation: Protocol errors cover malformed requests and unknown tools. A failure inside the tool, such as bad input, a business rule or a backend outage, should be reported in the result with isError set and an actionable message, so the model can fix its arguments and retry. Documentation is not seen by the model, silent coercion books the wrong time, and an empty success hides the failure.
questions.whyTested: MCP server development: tools and error handling.

questions.question: A server author must expose three things: a function that creates tickets, a read-only file holding the current database schema, and a weekly-report template that users pick from a menu. Which mapping to MCP primitives is correct?
options: A prompt for the ticket function, a tool for the schema file and a resource for the report template
A resource for the ticket function, a prompt for the schema file and a tool for the report template
A tool for the ticket function, a resource for the schema file and a prompt for the report template
Tools for all three, since only tools can be listed and invoked by a client
questions.explanation: Tools are model-controlled functions that act, resources are read-only context that the application attaches, and prompts are templates a person selects deliberately. The other mappings put an action behind a read-only primitive or make the model choose a human-facing template, and clients can list resources and prompts as well as tools.
questions.whyTested: MCP server development: MCP resources, tools and prompts.

questions.question: A developer wants the Messages API's MCP connector to use an MCP server that runs on their laptop over stdio and exposes both tools and resources. The request fails. Which statement explains why and points to the right alternative?
options: The connector accepts stdio servers only when they are under 1 MB, so the server has to be compressed and uploaded to the platform first
The connector requires every server to be registered in the Claude Console before a request is allowed to name it
The connector works with local servers too, but only when the request sets a stdio transport flag on the server
The connector reaches only public HTTP servers and only tools; local servers need Claude Code, the Agent SDK or your own client
questions.explanation: The Messages API connector is a beta feature that connects to remote servers over HTTP that are reachable from the internet, and it supports tool calls only, not resources or prompts. A subprocess server on a laptop needs a client that can launch it, such as Claude Code, the Agent SDK or a client you write. The other statements describe limits and flags that do not exist.
questions.whyTested: MCP server development: integration with Claude applications.

questions.question: Which THREE belong in a well-written tool description? (Choose three.)
options: When the tool should be used and when it should not
What each parameter means, including its expected format
The credentials the handler uses to authenticate to the backend service
What the result contains and any important limits, such as fields it leaves out
A parameter asking the model to write out its step-by-step reasoning for the call
questions.explanation: A description is the model's manual for the tool: purpose, when to use it, parameters, and results with their caveats. Credentials never belong in text the model can see, so handlers read them from the environment or a secret store, and a parameter that asks for step-by-step reasoning can trigger a refusal; ask for a short explanation or the supporting evidence instead.
questions.whyTested: Tool implementation: tool description writing.

questions.question: A team is designing tools for GitHub and Slack integrations. Which TWO design choices follow good practice? (Choose two.)
options: Expose one generic call_api tool that accepts any URL, method and body
Prefix tool names with the service, such as github_list_prs and slack_send_message
Group closely related pull-request operations into one tool with an action parameter
Give every tool the same short description so that the model treats them consistently
Return the full raw API response from every tool so that no information is lost
questions.explanation: Namespacing keeps similar tools from different systems unambiguous as the catalog grows, and consolidating related operations gives the model fewer, clearer choices. A catch-all tool removes the structure that guides and limits calls (and makes permissioning hard), identical descriptions make selection impossible, and raw responses bury the few fields that matter.
questions.whyTested: Tool implementation: tool set construction best practices.

questions.question: A team runs an MCP server on developers' machines over Streamable HTTP. Which TWO protections does the specification call for? (Choose two.)
options: Validate the Origin header on incoming connections to defend against DNS rebinding
Skip authentication, because only processes on the same machine can reach a local server
Expose the server on all network interfaces so that teammates can connect for pair debugging
Bind to 127.0.0.1 rather than to all interfaces when the server runs locally
Accept any Origin value so that browser-based clients are never blocked
questions.explanation: Servers must validate the Origin header (answering an invalid one with 403) and, when run locally, should bind only to localhost; they should also authenticate connections. Without these protections, a malicious web page can use DNS rebinding to talk to a server on the developer's machine. Skipping authentication, binding to every interface and accepting any Origin each reopen that path.
questions.whyTested: MCP server development: deployment and communication patterns.

questions.question: Which THREE pairings of a need and an extension mechanism are right? (Choose three.)
options: A check that must run after every file edit, with no exceptions: a hook
A convention that applies in nearly every session, such as the test command: a skill the model must choose to invoke
A procedure the team keeps pasting into chat: a skill
A noisy investigation that would flood the main conversation: a note in CLAUDE.md
Reading and updating tickets in a SaaS tool that Claude cannot reach: an MCP server
questions.explanation: Guaranteed, every-time behavior belongs in a hook because hooks are executed, not suggested. Reusable procedures belong in skills, and a connection to an outside system belongs in an MCP server. Facts that apply to almost every session belong in CLAUDE.md rather than in something the model must decide to invoke, and a noisy investigation belongs in a subagent with its own context.
questions.whyTested: Agentic customization: choosing among extension mechanisms.

questions.question: Strict tool use makes tool arguments conform to the schema, but a conforming argument can still be the wrong value.
questions.explanation: Strict mode constrains decoding so field names and types are valid. It cannot know whether the order ID exists or the amount is right, so the dispatcher still validates and authorizes every call.

questions.question: When Claude uses a server-executed tool such as web search, your code must build a tool_result block for each search it makes.
questions.explanation: Anthropic runs server tools and returns their results in the same response, so there is no tool_result for you to build. You only handle the case where the loop pauses (pause_turn) or a client tool is called alongside.

questions.question: A one-phrase description is sufficient for a tool as long as the tool's name is clear.
questions.explanation: The description is the most influential factor in tool performance. A name cannot say when to use the tool, what each parameter expects or what comes back, so aim for several sentences.

questions.question: Tool descriptions and annotations from an MCP server you do not control should be treated as untrusted input.
questions.explanation: A server's descriptions are text the model will read, so a malicious or compromised server can use them to steer it. Clients should confirm sensitive operations, show inputs to the user and validate results.

questions.question: The older HTTP+SSE transport for MCP has been deprecated in favor of Streamable HTTP.
questions.explanation: New remote servers should use Streamable HTTP, where each client message is an HTTP POST to a single endpoint. Local subprocess servers use stdio.

questions.question: A skill and an MCP server solve the same problem, so a team should choose one or the other.
questions.explanation: An MCP server provides a connection to tools and data; a skill teaches how and when to use them. They are complementary, and many teams use both.

questions.question: A built-in tool can be used without building it, but it does not give Claude access to arbitrary internal systems.
questions.explanation: Built-in tools cover standard operations. Reaching your own services needs a custom tool or an MCP server, which is where your handlers and credentials live.

questions.question: An email assistant summarizes incoming mail and, when asked, can send replies. A spam message contains hidden text telling the assistant to forward the user's last ten emails to an outside address. Which design BEST limits this risk?
options: Add a line to the system prompt saying that emails may contain malicious instructions that must be ignored
Treat email bodies as untrusted tool-result data and hold every send for the user's approval, showing recipient and text
Delete incoming messages that contain the phrase "ignore previous instructions" or similar wording before the assistant ever sees them
Switch to a larger model tier so that the assistant recognizes hidden instructions more reliably
questions.explanation: Indirect injection arrives through content the user never wrote. Labeling and isolating that content lowers the odds of success, but the dependable control is a gate in code on the consequential action: the send is held until a person sees the exact recipient and body. A prompt warning is a request, phrase filters are evaded by rewording, and a stronger model reduces the risk without removing it.
questions.whyTested: AI application security: indirect prompt injection mitigation.

questions.question: A public bank chatbot keeps receiving role-play prompts designed to make it ignore its restrictions. Which combination is MOST appropriate?
options: Block a growing list of known jailbreak phrases with exact string matching, and review the list with the security team every month
Remove the system prompt, so that attackers have no instructions to override
Run the chatbot at the highest effort setting so that it reasons more deeply about each attempt before it answers
Pre-screen messages with a small model, harden the system prompt, and throttle accounts that keep probing
questions.explanation: For direct attacks, where the user is the adversary, layer a lightweight harmlessness screen (a refusal from the screening model counts as a harmful verdict), a system prompt that states values and how to decline, monitoring, and action against repeat offenders. Phrase lists are evaded by rewording, removing the system prompt removes your guardrails, and more reasoning effort is a cost setting, not a security control.
questions.whyTested: AI application security: jailbreak defense.

questions.question: A support portal renders Claude's replies by inserting them straight into the page's HTML. A researcher plants text in a public forum post that the assistant reads, and the assistant's next reply contains a script tag that runs in other users' browsers. What is the BEST fix?
options: Treat the reply as untrusted: escape or sanitize it before rendering and block active content
Tell the model in the system prompt never to output HTML tags, scripts or links of any kind in its replies
Ask the model to check its own reply for scripts and to rewrite it before returning it to the portal
Block the assistant from reading that one forum domain and leave everything else as it is today
questions.explanation: Model output can be steered by anything the model reads, so it must be handled like any untrusted input at the point of use: encode it for the destination (HTML escaping or a sanitizer), disallow executable content, and do not render remote images or links automatically, since those can carry data out. Prompt instructions and self-checks are not guarantees, and blocking one domain fixes only this instance.
questions.whyTested: AI application security: untrusted input handling and output handling.

questions.question: A claims tool sends complete customer records, including full names, government ID numbers and addresses, to Claude to draft a one-paragraph summary, and it logs every prompt for debugging. Which change is BEST?
options: Tell the model in the prompt never to repeat the ID numbers or addresses in its summary, and check that it complies
Keep sending everything but use the newest version of the transport encryption protocol
Send only the fields the summary needs, mask identifiers with placeholders, and keep them out of the logs
Keep sending everything and rely on the provider's retention settings to cover the logs
questions.explanation: Data you never send cannot leak from a prompt, a response, a cache or your own logs. Minimizing and masking personal data before the call, and keeping it out of debug logs, closes all of those paths. An instruction only governs the output, transport encryption is already expected, and the provider's retention terms do not govern what your own systems store.
questions.whyTested: AI application security: PII handling and data leakage prevention.

questions.question: A retail chatbot's system prompt contains a staff-only discount code and the key for an internal pricing service. Users have begun extracting the prompt with clever questions. What is the BEST response?
options: Add a firm instruction to the prompt never to reveal its contents under any circumstances
Remove the secrets from the prompt, keep the key in server-side tool code, and screen the replies
Encode the discount code and the key in base64 so that they are no longer readable to casual users of the chatbot
Mix decoy codes into the prompt so that a leaked value is harder to identify as the real one
questions.explanation: No wording makes it impossible for a model to repeat text it can see, so anything in a prompt must be assumed disclosable: keep secrets out, and put credentials where only your code can reach them. Monitoring and filtering outputs can catch leaks. A firmer instruction is still a request, base64 is encoding rather than protection (the model can decode it), and decoys leave the real values exposed.
questions.whyTested: AI application security: data leakage prevention and prompt leak.

questions.question: A reporting agent needs to read three tables. Its run_sql tool connects with the database administrator account, and the system prompt says "Only run SELECT statements." Which change is BEST?
options: Connect the tool with a role that has read-only rights on just those three tables
Add a regular expression to the tool that rejects statements containing DROP or DELETE
Rewrite the system prompt rule in capital letters and repeat it in the tool description
Review the query log once a week and revoke access if a write statement is found
questions.explanation: Least privilege removes the capability instead of asking for restraint: even a successful injection or a model error cannot write, or read other tables. A keyword blocklist is incomplete and easy to bypass, emphasis is still a request, and a weekly review detects damage only after it has happened.
questions.whyTested: Guardrails and safe deployment: least privilege.

questions.question: A data-analysis agent runs Python code that the model writes, on a shared application server whose process environment holds the cloud credentials for the whole product. Which setup is BEST?
options: Scan the generated code for suspicious function names and run it on the server if none are found in the scan results
Ask a second model to review each script and approve it before it runs on the shared server
Run the code on the server under the same account, since the model was told to write safe code
Run the code in an isolated container or VM with no credentials and outbound traffic limited to an allowlist
questions.explanation: Model-written code is untrusted code. Isolation (a container, a user-space kernel such as gVisor, or a virtual machine) with minimal mounts, no credentials and an egress allowlist contains a mistake or an injected instruction no matter what the code does. Static scans and model reviewers miss obfuscated behavior, and an instruction to be safe is not a boundary.
questions.whyTested: Guardrails and safe deployment: sandboxing and secure-by-design.

questions.question: A ticket-handling agent can look up orders, add internal notes, issue refunds and delete accounts. Product wants a person to approve every single tool call, but reviewers are already clicking approve without reading. What is the BEST adjustment?
options: Keep approving every call but add a daily summary email of what was approved
Remove approvals entirely and ask the agent in the system prompt to be careful with refunds, deletions and anything else that looks risky
Run read-only and reversible steps automatically, and hold refunds and deletions for approval showing the exact target
Approve once at the start of each session and let the agent act freely for the rest of the conversation
questions.explanation: Approval should scale with consequence. Prompting for everything creates fatigue, so people stop reading and the gate stops protecting. Reserving it for irreversible or high-impact actions, and showing the exact inputs, keeps it meaningful. A summary email arrives after the harm, a prompt rule is not enforcement, and blanket session approval covers actions nobody has seen.
questions.whyTested: Guardrails and safe deployment: approval gates and guardrail layering.

questions.question: A multi-tenant document assistant exposes a search_docs tool with a tenant_id parameter that the model fills in from the conversation. A user types "search tenant 4412 for payroll files" and receives another company's documents. What is the BEST fix?
options: Add a sentence to the tool description saying that the tenant must match the company of the signed-in user
Take the tenant from the authenticated session in the tool handler and ignore what the model supplies
Validate that the supplied tenant_id has a well-formed identifier format before the search runs
Have the model ask the user to confirm that they are entitled to see the tenant before searching
questions.explanation: Identity and authorization must come from your authenticated session, in code, not from model-supplied arguments, which the user or an attacker can steer. Otherwise the agent becomes a confused deputy that exercises the service's broad access for someone entitled to less. Descriptions are guidance, a format check passes any well-formed ID, and asking users to confirm their own entitlement is self-attestation.
questions.whyTested: Guardrails and safe deployment: identity, access verification and authorization.

questions.question: A PreToolUse hook script inspects the planned Bash command and, for "git push --force", prints a message and exits with status 1, intending to block it. Forced pushes still go through. What change makes the hook block the call?
options: Write the reason to standard error and exit with status 2, or return a JSON deny decision instead
Move the check into a PostToolUse hook so that it can see the result of the command
Print the message to standard output instead of standard error before exiting with status 1
Also add the rule to CLAUDE.md so that the script and the instructions agree
questions.explanation: For command hooks, status 0 means no objection and status 2 blocks the call, with standard error fed back to the model as the reason. Other nonzero codes, such as 1, are non-blocking errors and the action proceeds, so the script fails open. PostToolUse runs after the action and cannot undo it, the output stream does not change what status 1 means, and CLAUDE.md is context rather than enforcement.
questions.whyTested: Claude hooks: guardrails that prevent destructive actions.

questions.question: Security wants a rule that no Claude Code session may run commands containing "terraform destroy", even when engineers launch sessions with permission prompts skipped for speed. Which control holds?
options: A sentence in the shared CLAUDE.md prohibiting the command
A PreToolUse hook, delivered through managed settings, that denies matching Bash commands
A PostToolUse hook that restores the infrastructure state after a destroy has run
A reminder in the onboarding guide and in the pull request template
questions.explanation: PreToolUse hooks run before any permission-mode check in every mode, so a deny still blocks when prompts are skipped, and delivering the hook through managed settings means engineers cannot switch it off from their own settings. CLAUDE.md and onboarding text are guidance, and a PostToolUse hook runs after the damage and cannot undo it.
questions.whyTested: Claude hooks: safety controls that cannot be bypassed by permission mode.

questions.question: A company runs its Claude-based service on Kubernetes in a major cloud. Security policy forbids long-lived secrets in the cluster, and an audit flagged the static API key stored in a Kubernetes secret. Which approach BEST meets the policy?
options: Keep the static key in the cluster but rotate it monthly with a scheduled job and an audit reminder
Base64-encode the key in the manifest so that it is no longer stored in clear text in the repository
Give every developer a personal key and have the service use the key of whoever deployed it most recently
Use Workload Identity Federation: exchange the pod identity token for short-lived Claude API tokens
questions.explanation: Federation replaces a stored key with a short-lived token exchanged from an identity the platform already issues, so there is nothing long-lived to leak or rotate (its strength depends on the identity provider setup). Monthly rotation still leaves a static secret in the cluster, base64 is encoding rather than protection, and a personal key ties the service to one person's access and lifetime.
questions.whyTested: Identity, secrets and key management: authentication for production workloads.

questions.question: An engineer accidentally pushes an API key to a public repository and notices a few minutes later. What should happen FIRST?
options: Rewrite the repository history to remove the commit and watch whether the key is misused afterwards
Leave the key active until it expires, since expiry already limits the exposure to a short window
Disable or delete the key in the Console so it stops working, then issue a replacement
Message the team to avoid using that key while the repository is cleaned up and the history is rewritten
questions.explanation: A published key must be assumed compromised the moment it is public, so revocation comes first (disable is reversible, delete is permanent), followed by a replacement, a review of usage and a root-cause fix such as secret scanning. Cleaning history does not un-leak copies that already exist, waiting for expiry leaves the key usable meanwhile, and asking colleagues to avoid it does nothing about an attacker.
questions.whyTested: Identity, secrets and key management: managing and revoking compromised credentials.

questions.question: A research agent browses the web and summarizes pages for users. Which THREE measures reduce the damage from indirect prompt injection? (Choose three.)
options: Return page text inside tool results, labeled with its source, under a system prompt policy that treats it as data
Give the agent only read-only tools and run it in a sandbox with a network allowlist
Place the fetched text in the system prompt so that the model weighs it carefully
Ask users to avoid submitting URLs whose pages might contain malicious text
Test the agent before launch with pages that deliberately contain injected instructions
questions.explanation: Isolating and labeling third-party content, limiting what a fooled agent can do, and red-teaming with hostile pages are all parts of a layered defense. The system prompt carries the highest authority, so fetched text never belongs there, and asking users to avoid risky pages is not a control: the attacker plants the text, not the user.
questions.whyTested: AI application security: prompt injection awareness and mitigation.

questions.question: An agent that processes confidential documents also has outbound network access. Which TWO controls best limit the damage if an injected instruction turns it against you? (Choose two.)
options: A system prompt line telling the agent never to send data to unknown domains
An egress allowlist enforced by a proxy or firewall outside the agent's environment
A higher effort setting so that the agent reasons carefully about every outbound request
Credentials kept outside the agent's boundary, with a proxy that injects them into approved requests
A log of the agent's outbound requests that the agent itself is able to edit
questions.explanation: Network controls outside the agent stop exfiltration even when the agent has been fooled, and a credential proxy means there is no secret for it to leak while also giving you a place to enforce the allowlist. A prompt line is guidance, effort is a cost and quality setting, and a log the agent can edit cannot be trusted to detect anything.
questions.whyTested: AI application security and guardrails: data leakage prevention.

questions.question: Which TWO practices limit the damage if a Claude API key leaks? (Choose two.)
options: Create keys with an expiration suited to their purpose and rotate them on a schedule
Share one production key across all services so that only a single key has to be tracked
Use separate keys scoped to separate workspaces for development, staging and production
Embed the key in client-side code so that it can be replaced without a server deployment
Keep the key in a private repository so that only employees can read it
questions.explanation: Expiry and rotation cap how long a stolen key works, and per-environment, workspace-scoped keys keep a leak in development from exposing production. A single shared key widens the blast radius, client-side code exposes the key to every user, and a private repository still spreads the secret to everyone with access and into history.
questions.whyTested: Identity, secrets and key management: limiting blast radius.

questions.question: A security team wants to detect misuse of its Claude credentials and agent actions. Which TWO practices support authorized access monitoring? (Choose two.)
options: Give all services one shared key so that the usage dashboard has a single line to watch
Give each workload its own identity-backed key so that usage can be attributed and unusual patterns stand out
Turn off request logging in the tool layer to avoid storing sensitive inputs
Write each tool call, its caller identity and its outcome to a log that the agent cannot modify, and review it for anomalies
Rely on end users to report anything that looks wrong
questions.explanation: Attribution and tamper-resistant records are what make monitoring possible: separate identities show who or what is acting, and an audit log the agent cannot edit lets you reconstruct events and spot odd behavior. A shared key hides which workload is responsible, disabling logging removes the evidence (keep secrets and unnecessary personal data out of the log instead), and user reports are not systematic monitoring.
questions.whyTested: Identity, secrets and key management: authorized access monitoring.

questions.question: No system prompt wording can guarantee that its contents stay hidden, so a system prompt should never contain secrets.
questions.explanation: A model can be induced to repeat text it can see. Keep credentials and sensitive logic in server-side code, and treat output monitoring as a way to catch leaks rather than a guarantee against them.

questions.question: Prompt injection can only come from the typed input of the application's own end users.
questions.explanation: Indirect injection arrives through content the model reads on a user's behalf, such as web pages, emails, documents and tool results, where the user is honest and an attacker has planted the text.

questions.question: A zero data retention arrangement covers the Message Batches API and the Files API in the same way that it covers standard Messages API calls.
questions.explanation: Stateful features such as batch jobs and stored files are not ZDR-eligible; using them is a choice to step outside the arrangement for that data. Check the feature eligibility table before designing a regulated workflow.

questions.question: A personal API key keeps working after its owner is removed from the organization.
questions.explanation: Personal keys act as the user and are archived when that person leaves the organization, which is why shared or unattended workloads should use a service account key or federation instead.

questions.question: A PostToolUse hook can undo a tool action that has already run, so it prevents destructive commands as well as a PreToolUse hook does.
questions.explanation: PostToolUse fires after the tool has succeeded and cannot reverse it. To prevent an action, deny it in a PreToolUse hook (or with a deny rule); use PostToolUse for follow-up work such as formatting or logging.

lessons.title: Choosing Between Workflows and Agents
lessons.summary: Who steers the process, code or the model: the decision criteria, the five workflow patterns, and how subagents and supervisor hierarchies split work.
lessons.reading:
Most Claude applications sit between two designs. In a workflow, your code decides the order of the steps and calls the model at each step for a piece of language work. In an agent, you give the model a goal and some tools, and the model decides what to do next, looks at the result, and decides again until it judges the task done. The difference is who holds the steering wheel: your code, so the path is the same every run, or the model, so the path depends on what it finds. Neither is better in general; the exam tests whether you choose the least autonomy that still solves the problem.

Ask four questions. Can you write the steps down in advance? Build a workflow. Must the same audited sequence run every time? Workflow again, because code can guarantee an order and a prompt cannot. Do you need predictable latency and cost? Workflows win, since an agent may take five turns or fifty. Is the problem open-ended, each next action depending on what the last tool returned? That is where an agent earns its extra cost and variance, and it needs guard rails: a turn cap, a spend budget and a clear definition of done. Start with one good call, add steps when measurements demand them, and add autonomy last.

Five workflow patterns cover most needs. Prompt chaining runs a fixed sequence of calls, each using the previous output, with code checking each intermediate result. Routing classifies the input first and sends it to a specialised prompt or a cheaper or stronger model. Parallelization runs calls at the same time, on independent slices of one job (sectioning) or on the same job several times to compare answers (voting), and merges the results. Orchestrator-workers lets a central call decide at run time how to split the job and hand pieces to workers, which fits work such as a change touching an unknown number of files. Evaluator-optimizer pairs a generator with a critic that checks drafts against explicit criteria until they pass or a round limit is reached. What separates parallelization from orchestrator-workers is who creates the pieces: you in advance, or the model on the fly.

When one agent is overloaded, with dozens of tools and a context full of tangents, split it. A subagent is a separate agent instance, started by a lead agent, that works on one focused task in its own fresh context window and returns only its final message. That gives context isolation, parallelism, tailored instructions and restricted tools, such as a reviewer that can read but not write. A manager or supervisor hierarchy is the result: a lead breaks the goal down, delegates and combines the reports. Every layer adds latency and tokens, so justify it with real differences in tools, permissions or context.

The most tested detail is that a subagent does not inherit the lead's conversation. If the lead spent ten turns learning that the public API must not change, the subagent knows none of it unless the task prompt says so. A good delegation names the files and functions, quotes the exact error, states the constraints and decisions so far, and says what the answer should look like. "Fix the bug we discussed" fails; "In services/billing/invoice.py total() raises on an empty cart; reproduce with test_empty; keep the public signature; report the diff and test output" works.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to agents? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: A workflow is a restaurant kitchen following a recipe card: the cook may be skilled, but the sequence of steps is fixed and every plate comes out the same way. An agent is a personal chef told "make dinner for six" who opens the fridge, decides what is possible, tastes as they go and changes plan. A head chef who sends an assistant to the pantry must write the shopping list, because the assistant was not in the earlier meeting. That list is the task prompt, and it is the only thing the assistant knows.
commonTraps: Choosing an agent because it sounds more advanced. If the steps are known and must repeat, a workflow is the better, cheaper and more testable answer.
Mixing up parallelization and orchestrator-workers: fixed slices you define in advance versus subtasks the model invents at run time.
Assuming a subagent can see the parent conversation. It receives only the task prompt you write, plus its own system prompt and project context.
Treating a prompt instruction as a guarantee of order. When a sequence must hold every time, put it in code.
Forgetting a stop condition on evaluator-optimizer loops and on agents: cap the rounds, turns and spend.
lessons.scenario: A retailer builds a returns assistant. Order lookup, eligibility checks and label creation always happen in that order, so the team implements them as a prompt chain with a validation gate before the label step. A separate "why was my order late?" feature involves unpredictable investigation across carrier notes and warehouse logs, so it runs as an agent with a turn cap and a read-only toolset. When the late-order agent grows to forty tools, the team splits it into specialist subagents for shipping, billing and inventory, each with a narrow tool list and a delegation prompt that carries the order number and what the customer said.
lessons.onTheJob: Resist designing the architecture before you have a baseline. A single call with good instructions often beats a clever pipeline, and a chain you can unit test beats an agent you can only watch. When you do use an agent, write the end condition and the budget first, log every tool call, and review transcripts: most agent failures are visible there as repeated searches, missing context in a handoff, or a tool whose description misled the model. Treat each added layer, whether a subagent, a supervisor or an evaluator, as something that must pay for its latency and tokens with a measurable gain.

lessons.title: Building Agents: Loops, Harnesses, Hooks and Hosting
lessons.summary: The tool-use loop, three ways to own the harness (custom loop, Agent SDK, Managed Agents), limits, permissions and hooks, plus memory, context and frameworks.
lessons.reading:
Under every agent is the same loop. You send the model a prompt and a list of tools. If it replies with a tool request (stop_reason tool_use on the Messages API), your code runs the tool, appends the outcome as a tool_result, and calls the model again. When a reply arrives with no tool request, the loop ends. The model never executes anything itself; it emits structured requests, and the software around it, the harness, runs the loop, enforces permissions, manages context and persists state.

There are three ways to own it. You can write it yourself on the Messages API: a loop that checks stop_reason, runs every requested tool, and sends back one user message holding a tool_result per tool_use ID, results first. That costs code but gives full control for approval gates and custom logging; the SDK tool runner automates the plain case. You can embed the Claude Agent SDK for Python or TypeScript, which brings Claude Code's loop, built-in tools such as Read, Edit and Bash, permissions, sessions, hooks and subagents into your own process. Or you can use Claude Managed Agents, where Anthropic hosts the harness: you define an agent (model, prompt, tools) and an environment, then start sessions that stream events and keep history server-side. The environment is either an Anthropic-managed cloud sandbox or a self-hosted sandbox, where tool execution, files and network egress stay on your infrastructure while orchestration stays on Anthropic's side. Managed Agents suits long-running, asynchronous work; because it is stateful, it is not currently eligible for zero data retention.

Control comes from code, not prose. Give every run turn and budget limits (max_turns and max_budget_usd in the Agent SDK). When one is hit, the final result message carries an error subtype such as error_max_turns and no result text, so check the subtype first and use the session ID to resume. Permission modes set how much approval tools need, from asking by default up to bypassPermissions, which belongs only in containers and CI. Hooks run your code at fixed points: a PreToolUse hook can deny a call before the tool runs, a PostToolUse hook can audit it, and neither costs context tokens. The principle behind all of it is programmatic enforcement: a rule in a prompt or CLAUDE.md makes the behavior likely, while a hook or permission rule makes it certain, so anything that must always hold belongs in code.

Long runs also need memory and context care. The window accumulates every prompt and tool result, so older turns get compacted into summaries and a rule stated only in the first message can be lost. Keep persistent rules in the system prompt or CLAUDE.md, push noisy investigation into subagents so only summaries return, and give the agent a persistent memory store for facts that must outlive a session. Frameworks package these ideas: LangGraph models a flow as a graph of deterministic and model-driven steps with durable state and human-in-the-loop pauses, PydanticAI offers typed tools and validated outputs, and Strands Agents is an open-source toolkit for production agents. They save work on state, tracing and orchestration but add abstraction, and underneath they still run the same tool-use contract. Start with the simplest loop that works.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to agent harnesses? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Picture a capable new employee (the model) and the office around them (the harness). The employee proposes actions: "I would like to email this customer." The office decides what happens: a checklist runs first (hooks), there is a spending limit (budget), large amounts need a manager's signature (approval), and the cash drawer is locked (permission rules). A memo reminding the employee to be careful (a prompt) helps, but it is the locked drawer that actually protects the money. You can run the office yourself, rent a managed one from Anthropic, or put the office on your own premises while the manager works remotely.
commonTraps: Treating a prompt or CLAUDE.md rule as enforcement. Only hooks, permission rules, validation in code and sandboxes hold every time.
Reading the result field without checking the result subtype. Only the success subtype carries result text.
Leaving a tool_use unanswered, or placing text before the tool_result blocks, which produces a 400 error. Answer every ID, results first.
Thinking a self-hosted sandbox keeps everything from Anthropic. Execution and files stay with you, but tool inputs and results still reach the model.
Adopting a heavy framework before a short loop or the SDK has proved insufficient.
lessons.scenario: A bank's platform team wants an agent that reconciles ledger exports overnight. The work takes hours and nobody waits for it, so they compare options. Building a loop gives control but means writing sandboxing and tool execution. The Agent SDK in their own service gives the Claude Code toolset but they must host it. Managed Agents with a self-hosted sandbox keeps the ledger files inside their network while Anthropic runs the loop. They choose that, add a spend budget and turn limit, deny any write outside the working directory with a PreToolUse rule, and require a person to approve any adjustment above a threshold.
lessons.onTheJob: Log every tool call with its arguments, result and the request ID of the model call that asked for it; those traces are how you debug an agent. Decide in advance what happens at each limit: a run that hits its turn cap should save its session ID and report partial progress, not crash. Keep hooks small and fast, because they run on every matching tool call. Test the failure paths on purpose, for example a tool that times out, a denied call and a refused request, since the happy path is rarely where an agent breaks.

lessons.title: Claude API Mechanics: Messages, Stop Reasons, Streaming and Files
lessons.summary: The request and response shape, stateless multi-turn conversations, every stop_reason, streaming events, structured outputs with defensive parsing, files and the Batches API.
lessons.reading:
A request to POST /v1/messages needs a model, a max_tokens cap and a messages array of turns tagged user or assistant, with standing instructions in the top-level system field. The API is stateless: the server remembers nothing, so your application resends the whole conversation, earlier assistant replies included, on every call, and decides how to trim or summarise it as it grows. A reply's content is an array of blocks such as text, tool_use and thinking, so loop over the blocks and check each type instead of assuming the first is text. Log the usage object, which holds the token counts, on every call.

Every successful response carries a stop_reason, and handling it is the heart of a robust client. end_turn means the model finished. max_tokens means it hit your cap, so the text may stop mid-sentence, mid-JSON or mid-tool-call: raise the cap, ask it to continue, or stream. stop_sequence means it emitted one of your stop strings. tool_use means it wants tools run, and every ID needs a tool_result. pause_turn means a server-side tool loop, such as web search, hit its iteration limit, so send the assistant content back unchanged. refusal means the safety classifiers declined; it is a normal 200 response, so no exception fires, and the content may be empty. model_context_window_exceeded means input plus output filled the window. Truncation and refusal are successful responses that need their own branches, not errors.

Set stream to true and the API sends server-sent events: message_start, then for each content block a content_block_start, a run of content_block_delta events and a content_block_stop, then message_delta, which carries the stop_reason and cumulative usage, and message_stop. An error event such as overloaded_error can arrive after the 200 status, so streaming code needs its own failure handling. Text arrives as text_delta; tool arguments arrive as input_json_delta fragments that are valid JSON only once the block stops, so accumulate, then parse. Streaming makes answers feel instant and suits very large max_tokens, since the SDKs reject non-streaming calls expected to run beyond about ten minutes.

When code consumes the output, do not rely on "please reply in JSON". Structured outputs (a JSON Schema in output_config.format) constrain decoding so the text parses and matches. Assistant prefill is rejected with a 400 error on Claude 4.6 and later. Constrained output guarantees shape, not truth, and a refusal or a reply cut off at max_tokens can still escape the schema, so parse defensively: check stop_reason, catch failures, validate business rules, and keep a retry or fallback.

Images and PDFs enter as image and document blocks from base64, a URL or a Files API file ID. Upload once and reuse the ID, but files are visible workspace-wide, so never accept file IDs from end users; Word and Excel files must first become text or PDF. For bulk work nobody waits on, the Message Batches API costs half the standard price, takes up to 100,000 requests or 256 MB, and returns results within 24 hours. Give each request a unique custom_id because results arrive in any order, dry-run the request shape on the Messages API because validation happens after submission, and handle all four outcomes: succeeded, errored, canceled and expired.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to the Messages API? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Think of a postal chess game where the other player has no memory. Each time you write, you must enclose the entire game so far, because they will read it fresh. Their reply always ends with a note on why they stopped: they finished, they ran out of paper (the output cap), they want you to look something up and report back (a tool request), or they declined to answer. Streaming is the other player reading their reply aloud as they write it. A batch is mailing a thousand games overnight at a discount and collecting the answers in the morning, in whatever order they finish.
commonTraps: Sending only the newest message and expecting the model to remember. The API is stateless, so the full history goes in every request.
Treating a max_tokens or refusal response as a failure to retry unchanged. Both are successful responses; truncation needs a higher cap or a continuation, a refusal needs a fallback.
Parsing partial_json fragments before the block stops, or reading the stop reason from the first streaming event, where it is null.
Believing structured outputs make values correct. They guarantee shape, so semantic validation is still required.
Pairing batch results with inputs by position instead of custom_id, or sending prefill to a 4.6-generation or later model.
lessons.scenario: A document-intelligence team extracts fields from supplier invoices. Interactive uploads stream to a review screen as they are processed, using the Messages API with a schema in structured outputs and a check on stop_reason before parsing. Truncated replies on very long invoices are retried with a higher cap and a streamed call. A nightly job re-extracts the archive: it is submitted as batches with the supplier ID as custom_id, one request of each shape having been tested synchronously first, and the results are joined back by ID. PDFs that are reused are uploaded once and referenced by file ID.
lessons.onTheJob: Wrap the SDK in one small module so retries, logging, model IDs and the stop_reason switch live in a single place. Log the usage object, the stop reason and the request ID for every call; those three fields explain most production mysteries. Write unit tests with canned responses for each stop reason, including an empty refusal and a truncated tool call, because those rarely appear in manual testing. Keep a dry-run script that sends one request of every shape through the Messages API before any big batch is submitted.

lessons.title: Application Design and Configuration Management
lessons.summary: How instructions differ across claude.ai, the API and Claude Code, content boundaries, schema design, session hygiene, plugins, and the configuration that keeps behavior stable.
lessons.reading:
Claude never works alone, because each interface wraps it in different instructions. The claude.ai site and the mobile apps add an Anthropic-written system prompt that supplies things like the current date and formatting habits. The raw API adds nothing, so everything you want must be in your own system prompt and messages. Claude Code adds its own instructions and loads your CLAUDE.md files, and the Agent SDK embeds that same loop in your code. The consequence is practical: a prompt that works beautifully in a chat window has to be rebuilt, and retested, inside your application.

Two design habits matter in every interface. The first is a content boundary: keep your trusted rules in the system prompt and place documents, web pages and tool output in clearly delimited, labelled blocks, with tool output inside tool_result, and say that the block is data. It is a design aid, not a guarantee, so pair it with least-privilege tools. The second is schema design. A schema is both a contract and documentation, so name fields clearly, describe the ones that are not obvious, use enums for closed sets, mark fields required where you can, keep nesting shallow, and set additionalProperties to false. Every optional parameter and union type adds ambiguity and, with strict schemas, compile complexity, so when the API says a schema is too complex, simplify it instead of retrying.

In Claude Code the scarce resource is context, so practice session hygiene. Clear the session between unrelated tasks. If you have corrected the same mistake two or three times, clear and restart with a sharper prompt that includes what you learned. Send broad research to a subagent so only a summary returns, compact with instructions when a long task must continue, and name sessions you will resume. Plugins package skills, subagents, hooks and MCP servers as one installable unit from a marketplace. Pick an install scope: user (you, every project), project (everyone, through the committed settings, although each teammate still installs it) or local (you, this repository). Every enabled plugin places its skill and agent descriptions in context on every turn, so disable the ones you do not use, and review a plugin before installing because it runs code with your privileges.

Configuration management keeps behavior stable. CLAUDE.md files at managed, user, project and local levels are concatenated rather than overridden, with instructions nearer the working directory read last. Keep them short, specific and free of contradictions, move situational guidance into path-scoped rules or skills, and remember they are guidance, not enforcement. Settings have a precedence order: managed settings, then the command line, then local project, shared project and user settings, with list-type keys such as permission allow rules merging across scopes. Put team defaults in the committed project file, personal overrides in the local file, and non-negotiable policy in managed settings. Finally, pin versions: use the full model ID rather than an alias that follows the newest release, version prompts in source control with an identifier you log, and declare a tested range such as ~2.1.0 on plugin dependencies so an upstream release cannot silently break you.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to application design? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Imagine hiring a translator through three agencies. One agency briefs the translator with its own house rules before every job (the chat apps). Another sends the translator to you with no briefing at all (the API), so you must supply every instruction. A third sends the translator with your company handbook already in their bag (Claude Code and CLAUDE.md). Documents you hand over for translation go in a labelled folder so no one mistakes a sentence inside them for an instruction from the boss. And you write in the contract which translator you want by name, not "whoever is newest this month".
commonTraps: Expecting API behavior to match claude.ai. The chat apps add their own system prompt; the API does not.
Believing CLAUDE.md or a boundary tag enforces anything. Both are guidance the model weighs; hooks and permission rules enforce.
Using an alias in shared production configuration. Aliases move to the newest release, so pin the full model ID and migrate after evals.
Assuming project-scope plugins appear on every teammate's machine automatically; each person still installs them, and every enabled plugin costs context.
Putting a personal preference in the shared project CLAUDE.md instead of the local file, or putting a mandatory policy anywhere but managed settings.
lessons.scenario: A platform team rolls out Claude Code to eighty engineers. The managed settings file forbids bypassing permissions and sets the allowed model list. The repository's CLAUDE.md is trimmed to 150 lines of build commands and conventions, with API rules moved to a path-scoped rules file and personal sandbox URLs left to each developer's local file. The shared settings pin the full model ID. A review plugin is enabled at project scope, with its dependency constrained to a tested range. Engineers are told to clear sessions between tasks and to hand research to subagents.
lessons.onTheJob: Audit instructions the way you audit code: run the context command to see what actually loaded, delete rules that nobody can verify, and resolve contradictions between nested files. Treat model and prompt changes as releases with a changelog and an eval run, and keep the previous pinned ID available for rollback. Review plugins before approving them for a team, check their context cost, and prefer a short list that people actually use. When behavior surprises you, ask first which interface and which instruction layers were involved.

lessons.title: Requirements, Life Cycle and Reliable Engineering
lessons.summary: Turning business needs into measurable requirements, choosing realtime or batch and a platform, handling errors and rate limits, and running the system through its life cycle.
lessons.reading:
Start with requirements. A functional requirement says what the system must do, such as extract an invoice total or call a refund tool. A non-functional requirement says how well: p95 latency, throughput, availability, cost per request, data residency, compliance. "Fast and accurate" is not a requirement until it becomes numbers you can test. These choices drive the architecture. A person watching a screen needs a streamed, synchronous call, while an overnight job belongs in a batch at half price. Residency may call for inference_geo set to us, or for a cloud platform such as Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud, Microsoft Foundry or Claude Platform on AWS, with their own IAM and billing but different features and limits. A zero-data-retention arrangement rules out the Files API, batches and Managed Agents for that data.

Capacity is part of the requirement. Limits are requests, input tokens and output tokens per minute, enforced as a token bucket, so a burst can fail even when the minute total looks fine. Do the arithmetic: 800 requests a minute at 4,000 input tokens each is 3.2 million input tokens per minute, which a 2 million limit will not allow. For most models cached input does not count toward the input limit, so caching a shared prefix is also a throughput fix. Spend limits are separate: a limit you set returns 400, the tier cap returns 429 with no retry-after, and retrying cures neither.

Reliable calls start by sorting errors by whether a retry can help. Transient errors, namely 429 with a retry-after header, 529 overloaded, 5xx, timeouts and dropped connections, are retried with exponential backoff and jitter, capped in attempts and wait, honoring retry-after. The SDK already retries twice by default, so do not stack your own loop on top without deciding which layer owns retries. Errors like 400, 401, 403, 404 and 413 will fail again until you change the request or credential. Make operations that charge or send idempotent, bound concurrency with a semaphore so asynchronous fan-out does not cause a wall of 429s, and add a circuit breaker and a fallback so a bad hour does not take the product down.

A Claude application is never finished. The life cycle loops through requirements, design, build, test, deploy, operate, maintain and retire. Test with evals gated in the CI pipeline. Deploy gradually behind a feature flag so you can roll back. Operate with monitoring that scores sampled live output and logs the prompt and model version per request. Maintain by tracking the model lifecycle of active, legacy, deprecated and retired, with at least 60 days' notice before a public model retires, and migrate by running your own evals on the replacement. Pinned IDs and versioned prompts are what make a rollback possible.

Ordinary habits still apply. Keep prompts, schemas and settings in version control and change them through reviewed pull requests. Review model-generated diffs as carefully as human ones, because passing tests prove only what the tests cover. Refactor in small tested steps, and migrate a large system incrementally behind an interface, the strangler pattern, instead of rewriting it. In CI, run Claude Code non-interactively with claude -p, preferably in bare mode, with the key coming from the pipeline's secret store.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to systems engineering? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Running a Claude application is like running a food truck. Requirements are the menu and the promises you make: what you serve (functional) and how fast, how cheaply and under which health rules (non-functional). Capacity limits are the size of the kitchen window; a lunch rush can overflow it even if the daily total is fine, so you queue orders instead of shouting them all at once. When the supplier is out of an ingredient (a 529), you wait and try again, but if your licence has expired (a 401) waiting will not help. Over the years the supplier retires products, so you keep a tested replacement and change the menu gradually.
commonTraps: Retrying every error. A 400, 401, 403 or a spend-cap 429 needs a code, credential or limit change, not another attempt.
Stacking a custom retry loop on top of the SDK's default retries and multiplying traffic during an incident.
Putting a latency-sensitive feature on the batch endpoint, or an overnight job on full-price synchronous calls.
Waiting for a model's retirement date before testing a replacement; deprecation notices exist to give you time to run evals.
Treating green tests as proof that a model-generated change is safe to merge without human review.
lessons.scenario: A telecom builds a support assistant and a nightly churn-analysis job. The team converts "fast and accurate" into a p95 first-token time of three seconds, an accuracy threshold on a labeled set and a cost per conversation. Chat streams synchronously; the analysis runs as batches at half price. At launch day 429s appear: the arithmetic shows input tokens per minute, not requests, are the binding limit, so a shared policy block is cached. The client retries only transient errors with capped backoff, evals gate every prompt change in CI, and a new model is rolled out to five percent of traffic behind a flag before everyone.
lessons.onTheJob: Write the non-functional requirements down before choosing a model, and do the token arithmetic against your real limits at peak, not average. Keep one place in the codebase that owns retries, timeouts and logging. Put an alert on spend before the tier cap, and another on the share of responses that end in max_tokens or refusal, since those quietly degrade quality. Put the model deprecation page on the team calendar, export the usage by model to find stragglers, and rehearse a rollback before you need one.

lessons.title: Model Selection, Effort, Caching and Cost Control
lessons.summary: Tokens, context windows, sampling and next-token generation; thinking, effort and fast mode; Opus, Sonnet, Haiku and Fable tradeoffs and migration breaking changes; token budgeting, cost modeling, prompt caching and batch processing. Covers Domain 5: LLM Fundamentals, Technical Fundamentals, Model Selection and Tradeoffs, and Cost and Token Management.
lessons.reading:
Everything starts with tokens: small chunks of text, often word fragments, in which prices, rate limits and the context window are measured. Claude 4.7 and later models split the same text into about 30 percent more tokens than older ones, so estimates must be recounted for the target model. A model writes one token at a time, so after the first token the wait grows with output length; asking for three sentences instead of a memo is often the biggest latency win. The context window holds input and reply together, thinking included, and caching makes repeated input cheaper without shrinking it. Output varies between calls, and current models reject non-default temperature, top_p and top_k with a 400, so tests check properties, never exact strings.

Pick the tier by the work. Haiku 5.5 is fastest and cheapest, for classification, extraction, routing and subagents. Sonnet 5.5 balances speed and intelligence for everyday coding and agents. Opus 5.5 is the documented starting point for long-running agentic coding and knowledge work. Fable 5.1 is the most capable model open to all, slower and dearest; as a Covered Model it needs 30-day data retention, so zero retention is unavailable by default. Start efficiency-first (begin small, move up where tests show gaps) or capability-first (begin strong, then trade down while evals still pass). Either way, decide on an evaluation set built from your own prompts and compare cost per completed task, since retries can make the cheaper token price the dearer outcome.

Thinking depth is a dial. Adaptive thinking lets the model decide whether and how long to reason; it is always on for Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1, and the old budget_tokens mode returns a 400. Effort, from low to max, is a soft signal that scales reasoning, tool calls and answer length together, and tuning effort often beats switching models. Thinking is billed as output and counts toward max_tokens, the hard ceiling, so leave room. Fast mode on some Opus models gives up to about 2.5 times the output speed for a premium, but not a quicker first token. Before moving to a new release, read its migration notes and run evals: prefill, forced tool_choice and thinking disabled are rejected on newer models.

Money follows tokens. Output costs about five times input, and an agent that resends its history each turn pays for it again every turn. Prompt caching is usually the biggest free win. The prefix runs tools, system, then messages; put a breakpoint (up to four) on the last block that stays identical, never on a timestamp. A five-minute write costs about 1.25 times normal input and a read a tenth or less, so a 10,000-token prefix sent 11 times in five minutes costs about a fifth of the uncached price. Use the one-hour lifetime when users pause 8 to 40 minutes. Editing tools or the system prompt, or changing effort or tool_choice, invalidates the cache; the usage fields show whether it worked. Work that can wait a day goes to the Batch API at half price, stacking with caching.

Official SDKs wrap the REST API and add headers, retries, timeouts and streaming helpers. Replies stream over server-sent events, not WebSockets, which belong between your backend and the browser. Read capabilities from the Models API instead of hard-coding model names.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to model selection? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Choosing a model is like choosing a vehicle for deliveries. A scooter (Haiku) is cheap and quick for small parcels across town, a van (Sonnet) handles most routes, a truck (Opus) hauls the big, long jobs, and a heavy-haul rig (Fable) is for the loads nothing else can move. Effort is how carefully the driver plans the route: more planning costs time and fuel, and on an easy trip it is wasted. Prompt caching is leaving the standard boxes loaded on the vehicle between trips, and the Batch API is the overnight freight service: slower, but half the price. You decide with test deliveries on your own roads, not from the brochure.
commonTraps: Treating temperature 0 as a determinism switch. Current models reject non-default sampling values and no setting makes output byte-identical, so tests must check properties rather than exact text.
Comparing models by price per million tokens instead of cost per completed task on your own evals; retries, extra turns and failures change the answer.

Capping max_tokens to save money. It truncates (and still bills) rather than making the model economize, and at high effort hidden thinking can use the whole allowance; control cost with effort and a request for brevity.

Assuming caching shrinks the context window, or that any prompt gets cached. It changes price only, needs a stable prefix of at least the minimum length, and any edit before the breakpoint or a change of effort or tool_choice invalidates it.

Carrying settings across releases. Manual budget_tokens, prefill, forced tool_choice, thinking disabled and non-default sampling fail with a 400 on newer models, and the new tokenizer changes token counts.
lessons.scenario: A travel company runs three Claude features. A fare-rule classifier handles 30 million short messages a month and must answer in under a second, so the team starts with Haiku 5.5, scores it on a labeled sample and keeps it. A trip-planning agent runs for an hour with many tool calls; it starts on Opus 5.5, sweeps effort downward on its eval set and keeps the cheapest level that still passes. Both resend a 12,000-token policy prefix, so the team puts a cache breakpoint on the last stable block, moves the timestamp after it, uses the one-hour lifetime for the agent whose users pause, and sends a nightly quality run through the Batch API.
lessons.onTheJob: Build the eval set before arguing about models, and re-run it whenever the model, effort, tools or system prompt change. Log the usage object for every call, including the cache fields, and watch the cache-read share: a sudden drop usually means someone put a timestamp or reordered tools in the prefix. Set max_tokens generously and treat max_tokens stops as failures to handle. Pin full model IDs in production, read migration notes before upgrading, and recount tokens for a new tokenizer. Give each feature and environment its own workspace so the Usage and Cost API shows where the money goes.

lessons.title: Evals, Debugging and Claude Code Operation
lessons.summary: Designing evals, choosing graders and running regressions; identifying error types and silent failures, choosing recovery strategies, analyzing traces and isolating whether the integration or the model is at fault; and operating Claude Code: CLAUDE.md placement, rules, commands, subagents and memory, sessions, headless output and permission modes. Covers Domain 4 (Debugging and Error Handling) and Domain 3 (Claude Code Operation).
lessons.reading:
You cannot tune what you cannot measure. Start with success criteria that are specific, measurable, achievable and relevant, such as 95 percent of invoice totals exact. Build an evaluation set that mirrors real traffic and includes edge cases: irrelevant, overlong, ambiguous or harmful inputs. Use the fastest reliable grader: code-based grading for checkable answers, an LLM judge with a detailed rubric and a constrained verdict for tone and completeness (tested against human labels first), and humans sparingly. Re-run the whole set after every prompt, tool or model change and compare with the baseline; that regression run catches the fix that broke something else.

Debugging starts with naming the failure. Transport and request errors raise exceptions: 429, 5xx and 529 are retried with backoff, while 400, 401 and 403 need a code or configuration fix. The subtle class is the silent failure, an HTTP 200 with a bad result: a reply cut off at max_tokens, a refusal, output that breaks the schema, or a confident wrong answer. Only stop_reason checks and validation in code see these. Match the recovery to the cause: retry transient faults, correct and resend invalid requests, continue after truncation, feed a validation error back for one bounded second attempt, and fall back or escalate when it persists.

When behavior is wrong, read evidence instead of guessing. A trace is the full record of one request and a span is one step in it, such as a model call; the Claude API and SDK can export them with OpenTelemetry, by default with metadata only. Failing traces reveal patterns such as a repeated search. To tell your integration from the model, capture the exact request the app sent and replay it on its own. If the replay is fine, suspect history assembly, headers, truncation, parsing or tool-result formatting; if it fails the same way, work on the prompt, tool descriptions, model or validation. For cache misses, cache diagnostics reports where consecutive requests first differed.

Claude Code offers several homes for guidance. CLAUDE.md files (managed, user, project, local) are concatenated into context at launch; /init drafts one from your codebase or suggests improvements to an existing one. Keep it short and move topic conventions into .claude/rules files with a paths pattern, which load only for matching files. Reusable procedures live in skills or command files; helpers with their own context live in .claude/agents files, whose memory setting (user, project or local) decides where their notes persist. Auto memory is written by Claude, on your machine. All of this is context, not enforcement; what must always hold belongs in a hook or permission rule.

For sessions, /clear starts fresh, /compact summarizes, --continue or --resume returns, and /branch (or --fork-session) copies a conversation so the original stays intact. In scripts, claude -p runs headless: --output-format json returns one object (add --json-schema for a structured_output field), stream-json emits one event per line, and --bare skips local configuration so CI runners behave alike. Permission modes run from asking, through acceptEdits and plan, to auto mode, where a classifier reviews actions; bypassPermissions is for isolated sandboxes only.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to evals and debugging? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Evals are the driving test for your prompt: a fixed route with known hazards that every new version must pass before it is allowed on the road. Debugging a failed run is accident investigation. You do not repeat the journey from memory; you read the black-box recording (the trace) and replay the exact conditions on a test track (the isolated request) to learn whether the car, the road or the driver was at fault. Claude Code's configuration is the workshop: a posted rulebook (CLAUDE.md), drawers that open only for matching jobs (path rules and skills), and a locked gate (hooks and permissions) for what must never happen.
commonTraps: Retrying every failure. A 400, a refusal or a schema error fails the same way each time, so match the recovery to the cause and cap the attempts.
Trusting HTTP 200. Truncated, refused or malformed replies are successful responses; check stop_reason and validate the output in code.
Blaming the model first. When the same prompt works elsewhere, replay the exact logged request to learn whether your integration changed it.
Judging a prompt change on three hand-picked examples, or building an eval set from clean inputs only; real regressions hide in the cases you did not look at.

Treating CLAUDE.md, rules or auto memory as enforcement. They are context; a rule that must hold needs a hook or permission rule, and auto memory is machine-local while the committed CLAUDE.md is the shared file.
lessons.scenario: A claims-intake service starts rejecting about 4 percent of its model replies as invalid JSON after a Friday deploy. The on-call engineer does not touch the prompt. She pulls logged request bodies from before and after the deploy, sees that the new code sets max_tokens to 400 instead of 4,000, and confirms from the raw responses that the failing calls ended with stop_reason max_tokens. She restores the limit, adds a check that treats max_tokens as a failure and retries once with a larger ceiling, and adds the failing inputs to the eval set. Meanwhile the team trims its CLAUDE.md, moves the claims-schema conventions into a path-scoped rule, and has CI call claude -p with --output-format json and a schema.
lessons.onTheJob: Log the request ID, model, stop_reason and usage for every call, and keep the exact request body for failures, so a replay is possible a week later. Decide per failure type what the app does (retry, repair, fall back, escalate) and test those paths with injected faults. Add every production failure to the eval set. Keep trace content modes in line with your privacy rules: metadata only is the safe default, full content is for debugging with retention you control. In Claude Code, trim what /init writes before committing it, keep CLAUDE.md short, move situational guidance into rules and skills, and use --bare in CI so every runner behaves the same.

lessons.title: Prompt and Context Engineering: Clear Instructions, Lean Context, Checked Output
lessons.summary: Domain 6: Context Engineering (window management, preventing drift and bloat, isolation), Prompt Engineering (clarity, examples, placement, output constraints, iteration, sanitization) and Output Handling (structured output patterns, validation, defensive parsing, skepticism toward confident output).
lessons.reading:
Claude knows only what is in front of it: the system prompt, the conversation, tool definitions and results, and attached documents. Prompt engineering is writing that text so the model does the right thing; context engineering is deciding what belongs in the window at all, and what to remove as work goes on.

Start with clarity. Test it on a capable colleague with no project context: would they know the audience, goal, format and limits? "Summarize this ticket" gets a different answer every run; "Summarize this ticket for the on-call engineer in three sentences: symptom, suspected component, customer impact" does not. Give the reason behind a rule ("replies are read aloud, so avoid symbols"), because a reason lets the model handle cases the rule never listed, and say what to do, not only what to avoid. Put the stable role and policies in the system prompt, the task and its data in the user turn, and wrap each kind of content in consistently named tags such as <instructions>, <document> and <example>. Three to five varied examples teach a format better than paragraphs of description; examples that are all positive teach the model to say yes.

Long inputs follow their own rules: put long documents first and the question last, wrap each document with its source, and for factual work ask for word-for-word quotes first and an answer built only from them, with "the documents do not say" as an accepted result. Treat prompts like code: keep a fixed test set, change one thing at a time, re-run everything, and re-audit after every model change. Newer models follow instructions more literally, so shouted warnings ("CRITICAL: you MUST ALWAYS..."), "verify twice" rules and hand-built scratchpads written for older models now cause over-action; use plain statements of when to act.

More context is not better. Accuracy and recall decline as the window fills (context rot), so a million-token window is a ceiling, not a target. Keep material small at the source: tools return only the fields the next step needs, lists are paginated, passages are retrieved on demand. In long runs, two features manage the window. Compaction replaces older turns with a model-written summary: the thread survives, detail is lost. Context editing clears the oldest tool results by rule and leaves a marker in their place: the right fit when bulky outputs are stale but decisions must stay word for word. Neither stores what must survive: rules belong in the system prompt or CLAUDE.md, and exact state, such as which of 300 tables are migrated, in a progress file the agent re-reads.
